text: For transport covered by the regulation, exceeding prescribed driving times incurs a fine; the amount depends on the infringement.

After four and a half hours of driving, a break of at least 45 minutes is required unless a rest period begins; it can be split into at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30. Failure to take the prescribed breaks incurs a penalty.
For services where it is required, the extract concerns the schedule established in advance for driving, other work, breaks and availability. Its absence, incompleteness or alteration is penalized.

A regular daily rest period is at least 11 hours; under certain conditions it can be reduced to at least 9. During rest the driver can freely dispose of their time; failing to take the prescribed rest is penalized.

A break interrupts driving: after four and a half hours, at least 45 minutes are required unless a rest period begins; it can be split into at least 15 and then 30 minutes. Regular daily rest is at least 11 hours, reducible to 9 under the prescribed conditions. Violations are penalized.
Exceeding driving times incurs a fine, not automatic revocation of the driving licence; documents may be temporarily withdrawn until the required rest is taken.

Taking a 45-minute break after four and a half hours of driving complies with the rule; it is not an offence. The break may instead already have been taken in two parts, at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30, distributed over the driving period; alternatively, a rest period may begin.

Four consecutive hours, considered alone, do not exceed the four-and-a-half-hour limit. After four and a half hours of driving, an uninterrupted break of at least 45 minutes is required before driving resumes, unless a rest period begins. Alternatively, the break may be split during the driving period into at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30. For occasional passenger services, two breaks of at least 15 minutes each, totaling at least 45 minutes, are also permitted.
An analogue record sheet must not be used beyond its intended recording period: a 24-hour sheet must be replaced within that period to avoid overlapping records.
Exceeding driving times incurs a fine; it does not automatically lead to revocation of the driver qualification card.
For transport within its scope, the regulation sets driving limits as well as breaks and rest periods.
The regulation includes a weekly limit: driving time must not exceed 56 hours in a week.
Limiting driving and ensuring breaks and rest helps improve the social conditions of the workers concerned.
By regulating driving, breaks and rest, the regulation also aims to improve road safety.
The daily driving limit is normally 9 hours; it may be extended to 10 hours no more than twice a week.
The regulation limits maximum driving time; it does not require a minimum number of driving hours.
Weekly rest is subject to minimum durations, not a maximum limit.
The regulation aims to improve working conditions and road safety, including by limiting driving and providing for rest.
The regulation governs driving, breaks and rest; it does not set minimum driver pay.
The rules cover both goods and passenger transport, within their respective scopes.
For goods, the general threshold is a maximum permissible mass over 3.5 tonnes, including any trailer or semi-trailer; exclusions apply.
The rules cover vehicles designed or adapted to carry more than nine people including the driver and intended for that purpose; exclusions apply.
The regulation applies to road transport within its scope undertaken in the EU, subject to the stated exclusions.
The territorial scope includes road transport between the EU and European Economic Area countries when the other conditions are met.

The 2025 quiz marks this FALSE: the general goods-transport threshold is over 3.5 tonnes, including a trailer. Since 1 July 2026, over 2.5 tonnes also covers certain international or cabotage operations, subject to exceptions such as qualifying own-account transport.
Using a taxi or a bus alone is not enough: for passengers, vehicle capacity and purpose and any exclusions matter.
The rules concern road transport. A vehicle carried by train may be subject to specific rest rules, but that does not extend the scope to rail transport generally.
The scope includes certain passenger vehicles as well as goods vehicles.
The normal daily driving limit is nine hours; it may rise to ten no more than twice a week.
Daily driving can reach ten hours at most twice a week; the normal limit is nine hours.
Eight hours is not the maximum: the normal limit is nine hours, extendable to ten no more than twice a week.
Nine hours is a normal daily driving limit, not a consecutive driving period: after four and a half hours a break is required unless a rest period begins.
The normal extension permitted twice a week is to ten hours, not eleven.
Breaks do not authorize twelve hours of daily driving: the normal limit is nine hours, extendable to ten at most twice a week.
Regular daily rest comprises at least eleven hours; it can also be split into at least three hours followed by at least nine.
A reduced daily rest is at least 9 but less than 11 hours. At most three are permitted between two weekly rests; that interval does not necessarily match the calendar week.

The ordinary rule requires weekly rest to start within six consecutive 24-hour periods after the previous weekly rest ends. This is not a count of six calendar days driving; certain occasional passenger services may defer it under specific conditions.
The limit of three reduced daily rests is counted between two weekly rest periods, not simply by calendar week.

The quiz marks this FALSE, treating 9 hours alone as insufficient for a regular daily rest. Regular rest is at least 11 consecutive hours, or split into at least 3 hours followed by at least 9; 9 to under 11 consecutive hours is reduced rest.
Daily rest has its own durations: regular rest is at least eleven hours, while reduced rest is at least nine and less than eleven. It need not equal driving time.
Regular daily rest is at least 11 consecutive hours; it can also be split into periods of at least 3 and 9 hours.
During rest the driver can freely dispose of their time; this distinguishes it from work.
The 45 minutes are a driving break, not reduced daily rest, which lasts at least 9 hours and less than 11.
Regular weekly rest consists of at least 45 consecutive hours, unlike reduced rest.
The reduction must be compensated by an equivalent rest period taken in one block by the end of the third following week.
Reduced weekly rest can be less than 45 hours, but must last at least 24 consecutive hours.
There are two forms: regular rest of at least 45 hours and reduced rest of at least 24 consecutive hours, subject to the applicable conditions.

The quiz marks this FALSE: 30 hours is not enough for a regular weekly rest, which must last at least 45 hours. A 30-hour rest may instead count as a reduced weekly rest if the applicable conditions and compensation requirements are met.
The 24 hours are the minimum, not the maximum: reduced rest lasts less than 45 hours and at least 24 consecutive hours.
The minimum regular weekly rest is 45 consecutive hours, not 90.
Weekly rest is mandatory: payment cannot replace the required rest time.
During availability the driver need not remain at the workstation, but must be ready to resume work; its foreseeable duration is known in advance.
When a vehicle is multi-manned, time spent beside the driver or in a bunk while it is travelling is availability.
The square crossed by a diagonal indicates availability on the tachograph; it does not indicate other work.
Technical maintenance is work other than driving and is recorded as other work.
The figure shown does not match the crossed hammers: on a tachograph, these indicate other work, such as loading and unloading.
Other work includes work activities other than driving, such as cleaning and maintenance; it is recorded separately from driving.
Being free to dispose of time characterizes rest. During availability the driver must be ready to resume work.
Cleaning the vehicle is a work activity and counts as other work, not availability.
The square crossed by a diagonal indicates availability. Crossed hammers indicate other work.
A distance-based bonus is prohibited if it endangers road safety or encourages breaches of driving and rest time rules.
Vehicle ownership does not exempt the driver from penalties for their own infringements; the undertaking may also be liable under the applicable rules.
The undertaking must organize work, give appropriate instructions and check that drivers observe the prescribed times.
The undertaking must organize work within the limits: daily driving is normally limited to 9 hours, extendable to 10 no more than twice a week.
Responsibility does not rest solely with the driver: the undertaking is also liable under applicable provisions and must give instructions compatible with the limits.
The undertaking may also be liable for infringements committed by its drivers in another country; national law may make liability subject to conditions.

To safeguard the safety of people, the vehicle or the load, the limits may be exceeded only as much as necessary to reach a suitable stopping place, without compromising road safety. Article 12 separately provides for an exceptional, conditional exemption to reach the driver's home or the employer's operational centre for weekly rest.
When using the exemption to reach a suitable stopping place, the reason must be recorded by hand on the record sheet or printout, no later than on arrival at the stopping place.

The quiz marks this FALSE: going home does not normally permit exceeding the limits. In exceptional circumstances, without jeopardising road safety, Article 12 permits return to the driver’s residence or employer’s operational centre for weekly rest: up to one extra hour, or two for regular weekly rest after an uninterrupted 30-minute break immediately before the extra driving. The reason must be recorded and the extension compensated by the end of the third following week.

The quiz marks this FALSE: reaching the vehicle owner’s depot does not normally permit exceeding the limits. In exceptional circumstances, without jeopardising road safety, Article 12 permits return to the driver’s residence or employer’s operational centre for weekly rest, not just any owner’s depot: up to one extra hour, or two for regular weekly rest after an uninterrupted 30-minute break immediately before the extra driving. The reason must be recorded and the extension compensated by the end of the third following week.
A break is used exclusively for recuperation: the driver neither drives nor does other work during it.
Rest is an uninterrupted period during which the driver can freely dispose of their time, without remaining available for work.

Availability is neither a break nor actual work: it includes foreseeable waiting periods under the prescribed conditions and, in multi-manning, time beside the driver or on a bunk while the vehicle is moving. Not every wait at the workplace is availability.
A stop is not automatically a break: a break must be devoted exclusively to recuperation, without driving or other work.
Availability does not mean agreeing to work overtime: it is a period distinct from breaks and rest when the worker is ready to respond to a call, under the prescribed conditions.
The ordinary weekly driving limit is 56 hours; the limit of 90 hours in two consecutive weeks also applies.

The ordinary weekly driving limit is 56 hours; the maximum over two consecutive weeks is 90 hours. The exceptional return derogation for reaching the driver’s residence or employer’s operational centre can extend the weekly limit under its conditions, but not the 90-hour limit.
Split regular daily rest requires at least 3 consecutive hours first and at least 9 consecutive hours afterwards.
Regular weekly rest is at least 45 hours. It must normally begin within six 24-hour periods after the end of the previous weekly rest; reduced rest is also allowed under legal conditions.
Reduced weekly rest lasts at least 24 hours; the reduction must be compensated in one block by the end of the third following week, subject to the other weekly rest conditions.
In multi-manning at least two drivers must be available on board during the driving period concerned; only in the first hour is the second driver optional.
The order is reversed: split regular daily rest starts with at least 3 consecutive hours, followed by at least 9.
The ordinary rule does not require 48 hours after four driving periods: regular weekly rest is at least 45 hours and normally starts within six 24-hour periods after the previous weekly rest.
The second driver is optional only during the first hour of multi-manning, not the first three.
The ordinary weekly driving limit is 56 hours, not 48; the 90-hour limit over two consecutive weeks also applies.

The ordinary weekly limit is 56 hours, but the maximum over two consecutive weeks is 90 hours, not 100. The exceptional return derogation for reaching the driver’s residence or employer’s operational centre can extend the weekly limit under its conditions, but not the 90-hour limit.
After 4½ hours of driving a break of at least 45 minutes is required unless a rest period begins; the break may also be split under the prescribed conditions.
The circular steering-wheel-like symbol identifies driving time on the tachograph.
The bed symbol identifies breaks and rest periods on the tachograph.
The square crossed by a diagonal identifies availability on the tachograph.
The crossed hammers indicate other work, such as loading and unloading. Driving for commercial operations outside the scope of Regulation 561/2006 must also be recorded as other work.
Driving, other work, availability and breaks or rest have distinct symbols, so the recorded activities can be distinguished.
The picture shows a bed, the symbol for a break or rest. Driving is shown by a steering wheel.
The crossed hammers indicate other work; availability is shown by a square crossed by a diagonal.
OUT indicates an out-of-scope condition, not availability. Availability uses the square with a diagonal.
The T shown denotes a workshop or test station and inspection or calibration of the tachograph. Other work is indicated by two crossed hammers.
The square with a diagonal indicates availability; driving is represented by a steering wheel.
The device records both the driver’s driving activity and vehicle movement data, including speed.
By recording driver activities, the tachograph allows driving time to be checked and distinguished from other periods.
There are analog devices, which use record sheets, and digital devices, which use driver cards.
The different activities are recorded separately; the driver selects or enters periods other than driving as appropriate.
The tachograph records distance traveled and speed: these data let inspectors check vehicle movement alongside the driver’s activity periods.
The tachograph records movement data and driver activity, not conversations.
The tachograph records speed and distance, not individual braking actions as a driver activity.
The specified categories are analog and digital tachographs; hydraulic is not a specified tachograph type.
Recording is not started by pressing a START button on the dashboard: the driver uses a sheet or card and records activities according to the device’s procedures.

The tachograph records data such as distance and speed, not the complete path taken by the vehicle. A smart tachograph also retains specific positions, for example at the start and end of the working day: individual points do not describe the entire route.

Goods transport over 3.5 tonnes generally falls within the obligation, subject to exemptions. Since July 1, 2026, certain international transport or cabotage operations over 2.5 tonnes are also covered.

Vehicles built or adapted for more than nine people, including the driver, generally fall within the obligation. Regular services on routes no longer than 50 km are excluded, as are other exempt cases.
Vehicles with a maximum authorized speed of up to 40 km/h are outside the EU driving-time rules and the associated tachograph obligation.
The exemption applies to regular passenger services whose route is no longer than 50 km. Use for a non-regular service does not automatically qualify for that exemption and may require a tachograph.
Operating outside a city is not enough to require a tachograph: the general passenger rules cover vehicles built or adapted for more than nine people including the driver.

Exceeding 2 tonnes is not enough: the general goods threshold is over 3.5 tonnes. Since July 1, 2026, certain international transport or cabotage operations are covered above 2.5 tonnes, subject to exceptions.
Not all buses are covered: for example, regular passenger services on routes no longer than 50 km are excluded.

Not all goods vehicles are covered: mass, type of transport and exemptions matter. The general threshold is over 3.5 tonnes; since July 1, 2026, certain international transport or cabotage operations are covered above 2.5 tonnes.
Regular passenger services on routes of no more than 50 km are exempt from EU driving-time rules and the related tachograph requirement.
The exemption covers armed forces and fire service vehicles when transport is performed for their duties and under their control: ownership alone does not impose a tachograph requirement.
Specialised medical vehicles are exempt from EU driving-time rules and the related tachograph requirement; exceeding 3.5 tonnes alone does not make that requirement universal.
Specialised breakdown vehicles operating within 100 km of their base are exempt from EU driving-time rules and the related tachograph requirement.
Under normal storage conditions, the sheet’s records must remain clearly legible for at least one year.
The 24 hours are the sheet’s minimum recording capacity, not necessarily its exact duration: the capacity may be greater.
The dedicated area makes it possible to distinguish the speed trace from the other records on the sheet.
The dedicated area allows the kilometres travelled to be read and checked separately from the other records.
The sheet must be type-approved and suitable for the tachograph: compatibility allows the equipment to record correctly on the sheet.
The sheet provides space for handwritten details, such as the driver’s name and the vehicle registration number.
The required minimum capacity is 24 hours, not 48; several discs can be linked to increase it.
The sheet bears the manufacturer and approval marks for the sheet and compatible equipment, not the installing workshop’s mark.
The space on the sheet is for the driver’s entries, such as name, date, place and registration number; no area reserved for police entries is prescribed.
Sheets must be suitable for the equipment: the sheet indicates the tachograph types for which it is approved.
The first and last name identify the driver to whom the sheet belongs; they must be entered when its use begins.
The place where use of the sheet begins is entered with the date to identify the start of the recorded period.
The date when use of the sheet begins is entered with the place to identify the recorded period.
The registration number identifies the vehicle used and must be entered before the first journey recorded on the sheet.

The odometer readings are entered at the start of the first journey and the end of the last recorded journey. If the driver changes vehicles during the day, the readings of the first and the next vehicle are also entered: to calculate distance, compare readings from the same vehicle.
The owner company’s name is not among the entries the driver must make: these include the driver’s name and registration number.
The chassis number is not among the required entries: the vehicle is identified by its registration number.
The licence number and category are not required on the sheet; the driver is identified by first and last name.
The date of the last international transport is not required; instead, the date and place where use of the sheet begins are entered.
The date of birth is not required on the sheet: the driver enters their first and last name.
The switch allows activities such as other work, availability and rest to be recorded separately; driving time is recorded automatically.
Record the time of the vehicle change on the chart so the record can be linked to the vehicles used.
Enter the registration of every vehicle used, including the one taken over after the change.
Before departure, fill in the initial chart details, including name, date, place, registration and odometer reading.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but does not clearly distinguish distance travelled from the odometer reading. The initial and final readings are entered on the chart; their difference gives the kilometres travelled, which can be written down, but a separate total is not required by the regulation.
The owner's countersignature is not among the required entries. The driver fills in personal and journey details instead.
The chart follows the driver's activity: it should be kept for checks, not left in the vehicle at the end of the working period.
For a change, enter the time of the vehicle change, not the start time of the shift as the change detail.
The pictured square with a diagonal indicates availability. Select the bed symbol for rest.
The figure shown does not match the crossed hammers: on a tachograph, these indicate other work, such as loading and unloading.
The chart must be type-approved and compatible with the tachograph so its recordings suit the equipment used.
The initial details identify the driver, vehicle and start of chart use; the initial reading later helps establish the distance.
When changing vehicles during the day the chart continues to follow the driver. Enter the new vehicle's details on the back, using a chart compatible with both devices.
Document the change with the time, registration and odometer readings of both vehicles in the spaces provided on the chart.
Use approved charts suitable for the tachograph model, not just any chart.
The driver's first and last names are required, but driving licence and CQC details are not required entries on the analogue chart.
The driver's name and registration are analogue chart details; tachograph card details are not required to fill it in.
A vehicle change does not automatically require two charts: continue with the same compatible chart and enter the change details.
The digital tachograph records data in the unit's memory and on the inserted driver card, according to their respective functions.
The vehicle unit's memory is designed for at least 365 days of average activity.
The digital tachograph unit includes a printer for producing printouts of recorded data.

The quiz marks this TRUE: some devices can also sound a warning when driving without the appropriate card. The regulation requires a visual warning; sound is additional and is not mandatory on every device.
The internal memory is not the only store: relevant data are also recorded on the inserted driver card.
The data can be printed: the digital tachograph has a printer for the required printouts.
Seven days is not the maximum: the unit's memory is designed for at least 365 days of average activity.
The card covers the period when the driver uses the vehicle: insert it at the start and withdraw it at the end of the working period, except where authorised.
The personal driver card has a white background, distinguishing it from other tachograph cards.
In Italy, the competent Chamber of Commerce issues the driver card after checking eligibility.
The device permits card withdrawal only when the vehicle is stopped, after storing the relevant data on it.
The company card serves the company’s functions and cannot replace the driver’s personal card. If it is lost, request a replacement and make the required records.
The control card is for enforcement officers to check data; it is not a driver’s maintenance tool.
The workshop card is for persons authorised to work on the tachograph, not the driver repairing the vehicle.
Tachograph installation is reserved for fitters or workshops approved by the competent authorities.
The seals protect the integrity of the installation: the driver must not tamper with the tachograph or alter its records.
Calibration adapts the tachograph to the vehicle’s characteristics and is part of installation before entry into service.
The installation plaque records technical installation data, which are also useful for subsequent inspections.
The tachograph must be inspected at least every two years; some events require an earlier inspection.
Equipment alone is not enough: tachograph inspection requires an approved workshop.
Tachograph repair requires an approved fitter or workshop, not just any mechanical workshop.
Calibration is part of installation before entry into service: there is no general four-week period after installation.
Periodic inspection is required at least every two years, or earlier in certain circumstances.
Even a serious tachograph fault must be repaired by an approved fitter or workshop.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but the time limit runs from the failure, not the total length of the trip. An approved repair must be made as soon as circumstances permit; if the vehicle cannot return to the undertaking’s premises within a week of the breakdown or its discovery, it must be repaired en route.
Returning to base may precede repair if it occurs within one week of the breakdown or its discovery; the undertaking must still have the tachograph repaired as soon as possible.
A faulty tachograph must be repaired by an approved fitter or workshop as soon as circumstances permit.
During the breakdown the driver manually records activities no longer correctly recorded or printed, identifying themselves and signing the entries.
A breakdown does not remove the duty to document activities: those not correctly recorded must be entered manually.
Manual entries for activities not correctly recorded are required during the breakdown, regardless of the journey’s length.

There is no general 24-hour deadline: repair must be made as soon as possible and, if the vehicle cannot return to base within one week of the breakdown or discovery of defective operation, during the journey.
A breakdown does not always require the journey to stop immediately: manual records and repair as soon as possible are required under the applicable conditions.
Tachograph repair requires an approved fitter or workshop; the Chamber of Commerce issues cards and does not perform this repair.
In Italy, chambers of commerce issue the cards that identify users and let them access the digital tachograph’s different functions.
The four cards correspond to four users: driver, company, workshop and control authority.
The quiz marks this TRUE, but omits an exception: in Italy driver and company cards last five years, workshop cards one year and control cards two years.
The workshop card enables authorized technicians to perform their work and has an administrative validity of one year.
There are four cards, not two: driver, company, workshop and control authority cards.
In Italy, chambers of commerce issue the cards, not the Civil Motorization Authority.
The driver card lasts five years from issue, not three.
Twenty days is not the maximum: the memory must hold at least 28 days of activity under the average profile specified in the technical rules.
The tachograph records vehicle data such as distance and speed, and the driver’s activity periods, including driving and rest.
Records use UTC as a common reference; local time can differ with the time zone and daylight saving time.
The device has slots for the driver and co-driver and can record both their activities.
The tachograph printer can produce paper printouts of vehicle memory or card data, including daily activities.
The requirement does not apply to every vehicle. Specific conditions and deadlines apply to vehicles covered by the rules, including replacement of older equipment.
It also records vehicle data, such as distance and speed, as well as driver activities.
It is not limited to one driver: the driver and co-driver slots allow both drivers’ activities to be recorded.
A complete record of the last five years is not guaranteed: capacity varies by data type, and the oldest data are replaced when the allocated memory is full.
The tachograph can print daily activities recorded on the driver card or in the vehicle unit memory.
The microprocessor card interacts with the tachograph; the driver card stores changes of activity, among other information.
The driver card also stores data about vehicles used, in addition to activity information.
Each type has a distinct purpose: the driver card for driving activities, company card for managing data, workshop card for technical work and control card for inspections.
The card identifies its holder and is personal: it cannot be transferred to another driver.
The driver card is white and bears a photograph to identify its holder.
The driver card is valid for five years from issue and must be renewed when it expires.
In Italy, the driver applies for the card to the chamber of commerce responsible for their residence.

The quiz marks the listed categories TRUE, but a valid licence suitable for the vehicle is required along with the other applicable conditions, including residence and not holding another driver card. Since 2026, category B may also be suitable for certain international or cabotage operations with vehicles over 2.5 and up to 3.5 tonnes; exceptions apply.
The card identifies the company and lets it view, download and print tachograph data from its vehicles, helping it manage the fleet.
The company card can lock and unlock company data in the tachograph, protecting it from access by other companies.
The workshop card has a red background and is valid for one year.
The workshop card identifies the authorized technician and permits tachograph activation and calibration as well as maintenance work.
The control card identifies the competent authority and gives access to data needed for checks, including workplace safety and road police checks.
The control card gives competent authorities access to recorded data to check driving times and speed, among other things.
Cards interact with the tachograph: they identify the user and enable different functions, such as recording activities or viewing data.
There are four types: driver, company, workshop and control. Each enables functions suited to its user.
The tachograph card identifies the driver and records their activities; the CQC certifies professional qualification. Their functions differ.
The driver card is personal: it identifies the driver and stays with them when they change vehicle or employer.
The driver card is valid for five years, not ten.
In Italy the competent Chamber of Commerce issues the driver card, not employment offices.
Losing points concerns the driving licence; it does not automatically revoke the tachograph card. The card has its own withdrawal and suspension rules.
The driver card has a white background and is valid for five years. Yellow identifies the company card.
The company card can both lock and unlock company data in the tachograph; locking protects access to the company’s data.
The driver card is personal and a driver may hold only one valid card, even on international journeys.
The card identifies the driver and records their activities in the tachograph; it is not a toll payment card.
The cards are personal: each driver uses their own, even when two drivers take turns in the same vehicle.
Speeding can lead to penalties affecting the driving licence, but not an automatic three-month suspension of the tachograph card, which follows its own rules.
Drink-driving can lead to measures affecting the driving licence; it does not automatically revoke the tachograph card, which has its own rules.
The card is used with a digital tachograph. An analogue tachograph instead records activities on record sheets.

Before setting off, insert the card while the vehicle is stationary and follow the tachograph’s instructions. For example, the ADR version of the VDO DTCO 4.1x requires the ignition to be on for this function.
The driver at the wheel inserts their card in slot 1. After reading it, the tachograph displays the name associated with the card.
To remove the card the driver must request its ejection; this is done while the vehicle is stationary.

At the end of a shift, if rest begins, select rest before ejecting the card. If instead you are doing other work or are available, record the actual activity; enter subsequent periods away from the vehicle manually when required.
OUT signals to the tachograph that the use is outside scope; the driver enters this condition when it applies.
The card records driving and must be inserted before driving begins; there is no required sequence relative to inserting the ignition key.
Insert the card before starting to drive, not while moving, so activities can be recorded from the start.
OUT is a condition entered on the tachograph; the device cannot automatically infer that the service is outside scope.
OUT indicates use outside scope, not the end of a shift. It need not be selected to withdraw the card.
OUT identifies use outside scope; rest describes a driver activity. Driving outside scope does not become rest.
In Italy, the request to block and/or replace the card goes to the Chamber of Commerce within seven days of discovering the event.
Driving without the card is allowed for at most 15 calendar days, or longer only if necessary to return the vehicle to base and the inability to use the card can be proved.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but the rule requires a printout of vehicle details at the start of the journey, with name, card or licence number, signature and relevant periods; an activity printout is also needed at the end. A technical-data printout alone has not been shown to be equivalent.
At the end of the journey, print the time records, add any unrecorded periods, and identify and sign for the driver.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but seven days is not automatic permission: the undertaking must arrange repair as soon as possible. If the vehicle cannot return to base within one week of the breakdown or its discovery, it must be repaired en route.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but the rule requires the incorrectly recorded periods, name, card or licence number and signature on a record sheet or attached temporary sheet. The back of a printout and all the additional details listed are not a universally prescribed format and set of details.
The quiz marks this TRUE, but periods already captured on the analogue chart need not be duplicated on the digital card. Keep the chart, insert the card and record any genuinely missing periods.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but changing vehicles does not always require a printout. Complete and use the analogue chart, and retain the card and required records. A printout can help, but is not automatically required solely because of the change.
The deadline is not thirty days: the request must be submitted within seven days of discovering the event.
In Italy the request goes to the competent Chamber of Commerce, not the motor vehicle office.
There is no ordinary 45-day permission: the limit is 15 days, except for the time needed to return to base, with proof that the card cannot be used.
The driver must request a replacement and document activities using the required printouts; theft or loss must also be reported to the police.
Theft or loss is reported to the police, not the labour office; damage follows the replacement procedure.
Fifteen days is not the permitted delay for repair: it must be done as soon as possible and, if the vehicle cannot return within one week, en route.
Two working days is not the general deadline: repair must take place as soon as possible and, if the vehicle cannot return within one week, en route.
The analogue chart remains part of the activity records and must be available for inspection even when driving a vehicle with a digital tachograph.
The unit’s memory supports different printouts: daily activities, events and faults, overspeeding and technical data serve different checks.
The technical data printout identifies the unit and its software, allowing the device and installed version to be recognised.
The overspeed printout documents recorded events, including date, time and maximum speed. It concerns the tachograph’s overspeed threshold, not every road speed limit.
The printout shows overspeed events retained under selective criteria, not a complete record of the last ten years.
The card has limited capacity: older data can be overwritten, so a 365-day activity history is not guaranteed.
The technical printout concerns tachograph identification and calibration, not engine type or fuel supply.
The technical printout includes calibration data such as tyre size, but not the tyre brand.
The circular symbol resembling a steering wheel identifies driving and its duration.
The bed symbol identifies rest, distinct from driving and other work.
The crossed hammers indicate other work: work activities other than driving.
The square with a diagonal indicates availability, distinct from driving, work and rest.
The two vertical bars indicate a break and the cumulative duration of driving breaks.
OUT identifies an out-of-scope condition, not a driver activity.
The ship pictogram indicates a ferry or train crossing condition.
The T-shaped symbol identifies the workshop or test station, associated with inspection and calibration.
The rectangular symbol with a projection identifies the control authority, not a driving activity.
The rectangular symbol with a central projection at the top identifies the company and its mode.
The circle resembling a steering wheel indicates driving; tyre size has a different pictogram.
The circle with a hand represents the clock, not recreational activities.
The T-shaped symbol identifies the workshop; crossed hammers indicate other work.
The rectangular symbol with a projection indicates control; rest is represented by the bed.
The symbol with a central projection at the top indicates the company; ferry or train has a different pictogram.
The two bars indicate a driving break; OUT indicates an out-of-scope condition.
The square with a diagonal indicates availability; the company has a different symbol.
The crossed hammers indicate other work; the workshop is represented by the T-shaped symbol.
The ship indicates a ferry or train crossing; driving is represented by the steering wheel.
The two bars indicate a driving break; the control authority has a different symbol.
The numbered plate identifies the hazard and substance: 33 indicates a highly flammable liquid and 1203 identifies petrol.

The numbered plate identifies dangerous goods and their hazard. In the cases provided for by ADR, such as a tank carrying one product, it may appear at the front and rear; placement depends on the transport.

The quiz marks this TRUE. The orange ADR plate must meet technical specifications, including retroreflection, dimensions and resistance. The ADR provisions checked do not by themselves establish a separate type-approval procedure.
The lower number 1203 is the UN number for petrol; the upper number identifies the hazard.
The upper number 33 identifies a highly flammable liquid; the lower UN number identifies the goods.
The orange background must be retroreflective so the plate can reflect headlights.
For a tank with compartments carrying different substances, numbered plates normally appear on each side by the corresponding compartment. ADR provides exceptions for certain fuels.
The plate identifies dangerous goods and their hazard; it does not indicate the vehicle’s length.
This ADR plate identifies goods and their hazard, not a projecting load.
33 is an ADR hazard code, not the vehicle combination’s mass in tonnes.
The numbered plate identifies dangerous goods under ADR, not temperature-controlled ATP transport.
The plate identifies dangerous goods and their hazard; it does not indicate exceptional transport of concrete products.

Plates bearing the numbers of the individual substances normally appear on the sides by their respective compartments; the plates required for the transport unit go at the front and rear. Exceptions exist for certain fuels.
The plate identifies specific dangerous goods and their hazard, not vehicles carrying medicines generally.
The definition includes vehicles that complete the production cycle of building materials while moving, such as a concrete mixer.
Equipment suitable for emptying cesspits can also be among the equipment provided for construction vehicles; the vehicle must still meet the classification requirements.
The definition includes vehicles with special equipment for loading and carrying materials used in or resulting from construction.
A construction vehicle is designed for specific worksite use or mixed on-road and off-road use.
The mark proves payment of the road wear compensation required for the construction vehicle to circulate.
The classification is recorded on the registration document, where any vehicle-specific conditions can also be checked.
80 km/h concerns the calculated design maximum speed, which must not exceed it; it is not the speed limit when fully loaded.
When fully loaded, the specific limit in built-up areas is 40 km/h; any lower limits must also be respected.
When fully loaded, the specific limit outside built-up areas is 60 km/h; any lower limits must also be respected.
On motorways, an additional amount supplementing the road wear compensation is due along with the normal toll.
The road wear compensation is separate from the ownership tax: it is paid at the same time and proved by the mark.
They are not confined to worksites: the rules also provide for construction vehicles to travel on roads.
Work vehicles are not confined to roads outside built-up areas: they can also use urban roads and motorways, subject to applicable conditions and restrictions.
A vehicle equipped to load and transport sewage from cesspits can be classified as a work vehicle if it meets the required conditions.
Paying compensation does not authorize exceeding the vehicle’s payload. Exceptional transport requires a suitable vehicle and the required authorization, subject to its conditions.
A work vehicle’s maximum design speed must not exceed 80 km/h; it is not required to be 100 km/h.
When fully laden, the specific limit for work vehicles in built-up areas is 40 km/h, not 30 km/h; lower limits may also apply.
When fully laden, the specific limit for work vehicles outside built-up areas is 60 km/h, not 70 km/h; lower limits may also apply.
A work vehicle is classified by its particular equipment and uses; this does not mean every work vehicle is a special-purpose vehicle.
At least five axles are not required: the specifications for work vehicles also cover single vehicles with two or three axles.
Classification as a work vehicle does not give a general exemption from vehicle ownership tax. Road wear compensation is paid together with that tax.
Goods motor vehicles registered in Italy over 3.5 tonnes require approved retroreflective strips on the sides and rear to make them more visible.
Permitted side strips are white or yellow: they show the vehicle’s length when viewed from the side.
Permitted rear strips are red or yellow: they show the vehicle’s width when viewed from behind.
The requirement for side and rear retroreflective strips also applies to goods trailers registered in Italy over 3.5 tonnes.
Two rear panels are an allowed arrangement, but not the only one: a single long panel is also provided for.
For the motor vehicles described, two rear panels with diagonal yellow and red stripes can be used; a single long panel is another permitted arrangement.
For the trailers and semi-trailers described, two yellow rear panels with a red border can be used; a single long panel is another permitted arrangement.
Four separate panels are not a general requirement: arrangements with one or two yellow-and-red striped panels are also provided for. The corner arrangement shows separate segments.
Four separate panels are not a general requirement: arrangements with one or two yellow panels with red borders are also provided for. The corner arrangement shows separate segments.
Rear marking plates for heavy vehicles are rectangular, not two yellow triangles.
Green is not a permitted color for these strips: they are white or yellow on the sides and red or yellow at the rear.
Daytime-only use does not remove the requirement for side and rear retroreflective strips on the vehicles concerned.
The colors are not chosen according to whether the vehicle is a van or has a tarpaulin: strips are white or yellow on the sides and red or yellow at the rear.
Blue is not prescribed for tanker strips: they are white or yellow on the sides and red or yellow at the rear.
The red diagonal stripe, displayed at the front and rear, distinguishes carriage of goods on own account from carriage for others.
The white diagonal stripe, displayed at the front and rear, distinguishes carriage of goods for others from carriage on own account.
The stripe for transport for hire or reward is white; red distinguishes transport on own account. The marking is also repeated at the rear.
For carriage subject to ADR requirements, orange plates identify dangerous goods transport at the front and rear. The picture shows a numbered example; some ADR exemptions may apply.
The yellow front and rear panels warn other road users that the vehicle is exceptionally long; the black lettering identifies the exceptional transport.
The yellow panels on both sides make an exceptionally long vehicle visible from the side; the quiz identifies them as replacing the side reflectors.
The red and white stripes make the exceptional width visible: the panels mark the maximum outline at the front and rear.
The green panel with a d marks certain exempt categories, such as some fresh milk tankers. Exemption depends on the category and conditions, not just the panel.
The black a on a green panel identifies vehicles authorized by the prefecture to travel under an exemption. The conditions of the authorization must be met.

The a marks an exemption authorized by the prefecture, which may cover certain agricultural products to prevent deterioration. Carrying perishable food alone is not enough: the conditions for authorization must be met.
Exempt vehicles include tankers used for fresh milk, marked with a black d on a green panel on the sides and rear.

Under the 2007 calendar, vehicles carrying only newspapers and periodicals displayed a black d on a green panel. In 2026 the exemption applies to vehicles carrying only the categories listed in Article 8, including when empty; the d is not required for newspapers and periodicals.

Under the 2007 calendar, vehicles carrying only medical products displayed a black d on a green panel. In 2026 the exemption applies to vehicles carrying only the categories listed in Article 8, including when empty; the d is not required for medical products.
A black R on yellow identifies hazardous waste transport; the plate is placed visibly on the right at the rear.
Exceptional width is marked at the outer edges with red and white striped panels visible from the front and rear, not with the yellow squares described.
The supplementary signal for exceptional vehicles uses flashing yellow or orange light, not two red lights as claimed.
Red and white stripes, not black and white stripes, make the exceptional width visible.
The letter f is not the marking prescribed for these exemptions: a black d on a green panel identifies certain categories, while a indicates an authorized exemption.
The black a on a green panel indicates a vehicle authorized for an exemption from the ban; it does not identify liquid nitrogen transport.
The black d on a green panel marks certain categories of goods transport exempt from the ban; it is not a marking for buses carrying disabled people.
The black d on a green panel is prescribed for specific exempt goods categories, such as some perishables, not to identify pleasure boats.
A black R on yellow identifies hazardous waste transport, not refrigerated food.
A black R on yellow identifies hazardous waste transport, not registered mail.
The orange plate shown concerns dangerous goods: 33 is the hazard identification number and 1203 the substance’s UN number. They are not a food code and a weight.
The rectangular red and white striped panel marks a load projecting lengthwise so other road users can see it.
An indivisible load may project at the rear by up to three tenths of the vehicle length, within the overall size limits. It must be marked at its extremity with one or two panels like the one shown.
A load projecting lengthwise at the rear must be marked even if it projects only slightly: the panel goes at the end of the projection.
The red and white striped panel marks an indivisible load projecting beyond the rear, making it recognizable to other road users.
If the projection covers the full rear width, one panel is required at each end, placed across the load to mark its extent.
The panel is fixed at the end of the rear projection to mark where the load ends.
The red and white stripes must be retroreflective so the panel is visible at night too.
During emergency towing, if the towed vehicle has no flashing warning lights, this panel may be displayed on the side facing traffic; a portable warning triangle is also allowed.
The panel must be fixed at the end of the projecting load and kept visible so other road users can recognize its extent.
The panel warns of the projecting load: drivers behind should allow for its extent and proceed with care.
The picture shows the compulsory passing sign for roadworks vehicles: the arrow directs traffic to pass on the right. The projecting-load panel has red and white stripes without a blue disc.

The panel marks a rear projection even when it is less than three tenths of the vehicle length. Three tenths is the ordinary maximum allowed for an indivisible load, not a minimum threshold for the panel.
The picture is the compulsory passing sign for roadworks vehicles, recognizable by the blue disc and arrow. It is not the panel used for projecting loads.
The striped panel marks a load projecting at the rear; it does not identify trucks carrying construction materials.
The striped panel marks a load projecting at the rear; it does not indicate that the vehicle carries waste.
The picture shows the compulsory passing sign for roadworks vehicles, not the projecting-load panel. The latter marks a rear projection even below 50 centimeters.
The panel marks a load projecting at the rear; it is not required on every truck solely because of its weight.

The pictured panel indicates the compulsory passing side beside a roadwork vehicle: the arrow points to the side on which to pass it. When the vehicle is exposed to traffic, the prescribed panel must be fitted at the rear and cannot be replaced by a red flag.
The panel marks a rear load projection; the type of road does not require another at the front. In general, the load cannot project beyond the front.
The panel marks a load projecting at the rear, not the transport of schoolchildren.
The sign warns of an uneven road. Slowing down reduces the shocks transmitted to the load when the wheels meet irregularities.
The sign warns of an uneven road surface. Speed must be adapted to the road and to the characteristics of the vehicle and its load.
An uneven road has irregularities: driving over them too fast increases shocks transmitted to the load, which may be damaged.
Irregularities can destabilize the vehicle, especially at excessive speed. Slow down to maintain control.
Shocks from irregularities can shift or dislodge an inadequately secured load. Slowing down and securing the load properly reduce the risk.

The sign warns of an uneven road. Reduce speed in good time and drive smoothly: bumps can move the liquid, whose sloshing can affect stability. Slowing down does not, however, guarantee minimum slosh in every situation.
An uneven road transmits shocks to the suspension, which is under greater stress when the vehicle is fully loaded. Slowing down helps limit them.
Irregularities cause shocks to wheels and tires. When the vehicle is fully loaded, slowing down helps reduce the strain.
The sign warns of an uneven road. A fully loaded heavy vehicle should slow down: the irregularities cause impacts that also stress the steering.
The sign warns of an uneven road, but does not itself prohibit overtaking. Overtake only when conditions and the other rules allow it.
An uneven road requires an appropriate speed even when carrying goods other than liquids: the danger depends on the irregularities and the vehicle, not just the type of load.
Speed must be adapted to the uneven road even when the load is securely fastened. Securing the load is still necessary and does not eliminate impacts caused by the uneven surface.
A secured load and compliance with the general speed limit are not enough: on an uneven road, adjust speed to the actual road and vehicle conditions.
An uneven road may require slowing down even without rain: the surface irregularities themselves call for an appropriate speed.
An uneven road may require slowing down even without snow: the surface irregularities themselves call for an appropriate speed.
An uneven road may require slowing down even without strong wind: the surface irregularities themselves call for an appropriate speed.
A half-full cargo compartment does not remove the hazard of an uneven road. Adjust speed to the surface and the load.
A tanker is also affected by road irregularities. In a partially filled liquid tank, movement of the load can affect stability.
There is no rule requiring a half-full tanker to travel 20% faster. Adjust speed to the road and load; liquid can move in a partially filled tank.
The sign warns of an uneven road: slowing down limits the jolts transmitted to bus passengers.
An uneven road can cause jolts; slowing down helps prevent passengers losing their balance, especially when standing.
An uneven surface can cause jolts in the bus. Reducing speed helps make the journey more comfortable.
Jolts on an uneven road can make passengers, especially standing ones, lose balance and collide with one another. Slowing down reduces the risk.
An uneven road calls for slowing down, not unfastening seat belts. On a bus, seated passengers must keep them fastened while moving when their use is required.
The sign warns of an uneven road and calls for an appropriate speed; it does not require the driver to announce the danger over a microphone.
Accelerating would increase jolts on the uneven surface. The driver should instead adjust speed and slow down to protect passengers.
The sign warns of a hump; if it is a speed hump, slowing down limits jolts that could damage the goods carried.
The triangular sign warns of a hump ahead; it does not prohibit articulated goods vehicles. The stretch must be approached at an appropriate speed.
The triangle warns of a hump and does not by itself set a numerical limit of 50 km/h. Speed must still suit the hazard and any posted limits.
The sign warns of a hump; if it is a speed hump, slowing down reduces jolts and helps preserve passenger comfort.
The triangle warns of a hump; it does not prohibit articulated buses. Approach the section at an appropriate speed.
The triangle warns of a hump and does not by itself set a numerical limit of 30 km/h. Speed must still suit the hazard and any posted limits.
The sign warns of a dangerous right-hand bend. Slowing down helps limit the lateral forces that can shift the load and compromise stability; the load must also be properly secured.
The bend is to the right. A loaded tanker has a high center of gravity and its liquid can move, increasing the risk of rollover. Slow down before the bend.
The triangle warns of a dangerous right bend; it does not require the use of reduction gears. Speed must still be adjusted to the bend.
The sign warns of a dangerous right bend and can also be used on a motorway when that danger needs to be signaled.
The symbol shows a single right bend. A series of bends uses the double-bend sign with a supplementary panel showing the length of the section.
The right bend calls for moderate speed: smoother driving limits the lateral acceleration felt by passengers and improves comfort.
Lateral acceleration on a bend can make standing passengers lose their balance. Moderating speed reduces the risk of falls and collisions.
The sign warns of a dangerous right bend and can also be used on a motorway when that danger needs to be signaled.
The symbol shows a single right bend. A series of bends uses the double-bend sign with a supplementary panel showing the length of the section.
The sign warns of a right bend, but does not require everyone to sit. Where the vehicle is authorized to carry standing passengers, drive carefully and moderate speed.
The double bend produces lateral forces that can shift an inadequately secured load and affect stability. Secure the load and moderate speed.
A tanker requires particular care through the double bend: liquid in a partially filled tank can surge and affect stability.
A loaded tanker requires care through the double bend: liquid can move and a steep gradient makes the vehicle harder to control. Moderate speed.
The triangle warns of a double bend, the first to the right; it does not require the use of reduction gears. Speed must still be adjusted.
The double bend can also be signaled on mountain roads when its layout or visibility makes it dangerous.
The symbol indicates a double bend, the first to the right; a single left bend has a different symbol.
The triangle warns of a double bend, the first to the right: it is not a speed-limit sign and does not set that limit for trucks.
Moderate speed through the double bend limits the lateral acceleration felt by passengers and makes the journey more comfortable.
Lateral acceleration through the double bend can make standing passengers lose their balance. Moderating speed reduces the risk of falls and collisions.
The sign warns of a double bend, but does not require everyone to sit. Where the vehicle is authorized to carry standing passengers, drive carefully and moderate speed.
The triangle warns of a double bend, the first to the right: it is not a speed-limit sign and does not set that limit for buses.
The double bend can also be signaled on mountain roads when its layout or visibility makes it dangerous.
The symbol indicates a double bend, the first to the right; a single left bend has a different symbol.
The sign warns of a dangerous 10% descent. Excessive, prolonged use of the brakes can overheat them and reduce their effectiveness; engine braking should also be used.
The dangerous descent may call for the retarder, if fitted, to help control speed and reduce use of the service brakes.
The sign warns of a dangerous 10% descent. In a loaded tanker, moderate speed: the gradient and liquid movement make the vehicle harder to control.
The sign warns of a dangerous descent. Half-filling an empty tank does not guarantee stability: liquid can surge and make the vehicle harder to control.

The sign warns of a dangerous descent. Continuous braking can overheat the brakes and reduce their effectiveness; use a suitable gear and, if fitted and suitable for the conditions, the retarder as well.

A dangerous descent requires care: prolonged braking can overheat the brakes and reduce their effectiveness. A suitable gear and, if fitted and suitable for the conditions, the retarder help control speed.
The sign warns of a dangerous descent. If fitted and suitable for the conditions, the retarder helps control speed and supplements the service brakes.

The sign warns of a dangerous descent. Continuous braking can overheat the brakes and reduce their effectiveness; use a suitable gear and, if fitted and suitable for the conditions, the retarder as well.
The sign warns of a steep ascent. A heavy vehicle such as a loaded tanker accelerates more slowly uphill, so adjust speed to the gradient and load and proceed carefully.
The sign warns of a steep ascent. Half-filling an empty tank does not guarantee stability: liquid can surge and make the vehicle harder to control.
The sign warns of a soft or unusable shoulder. The vehicle’s weight can cause the edge to give way, so avoid getting too close to it.
The sign warns of a soft or unusable shoulder. If the edge gives way, a vehicle with a high center of gravity can roll over, so keep away from it.
The sign warns of a dangerous shoulder, not loose stones on the road. It warns that the edge may give way or that a vehicle may fall into a ditch if it moves too close.
The sign requires drivers to give way to oncoming vehicles at the narrow section. A bulky vehicle must wait and not enter when vehicles cannot pass each other.
The sign gives priority in the direction of the white arrow. With a bulky vehicle, carefully check that oncoming drivers are giving way before entering the narrow section.
The sign requires drivers to give way to oncoming traffic. The combination’s greater weight or size does not give it priority on this stretch.
The sign gives priority at the narrow section, but does not instruct drivers to accelerate. Speed must suit the available space and traffic conditions.
The sign requires at least 70 metres from the vehicle ahead. Spacing can create room between heavy vehicles where overtaking is difficult.
The sign requires at least 70 metres from the vehicle ahead. Spacing heavy vehicles can limit how many occupy a viaduct at once and spread the load.
The 70-metre spacing sign is a general restriction: it also applies to buses and heavy vehicles, not just cars.
The sign requires at least 70 metres from the vehicle ahead; it does not directly specify a maximum number of vehicles on the viaduct.

The prohibition applies to drivers of vehicles not designated for carrying people whose maximum laden mass exceeds 3.5 tonnes. It prohibits overtaking motor vehicles; vehicles without motors may be overtaken only while staying within your half of the road.
The prohibition also applies to special-purpose transport vehicles not designated for carrying people if their maximum laden mass exceeds 3.5 tonnes. They may not overtake motor vehicles.
The prohibition applies to vehicles with a maximum laden mass over 3.5 tonnes that are not designated for carrying people; it covers overtaking motor vehicles, including motorcycles.
The prohibition applies to vehicles over 3.5 tonnes not designated for carrying people. Buses are excluded even above that mass; other rules still apply.
The sign prohibits trucks over 3.5 tonnes from overtaking motor vehicles. Non-motor vehicles may be overtaken within the half of the carriageway, provided no other prohibition applies.
Buses are excluded from this specific prohibition, which applies to vehicles over 3.5 tonnes not designated for carrying people. They may overtake if the other rules allow it.
The prohibition applies above 3.5 tonnes maximum laden mass, not up to that value. Lighter trucks may overtake if the other rules allow it.
The ban applies to vehicles over 3.5 t that are not used to carry people. Buses are excluded even above that mass; other rules still apply.
The supplementary panel changes the usual 3.5 t threshold: above the indicated 5 t, vehicles not used to carry people may not overtake motor vehicles.
The ban also applies to special-purpose vehicles over 3.5 t that are not used to carry people: they may not overtake motor vehicles.
The sign prohibits goods vehicles over 3.5 t from overtaking motor vehicles, including cars.
The ban on overtaking cars applies even when the maneuver stays within the half of the road for that direction; staying inside the solid line does not remove it.
A motorhome is a motor vehicle: the ban applies even if its mass is under 3.5 t. The threshold concerns the overtaking vehicle.
A bicycle has no motor. The sign allows it to be overtaken if the maneuver stays within the half of the road for that direction and other safety conditions are met.
The ban concerns vehicles over 3.5 t not used to carry people; it does not apply to buses used for passenger transport.
Buses are used to carry people and are therefore excluded from this specific ban, which applies to vehicles over 3.5 t not used for that purpose.
Overtaking non-motorized vehicles is also allowed for special-purpose vehicles subject to the sign, provided the maneuver stays within the half of the road for that direction.
For vehicles subject to the sign, overtaking non-motorized vehicles is allowed only within their own half of the road, even without a solid line.
The sign concerns vehicles over 3.5 t not used to carry people. For trucks up to that mass it does not require the maneuver to stay within their half of the road; other overtaking rules apply.
Buses used to carry people are excluded from the specific ban even above 3.5 t; other overtaking rules still apply.
The sign prohibits overtaking motor vehicles, not passage. The panel changes the mass above which the overtaking ban applies.
Outside built-up areas, vehicles subject to an overtaking ban for specific categories must keep at least 100 m apart. This rule does not apply on sections with two or more lanes in each direction.
The sign prohibits goods vehicles over 3.5 t from overtaking motor vehicles, including cars.
The ban for goods vehicles over 3.5 t covers motor vehicles, including other goods vehicles.
A concrete mixer over 3.5 t that is not used to carry people is subject to the ban; a moped is also a motor vehicle.
A mobile crane over 3.5 t is subject to the ban for vehicles not used to carry people. A motorcycle is a motor vehicle and the ban applies even within the half of the road for that direction.
The panel sets the threshold at 5 t: construction vehicles above that mass that are not used to carry people may not overtake motor vehicles.
A concrete mixer over 3.5 t that is not used to carry people is prohibited from overtaking motor vehicles, including cars.
A mobile crane over 3.5 t that is not used to carry people may not overtake the motorcycle: the ban covers motor vehicles.
With the 5 t panel, the ban applies to construction vehicles above that mass that are not used to carry people. A slow motor vehicle ahead does not remove the ban.
The specific 100 m distance between vehicles subject to the ban does not apply on sections with two or more lanes in each direction. A safe following distance is still required.
The P indicates parking; the “except” panel with a bus symbol excludes buses from using the indicated area.
The P indicates parking, but the “except” panel excludes buses: the parking area is not reserved for them.
The circle with a bus symbol prohibits buses; trucks are not in that category.
The prohibition applies to the buses shown, not motor caravans, which are a separate vehicle category.
The prohibition applies to buses without a mass threshold, so it also applies below 3.5 tonnes.
The sign prohibits buses; tourist coaches are not exempt.
The red border indicates a prohibition on buses, not a lane reserved for them.
The sign prohibits buses, including school buses in that category.
The truck symbol without a number prohibits vehicles not used to carry people whose maximum laden mass exceeds 3.5 tonnes; this includes goods vehicles.
The 3.5-tonne limit applies to vehicles not used to carry people, so buses are not affected by this sign.
The prohibition applies above 3.5 tonnes maximum laden mass recorded on the registration document; a truck below that threshold may pass.
A closed body makes no difference: the prohibition covers vehicles not used to carry people with a maximum laden mass above 3.5 tonnes, not all vans.
An open body does not grant an exemption: trucks with a maximum laden mass above 3.5 tonnes cannot pass.
The sign concerns vehicles over 3.5 tonnes not used to carry people, not those intended to carry them.
The number inside the symbol changes the maximum laden mass threshold to 6.5 tonnes: a 5-tonne truck is below it.
The 6.5-tonne sign concerns vehicles not used to carry people; buses are not prohibited.
The number 6.5 is the maximum laden mass threshold on the registration document: a truck above it is prohibited.
The 6.5-tonne threshold applies to vehicles not used to carry people, not to those intended to carry them.
The prohibition above 6.5 tonnes applies to vehicles not used to carry people, including special-purpose motor vehicles; it is not limited to trucks.
Even above 10 tonnes, a bus carries people and is not covered by this sign’s prohibition.

The 6.5-tonne threshold refers to the maximum laden mass on the registration document, not the actual weight at the time: a truck with an authorized mass of 7.5 tonnes remains prohibited even when empty.
The prohibition applies to motor vehicles towing a trailer. Within the prescribed limits, a carrello appendice is an integral part of the towing vehicle and is not treated as a separate trailer.
The symbol prohibits motor vehicles towing a trailer, subject to any exemptions indicated on a panel.
An articulated bus has two sections joined by an articulation; it does not tow a trailer, so this prohibition does not apply.
An articulated vehicle consists of a tractor and semitrailer and is prohibited even when empty.
The prohibition applies to motor vehicles towing a trailer, without limiting it to goods transport: a trailer intended to carry people can also be covered.
The sign prohibits motor vehicles from towing a trailer; carrying a boat on the trailer does not change the prohibition.
The orange panel on the vehicle identifies the prohibition on vehicles carrying dangerous goods.
Gasoline is dangerous goods, so a tanker carrying it falls under the prohibition shown by the orange panel.
The sign concerns dangerous goods being carried, not whether the truck has a tarpaulin.
The prohibition concerns dangerous goods, not goods merely because they are perishable.
The sign concerns the transport of dangerous goods; having a refrigerated body is not in itself the criterion for the prohibition.
The flame symbol prohibits vehicles carrying explosives or highly flammable products.
The prohibition covers both explosives and highly flammable products, as indicated by the flame symbol.
This is not just a warning: the sign prohibits vehicles carrying explosives or highly flammable products.
The prohibition also covers highly flammable products; they do not have to be explosive.
The prohibition applies to vehicles carrying highly flammable products; towing the loaded vehicle does not remove it.
The waves beneath the tank identify the prohibition on vehicles carrying products liable to contaminate water.
This sign concerns products liable to contaminate water, not all dangerous goods. Any other applicable prohibitions must still be obeyed.
The prohibition concerns products liable to contaminate water, not tankers as such: carrying water does not fall under this prohibition.
The prohibition concerns the vehicle carrying products liable to contaminate water; an empty towing vehicle does not exempt the loaded trailer.
The waves indicate a prohibition on carrying products liable to contaminate water, not a flood warning.
The prohibition depends on the products carried, not merely on the vehicle being an empty tanker.
The indicated value is the actual length limit: vehicles over 10 metres are prohibited.
The limit applies to vehicles based on length, including buses: a bus over 10 metres cannot pass.
The length prohibition also applies at night; the sign shown has no time restriction.
The limit also applies to a combination of vehicles: its total actual length is compared with the indicated 10 metres.
The limit applies to vehicles and combinations according to length, not only to goods vehicles.
The number indicates the maximum permitted length of the vehicle or combination, not the distance from a following vehicle.
The length of the entire combination counts: if the coupled truck and trailer exceed 10 metres, passage is prohibited.
The prohibition also depends on actual length for articulated buses: those over 10 metres cannot pass.
The 7 t limit concerns the vehicle’s actual mass: vehicles exceeding it may not pass.
A supplementary panel can clarify the restriction, for example by prohibiting several vehicles from crossing a bridge at the same time.
The limit concerns actual vehicle mass regardless of whether it carries food: a truck exceeding 7 t may not pass.
The actual mass at the time of passage, including the load being carried, counts, not just the maximum mass in the documents.
The limit concerns actual total mass, not axle mass. If one axle alone exceeds 7 t, total mass also exceeds it, so passage is prohibited.
The passage restriction is not automatically limited to 8 a.m.–8 p.m.; that time range concerns urban parking restrictions unless otherwise indicated.
The 7 t limit also applies to buses: they may not pass if their actual mass exceeds the indicated value.
The actual mass at the time of passage counts, not just the laden mass recorded in the documents.
The axle symbol shows that the 2.5 t limit concerns the actual mass on the most heavily loaded axle.
The restriction applies to axle masses above 2.5 t: a truck with 2.5 t on each axle does not exceed the indicated limit.
The 2.5 t value limits actual mass per axle: if any axle exceeds it, the vehicle may not pass.
The value is compared with the mass actually borne by the axle at the time of passage.
The sign limits actual mass on an axle, not the truck’s total mass.
The drawing represents an axle: the limit concerns the mass borne by it, not only vehicles with twin wheels.
The 2.5 t limit concerns actual mass per axle, not the vehicle’s total laden mass.

The sign ends the specific overtaking ban for vehicles not used to transport people whose laden mass recorded on the registration certificate exceeds 3.5 t. The truck and trailer may overtake if the other rules and conditions allow it.

The sign ends the specific overtaking ban for vehicles not used to transport people whose laden mass recorded on the registration certificate exceeds 3.5 t; overtaking remains subject to the other rules and conditions.
The black bar across the symbols marks the end of the overtaking ban for vehicles not used to carry passengers with a laden mass over 3.5 t.

The sign ends an overtaking ban for vehicles not used to transport people whose laden mass recorded on the registration certificate exceeds 3.5 t; it does not prohibit the listed categories from passing.

The sign ends an overtaking ban for vehicles not used to transport people whose laden mass recorded on the registration certificate exceeds 3.5 t and does not require overtaking on the right. Overtaking is generally on the left, subject to the prescribed exceptions.
The sign also ends the specific overtaking ban for trucks with a laden mass of 7 t or more; they are not excluded from the end of the ban.
The prohibition disc refers to the two vehicles depicted: road trains and articulated trucks may not pass.
The prohibition disc applies to the categories shown below it: road trains and articulated trucks.
The restriction concerns the two illustrated categories, road trains and articulated trucks; this sign does not prohibit the other categories.
The red disc prohibits passage by the depicted categories, road trains and articulated trucks; it does not indicate a compulsory route.
The red circle and two silhouettes prohibit road trains and articulated trucks from passing; they do not indicate parking.
The silhouettes show goods vehicles with trailers and articulated goods vehicles, not articulated buses.
The white arrow in the blue circle warns of a mandatory right turn for the trucks shown, with a maximum authorized mass over 3.5 tonnes.
The mandatory right turn rules out going straight for the trucks shown, with a maximum authorized mass over 3.5 tonnes.
The mandatory right turn also rules out turning left for the trucks shown, with a maximum authorized mass over 3.5 tonnes.
The blue circle with a right arrow warns of a mandatory route for the category shown below: trucks over 3.5 tonnes.
This is not advice: the blue circle with a white arrow warns of a mandatory right turn for the trucks shown.
The arrow in the blue circle requires the vehicles shown to turn right; it does not prohibit that turn.
The blue circle with an arrow warns of a mandatory right turn for the trucks shown, not a parking area.
The arrow in the blue circle warns of a mandatory right turn for the trucks shown, not a dangerous bend.
The no-entry sign bars entry from its side; the “except” plate exempts buses from the prohibition.
The P indicates parking and the “except” plate excludes buses from that indication: the parking is for other vehicles.
The “except” plate can accompany a mandatory sign, exempting the category shown, buses, from the requirement.
The “except” plate can accompany a prohibition, exempting the category shown, buses, from it.
The “except” plate exempts buses from the no-entry restriction, so they may enter from the sign’s side.
The no-parking sign is accompanied by an “except buses” plate: buses are exempt from the prohibition.
This plate says “except”: it identifies the category exempt from the prohibition, not the category subject to it.
The symbol indicates buses without distinguishing urban from interurban buses, so both are included in the exception.
The arrow indicates a recommended right-hand diversion for the categories shown: road trains and articulated trucks.
The two silhouettes represent road trains and articulated trucks; the arrow indicates a recommended route to the right for them.
The black arrow indicates a recommended diversion for the vehicles shown; it is not the blue circle used for a mandatory direction.
The recommended diversion avoids crossing the built-up area or part of it; the silhouettes identify road trains and articulated trucks.
The arrow indicates a recommended right-hand diversion for road trains and articulated trucks, not a ban on turning.
The arrow recommends a diversion for the categories shown to avoid the built-up area or part of it, not a route toward its center.
The arrow indicates a recommended diversion for the vehicles shown; it does not require an immediate right turn.
The black arrow gives advance notice of a recommended right diversion for road trains and articulated vehicles, not a lane change to pass an obstacle.
The yellow background identifies temporary signage: this sign indicates a mandatory direction for the vehicles shown when approaching roadworks.
The blue circle with a straight arrow requires the categories shown below it, road trains and articulated vehicles, to continue straight.
This is a temporary roadworks sign: the indicated mandatory direction applies while it is needed for the works.
The requirement to continue straight applies to the road trains and articulated vehicles shown below the circle, not to all vehicles.
The blue circle with a white arrow indicates a mandatory direction for the vehicles shown, not a recommended route.
