The arrow in the blue circle requires the vehicles shown to follow that direction; it is not advice for everyone.
The white bars and yellow triangle distinguish the signal intended for public transport vehicles, including those on scheduled services.
For public transport vehicles the horizontal white bar means stop, like red on ordinary vehicle traffic lights.
The vertical white bar gives public transport vehicles for which the signal is intended permission to proceed straight.
The signal serves public transport vehicles and is not limited to rail vehicles: it can also apply to buses.
This is a signal for public transport vehicles, identifiable by the bars and triangle; it is not a level-crossing signal.
The bars and triangle identify a signal for public transport vehicles, not a ferry boarding signal.
The yellow triangle warns public transport vehicles that a stop signal is coming; it does not warn of roadworks.
The horizontal white bar is one of this signal’s lights and means stop when illuminated.
The vertical white bar is one of this signal’s lights and, when illuminated, permits straight-ahead travel.
The white bars and yellow triangle are the characteristic lights of the signal for public transport vehicles.
The figure shows a signal for public transport vehicles: its lights control movement and do not warn of roadworks.
The signal controls public transport vehicles with stop and proceed indications; it does not indicate rail switches.
The signal is intended for public transport vehicles; a military registration plate is not the criterion for its application.
The yellow markings delimit a stop for scheduled collective public transport vehicles, including buses.
The marked area is reserved for scheduled collective public transport vehicles to stop, such as buses and trolleybuses.
The yellow zigzags mark the beginning and end of the stop, needed for pulling in and rejoining traffic.
Parking is prohibited in the stop area, including the zigzag sections. A brief stop remains possible if it does not obstruct traffic and the driver is ready to move off.
The markings delimit a stop for scheduled collective public transport vehicles, including when the service uses articulated buses.
The yellow lines mark a scheduled bus stop, not a taxi parking space.
The lines mark the bus stop and its manoeuvring areas; they do not prohibit cars from passing through.
The parking prohibition applies to the marked stopping area, not to 20 metres before and after the zigzag.
The markings reserve the area for a bus stop; they do not prohibit trucks from passing through it.
A scheduled bus stop is marked in yellow; regional routes do not change the markings to blue.
The prohibition symbol is on the straight-ahead route and applies to goods vehicles with a maximum laden mass over 3.5 tonnes.
The straight arrow also leads to the town centre; on that route the symbol prohibits goods vehicles with a maximum laden mass over 3.5 tonnes.
The circular symbol on the straight-ahead route prohibits goods vehicles with a maximum laden mass over 3.5 tonnes.
The straight-ahead prohibition applies to goods vehicles with a maximum laden mass over 3.5 tonnes, not all vehicles; the sign gives no time restrictions.
The prohibition symbol is on the straight-ahead arrow, not a right turn.
The circular symbol on the straight-ahead arrow prohibits the indicated vehicles from passing; it does not recommend that direction.
When a CQC qualification is required for professional driving, the driver must have a valid qualification and prove it with the document showing code 95 and its expiry date.
Compulsory third-party liability insurance covers damage caused to others by road traffic; a truck must also be covered.
The driver tachograph card is personal and includes the driving licence number among its identifying details.
In Italy the driver tachograph card is requested from and issued by the competent local Chamber of Commerce.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but not every non-EU country requires a green card: for example, Switzerland and Norway do not require one for a vehicle registered in Italy. Insurance cover is still necessary; before travelling, check territorial cover and the destination’s document requirements with your insurer.
The CQC qualification is valid for five years; periodic training is required for renewal.
The ADR driver training certificate is valid for five years and must be renewed to remain valid.
When ADR requirements apply, the transport document accompanies the dangerous goods and contains the information needed to identify them.
ADR instructions in writing must be available in the cab to help the crew respond to an accident or emergency.
To renew an ADR driver certificate, the driver must complete refresher training and pass the corresponding examination.
For carriage subject to the ADR requirement, the driver must hold the appropriate training certificate; some operations are exempt.
Exceptional transport requires a specific authorisation from the authority responsible for the road or route concerned.
Milk in transport must be accompanied by the prescribed accompanying declaration identifying its origin and destination; an equivalent document allowed by the rules may be used.
For frozen goods carried under ATP rules, a compliant vehicle is used: the certificate concerns the body’s suitability for temperature-controlled transport.
CQC is renewed through periodic training. A medical examination concerns fitness to drive, not the ordinary renewal requirement for the qualification.
The tachograph card is requested from the competent Chamber of Commerce, not the Civil Motorization Office.
An EU citizen can travel to another EU country with a valid national identity card, so a passport is not always required. Different rules apply to non-EU citizens.
The driver card has its own expiry date: it normally lasts five years from issue.
The driver card is valid for five years from issue, so its expiry does not necessarily coincide with the driving licence expiry.
Ordinary driving licences are issued by Civil Motorization offices; the prefect is not the ordinary issuing authority.
For ADR transport subject to the requirement, the driver needs an ADR professional training certificate; a KC certificate does not replace it.
ATP concerns equipment for transporting perishable food. Dangerous goods instead are subject to ADR requirements, including driver training when required.
An escort is not required for every exceptional transport: the need for one and its type depend on the conditions and the permit’s requirements.
The road authority or the regional authority is responsible for the exceptional transport permit depending on the road network, not the stated Motorization office.
The driver’s ADR certificate is valid for five years, not the stated sequence of six and three years.
ADR renewal requires refresher training and passing the corresponding exam; an examination by the local medical commission is not the ordinary certificate renewal requirement.
Renewing an ADR certificate requires more than attending the course: the corresponding exam must also be passed.
ADR certificate renewal requires a specific refresher course as well as an exam; the exam alone is insufficient.
The own-account transport licence relates to the vehicle and must be produced during checks. For vehicles in the stated category, the licence for the vehicle used must be carried on board.
For own-account transport under a licence for a vehicle with a payload over 3 tonnes, the list accompanies the transport and allows checks that the goods are covered by the licence.
In this case, the declaration accompanies the list and documents the relationship between the holder and the goods, such as ownership or another permitted own-account condition.
When a driver attestation is required for transport under a Community licence, the original is carried on board and presented for checks; a certified copy remains with the undertaking.

The quiz marks this TRUE under the paper system. Since 2026 the ECMT licence is digital: a valid licence and its system-generated information document are required, with the document available on board digitally or printed for inspection.
ECMT licences may be annual or short-term; the 2026 guide specifies 30 days for short-term licences.
The applicable technical certificates document the vehicle’s compliance and roadworthiness and must accompany it throughout the ECMT journey.

The quiz marks this TRUE under the paper system. Since 2026 the journey logbook is electronic: it must be kept up to date, and its system-generated journey information document must be available on board digitally or printed for inspection.
For international transport covered by the CMR Convention, the consignment note documents the contract; one copy accompanies the goods.
Own-account transport with a vehicle under six tonnes does not require that licence, so its original cannot be required on board on that basis.

The list and declaration required for own-account transport concern that type of transport and its licence conditions; vehicle mass alone does not impose a general obligation on every hire-or-reward transport.

Own-account transport can include goods in the undertaking’s possession, not just goods it purchased. For the transport described, a list of the goods is required, not necessarily their purchase invoice.
The original Community licence stays with the haulier. A certified true copy must be kept in the vehicle and presented for inspection.

Subject to the stated conditions, the driver attestation concerns drivers who are neither nationals of a Member State nor long-term residents. An Italian driver is an EU national and does not need it for that reason.

The quiz marks this FALSE: under the paper system a simple photocopy did not replace the original licence. Since 2026 the licence is digital and must be valid; its system-generated information document is available on board digitally or printed for inspection.
ECMT licences are annual or short-term, not valid for five or ten years. The current guide sets a 30-day validity for short-term licences.

A certified copy of the registration document is not the document accompanying the ECMT licence. The system instead provides for licence and journey documentation and the relevant vehicle technical certificates.
ECMT refers to the multilateral licensing system for certain international goods transport. ATP concerns international carriage of perishable foodstuffs and the associated equipment.
For professional bus driving subject to the requirement, a valid passenger CQC qualification is needed in addition to the licence. The driver must be able to prove the qualification during a check.
A truck must have compulsory third-party liability insurance to circulate on roads. It covers damage caused to third parties by its circulation.
The driver’s personal card is used in the digital tachograph while driving to record activities. It must therefore be available for use and inspection.
The driver card identifies its holder and also records the driving licence number at the time of issue. It is not itself a driving licence.
In Italy, the competent chambers of commerce issue tachograph cards and also handle their renewal and replacement.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but whether a green card is needed depends on the country: for example, it is not required in Switzerland for an Italian-registered vehicle. Check the coverage and documents required for the destination.
Driving a trolleybus requires a specific certificate of fitness, distinct from the driving licence for the corresponding category. In the quiz’s terminology, USTIF issues the certificate.
The CQC qualification is valid for five years and is renewed through periodic training. The driving licence has its own renewal rules.
The CQC qualification is renewed every five years after the required periodic training; renewal keeps the professional qualification valid.
The certified copy connects the bus to the undertaking’s authorisation. The law requires it to be kept aboard each bus registered under that authorisation.
Renewing the CQC requires attendance at the prescribed periodic training. It updates the driver’s professional qualification.
Under current rules, the KD professional certificate is not the qualification required for professional bus driving. The appropriate driving licence and, where required, the passenger CQC are needed.
The CQC is renewed through periodic training; a medical examination instead concerns renewal of the driving licence under its own rules. The two procedures and expiry dates are separate.
In Italy, the competent chamber of commerce issues the tachograph card, not the Civil Motorization Office.
The trolleybus driving fitness certificate is not issued by the Prefecture. The quiz identifies USTIF as the competent office.
ATP concerns equipment for transporting perishable foodstuffs, not a professional certificate for driving trolleybuses. A specific driving fitness qualification is required for a trolleybus.
A passport is not always necessary: an EU citizen can travel to other Member States with a valid national identity card for travel. Rules for non-EU nationals may differ.
The driver tachograph card expires: in Italy it is valid for five years and must be renewed.
The driver card has its own expiry date: it normally lasts five years from issue. The driving licence has its own validity periods, so the dates do not necessarily coincide.
The Italian driving licence is issued by the competent motor vehicle office, not by the Prefect.

For an international regular service requiring authorisation, the competent authority of the departure state issues it. The original or a certified true copy must accompany the vehicle for inspection.
The journey form documents the occasional service: the company or driver completes it before departure and the original remains on board during the journey.
The type of service is one of the details identifying the occasional transport on the journey form.
The main itinerary identifies the route of the occasional service and is required on the journey form.
The form identifies the carrier or carriers providing the service; the company name serves this purpose.
For occasional cabotage the journey form accompanies the service: the original stays on the vehicle and must be shown to inspectors.
For occasional cabotage the form states the departure and arrival points, identifying the route of the service.
For occasional cabotage the departure and service end dates must be entered, defining the journey documented.
A copy is not enough: for an occasional service the original journey form stays on the vehicle and is shown at inspections; the copy stays with the company.
The form identifies the drivers but does not require the number and category of their driving licence or CQC. It documents the service and its itinerary instead.

The specific control document for an occasional service is the journey form. A certified copy of the last inspection result specifically is not prescribed: technical inspection rules permit the certificate or a copy, when available.
The journey form for occasional cabotage identifies the service, places and dates, but the model does not require a named passenger list.

For an international regular service, the authorisation or a certified copy is carried on board; it also specifies the stops and timetable. The claim that an original control document must contain both the timetable and fares is incorrect; fares must be available to users.
For an international regular service the document on board is the authorisation or a certified true copy, not a control document listing passengers.
A fallen load can obstruct traffic: the driver must remove it and clear the way as far as possible.
If the vehicle cannot be moved, the obstruction remains a danger to approaching traffic and must be signalled to other road users.

Outside built-up areas the triangle warns of a stopped vehicle in the specified conditions, for example when it cannot be seen from a sufficient distance. The obstruction must in any case be signalled.

For a small leak, you can try to stop it without exposing yourself to danger and by following the instructions for the substance; alternatively, you can contain it in suitable containers. If the leak is large and cannot be contained, notify the authorities.
Safety instructions help select measures suited to the substance and situation. Follow them while avoiding actions that create further risks.
Calling the police does not discharge all duties: the driver must also clear the way as far as possible and signal the obstruction.
The immediate duty is to clear the way as far as possible and signal the obstruction; there is no requirement to repair the vehicle immediately on the spot.
In built-up areas placing the triangle is not always mandatory. The obstruction must still be signalled by suitable means according to the circumstances.
Dangerous substances must not be channelled into a sewer: when safe and appropriate, prevent their entry and contain the spill instead.
Clear the obstruction as promptly as possible and warn other road users; also inform the road authority or the police.
Even when only property is damaged, a person involved in an accident connected with their conduct must stop and give the injured parties their details and other useful information.
Stopping and providing useful information helps the injured parties reconstruct what happened and pursue their claims, even when no one is injured.
The form collects the details of both vehicles and the circumstances in one document, making it easier to report the accident to the insurer.
The date, place and circumstances identify the accident and describe how it happened; the form has fields for them.
The form has driver details for each vehicle, identifying who was driving at the time of the collision.
The owner may be someone other than the driver; their details help identify the person associated with the vehicle involved.
Available witness details allow witnesses to be contacted to clarify what happened; the form provides space for them.
The sketch complements the circumstances boxes and helps show the vehicle positions at impact and how the accident happened.
Registration and insurance details link the vehicles to their cover and help process the report.

To clear the carriageway, remove the vehicle as soon as possible; if it cannot be taken off the road, place it at the right edge. Protect safety and, insofar as compatible with it, preserve the traces.
The warning triangle alerts approaching drivers to the vehicle or obstruction when the conditions set out in the Code apply.

Warn approaching traffic promptly without exposing yourself to danger, and notify the police or road authority. Use the warning triangle when required or other suitable means if it is unavailable: remaining to signal by hand is not always necessary.
A person involved in an accident connected with their conduct must stop and provide the assistance injured people need.
If the accident is connected with the driver’s conduct and people are injured, failure to assist is punishable by imprisonment; fleeing an accident involving personal injury is also punishable.
Fleeing an accident connected with one’s conduct can lead to arrest when people are injured; the rules differ when only property is damaged.
For negligent personal injury, a driver who stops, gives the necessary assistance and immediately makes themselves available to the judicial police is not subject to arrest in the act.
If the carriageway is obstructed, warn others and inform the road authority or a police body. If you cannot clear the road, their intervention can help manage the obstruction.
If the other vehicle’s insurance details cannot be obtained, the authorities may be called to establish the necessary information.
If people are injured, stop and provide assistance; call medical emergency services. It is also prudent to notify the police so they can respond and help manage the incident.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but the rule does not always forbid moving vehicles before police measurements. Help injured people and preserve traces as safety allows; where only property is damaged, avoid obstructing traffic as far as possible.
It is not optional: even with property damage alone, a person involved in an accident connected with their conduct must stop and give their details to the injured parties.
This is more than advice: stopping and providing personal details are obligations even when an accident connected with one’s conduct causes only property damage.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but a CAI accident form can also be used when more than two vehicles are involved: IVASS instructions provide for two forms for three vehicles. Using the form is distinct from the conditions for direct compensation.
The place and circumstances are not enough: the form also asks for other information, including the date and identification of the vehicles and insurers.
The other driver's details alone are not enough: the form also records the vehicles, policyholders, insurers and circumstances of the accident.

The quiz marks this FALSE. Complete all available details: the form also provides for the owner when different from the policyholder. The field alone does not prove a universal obligation to have every owner detail; if the other party will not sign, record at least the registration number and insurer.
A witness is not excluded simply because they were a passenger: record the details of people who witnessed the event, including passengers.
The two sides identify both vehicles and their respective information: the right side is not optional simply because it is on the right.
Columns A and B distinguish the two vehicles; they do not automatically assign fault. Each driver uses the column for their vehicle.
There is no permission to leave the danger in place for an hour: make traffic safe and, where possible, avoid obstructing it.
A warning triangle is not automatically required after every accident: its use depends on the vehicle's position, visibility and road conditions.
Do not force every driver to turn around. Instead, take appropriate measures to protect traffic from the danger created by the substance.
Stopping is not enough: anyone involved in an accident connected to their conduct must also provide necessary assistance to anyone injured.
When there is only property damage, failure to stop carries an administrative penalty; imprisonment for failing to stop applies to an accident involving injury.
Insurance does not remove the consequences of fleeing: if people are injured, failure to stop can be a crime and may lead to arrest in the cases provided by law.
Property damage exceeding €5,000 alone does not make the owner liable to imprisonment. Any liability depends on the facts and violations committed.
Do not wait until more than three people are injured: even one injured person may require emergency assistance and intervention by the authorities.

Failure to produce the insurance policy does not by itself require a call to the authorities: vehicle details can be recorded and coverage checked. Police assistance can be requested if problems arise.
Even one injured person needs attention: provide assistance and, as needed, call 112 and inform the police.
Helping injured people alone does not authorize destroying evidence: as far as safety permits, preserve the scene and traces useful to the investigation.
Hazard lights warn other road users of the broken-down vehicle and the danger in the tunnel.
If the vehicle can still be moved, reaching an emergency lay-by takes it away from the lane used by other traffic.
Where possible, the emergency lane allows the vehicle to stop outside the traffic lanes.
A stopped vehicle is a hazard in a tunnel: quickly request assistance via 112 or an SOS phone.
Hazard lights are necessary, but stopping immediately in a traffic lane is not the right choice if a safer place can be reached.
Do not rely on nearby drivers: signal the breakdown and request assistance through 112 or an SOS phone.
Towing by a passing motorist is not allowed on a motorway: request an authorized recovery service.
Do not simply wait for your own mechanic: on a motorway, signal the breakdown and request authorized assistance.
Hazard lights warn approaching drivers that traffic in the tunnel is stopped or moving very slowly.
After an accident in a tunnel, switch off the engine and leave the key in the ignition so emergency services can move the vehicle if necessary.
A reflective vest or straps make a person leaving the vehicle more visible to other drivers.
Alert the emergency services immediately, preferably using the tunnel emergency telephone if available, so they can respond quickly.
After calling the emergency services, give injured people first aid within your abilities and without exposing yourself to danger: it can help preserve life until professionals arrive.

Sounding the horn continuously is not the prescribed response: hazard lights warn other vehicles, while emergency services must be called. The horn should be used sparingly and under the conditions prescribed for safety.

Chocks prevent the vehicle from moving; they do not signal the accident. Securing the vehicle, for example by applying the brake, and calling emergency services take priority; getting out into traffic solely to place chocks is not an automatic response.

In a tunnel, hazard lights warn other drivers; there is no automatic duty to sound short horn blasts. A brief horn signal may be used when safety conditions permit; contact emergency services separately.
Do not make a U-turn in a tunnel: stop the vehicle safely and alert the emergency services.

Unloading immediately is not the priority: the load could be unstable and the operation could expose people to danger. Alert emergency services and help injured people; assess any unloading under safe conditions.
A fallen load can endanger approaching traffic: the driver must remove it and promptly clear the road as far as possible.

A load obstructing the carriageway must be signalled with the triangle or, if it is unavailable, with other suitable means: advance warning lets approaching drivers notice the obstacle and slow down in time.
An obstruction can endanger approaching traffic: the driver must remove it and promptly clear the road as far as possible.
A STOP sign is not the warning to use: mark the obstruction with the triangle or, if unavailable, other suitable means.
Remaining in the vehicle is not enough: the driver must try to clear the road, signal the danger and notify the road authority or police.
There is no requirement to set out flares: signal the danger with the triangle or, if unavailable, other suitable means.
The driver must promptly clear the road as far as possible by moving the vehicle: approaching vehicles may collide with an obstruction in the carriageway.

Push the vehicle off the carriageway; if that is impossible, place it at the right edge, parallel to the road. This frees as much space as possible for approaching traffic and reduces the risk of a collision.
Whatever its cause, an obstruction can endanger approaching traffic: the driver must remove it and promptly clear the road as far as possible.
Light traffic does not remove the obligation: clear the road as far as possible and move the vehicle off the carriageway or to its right edge.
Do not leave the load on the road to reconstruct the event: remove the obstruction as far as possible and signal the danger.
The rule requires clearing the road as far as possible, not that the driver can quickly repair every heavy-vehicle breakdown.
Besides signalling the danger, the road user must notify the road authority or a police body so they can take action to make traffic safe.
If the vehicles cannot be removed, signal the danger with the triangle or, if unavailable, other suitable means: advance warning lets approaching drivers notice the obstacle and slow down in time.
Notifying the police does not replace warning others: also signal the danger with the triangle or, if unavailable, other suitable means.
Warning others does not replace notification: also inform the road authority or a police body.
The sign warns approaching traffic in advance of the contaminated area. If necessary it is placed even in the center of the carriageway so the danger on the road can be noticed.
As well as placing the triangle, use hand signals to warn vehicles approaching from the side not covered by it and prevent them from crossing the danger area.
Remove the substances or, if possible, cover them with suitable material such as sand, earth or sawdust to restore grip.
Sound signals do not replace the triangle: warn of the area with the portable sign and take the other prescribed precautions.

There is no general duty to divert traffic while waiting for the road authority. Instead, give advance warning, use hand signals to stop vehicles approaching from the side not covered by the sign, and remove the substance or, if possible, restore grip.
Outside built-up areas at night, if the rear position or hazard lights are missing or insufficient, the triangle warns approaching drivers of the vehicle stopped on the carriageway.
Outside built-up areas at night, the triangle gives advance warning of a fallen load that cannot be removed, alerting approaching drivers to the obstacle on the carriageway.
Outside built-up areas, even in daylight, if a stopped vehicle cannot be seen clearly from 100 meters, the triangle warns approaching drivers in advance.
Outside built-up areas, even in daylight, if a fallen load cannot be seen clearly from 100 meters, the sign warns approaching drivers of the obstacle in advance.
Vehicles classified as autoveicoli under Italian law, such as cars, buses and trucks, must carry a warning triangle for use when stopped in the prescribed situations.
Place the triangle at least 50 metres behind the vehicle or obstacle, except where an intersection is closer; it must also be visible from 100 metres.
If an intersection is less than 50 metres away, place the triangle behind the vehicle where it can best be seen, rather than rigidly applying the usual distance.
The triangle must be fully visible to approaching drivers from at least 100 metres; this sighting distance is distinct from its distance behind the obstacle.
It is not optional: outside built-up areas at night, a vehicle stopped on the carriageway must be signalled when its rear lights are missing or ineffective.

150 meters is not the prescribed threshold. Outside built-up areas, the regulation specifies 100 meters for visibility in daylight: not seeing the vehicle at 150 meters does not necessarily mean it cannot be seen at 100. At night, advance warning is required if the rear position or hazard lights are missing or insufficient; the Road Code also requires advance warning at night if the vehicle cannot be seen from a sufficient distance.
It is not optional: outside built-up areas a fallen load not clearly visible from 100 metres must be signalled even by day, even if it occupies only one lane.
The specific triangle rule for a stopped vehicle with missing or ineffective lights applies to carriageways outside built-up areas; it does not automatically apply inside them.
Place the triangle on the road behind the obstacle, not on top of the load, to warn approaching vehicles in time.
The triangle must be fully visible to approaching vehicles from at least 100 metres; 50 metres is the ordinary minimum distance behind the obstacle.
Place the triangle in the same lane occupied by the vehicle or obstacle, to warn of the occupied part of the carriageway.
Place the triangle on the carriageway at least one metre from its outer edge, in the lane occupied by the vehicle or obstacle.
Place the triangle in the lane occupied by the vehicle or load, not necessarily in the lane immediately to its left.
The one metre is measured from the outer edge of the carriageway, not from the line separating directions of traffic.
In the prescribed stopped-vehicle situations, whoever places the triangle must use retroreflective devices to be visible; the driver wears a high-visibility vest or braces.
The device must meet the prescribed technical characteristics and approval requirements so that the person placing the warning is visible.
In the prescribed cases, the vest or reflective braces are also required on emergency lanes and in lay-bys: they help approaching drivers see the person placing the warning.
In the prescribed cases, the driver must put on the vest or reflective braces before getting out and walking on the road, so approaching drivers can better see the person placing the warning.
In the prescribed cases the vest or reflective braces are not optional: they make the person setting out the warning visible to other road users.
In the prescribed cases the duty also applies on emergency lanes and in lay-bys: the vest or braces make the person placing the warning visible.

A nighttime breakdown in a built-up area alone does not trigger the obligation to wear a reflective vest or braces. The rule links that obligation to the circumstances requiring advance warning with a triangle outside built-up areas.
The general rule permits only one vehicle to be towed and only one towing vehicle; exceptions include certain exceptional transports.
A motor vehicle may tow a vehicle unable to move because of a breakdown, using a secure connection and safe driving; the motorway ban does not apply on the ordinary roads mentioned.
In an emergency a chain may be used, provided the connection is strong and marked so other road users can clearly see it.
In an emergency a rigid bar may be used, provided the connection is strong and marked so other road users can clearly see it.
In an emergency a suitable cable may be used, provided the connection is strong and marked so other road users can clearly see it.
In an emergency a suitable rope may be used, provided the connection is strong and marked so other road users can clearly see it.
The emergency towing connection must be marked and visible; the towed vehicle also uses its hazard lights or, if these are unavailable, the panel or warning triangle.
On a motorway, private motorists cannot tow a broken-down vehicle; an authorized roadside rescue service can do so. The armed forces and police are exempt from rescue authorization.
The towed vehicle uses its flashing hazard lights; if these are unavailable, it displays the projecting-load panel or warning triangle facing traffic.
If the hazard lights are unavailable, the towed vehicle displays the projecting-load panel or warning triangle facing traffic, so approaching road users can spot it even without the flashing lights.
The connection must be strong and marked: another road user might mistake a hard-to-see rope or bar for a clear gap between the vehicles, risking a collision.
The hazard-light obligation applies to the towed vehicle, with the prescribed alternatives; the towing vehicle uses its yellow recovery beacon if fitted.
No fixed 60% weight difference is prescribed: the connection and towing arrangements must meet safety requirements.
Not always: towing requires safe conditions, and private motorists cannot tow a broken-down vehicle on a motorway. Exceptions include authorized rescue and certain motorway service needs.
Chain and bar are not the only options: in an emergency a rope, cable or similar equipment is also allowed, with a strong, well-marked connection.
Warning is required: the towed vehicle uses hazard lights or, if unavailable, displays the panel or triangle facing traffic.
The rear fog light is not the prescribed alternative: if hazard lights are unavailable, display the panel or triangle facing traffic.
An electrical cable is not required: the emergency connection must be strong and may use, for example, a well-marked rope, chain, suitable cable or rigid bar.
Emergency towing does not necessarily require an approved trailer hitch: a strong, properly marked connection, such as a rope, may be used.
There is no general one-metre limit: in an emergency the connection must be strong and marked so other road users can clearly see it.
Do not leave only the right indicator on: the towed vehicle uses hazard lights or, if unavailable, displays the panel or warning triangle on the side facing traffic.
The engines’ displacement is not the required criterion: emergency towing requires a strong, clearly marked connection, subject to the other applicable conditions.
A safe place, preferably off the carriageway, reduces exposure to traffic while working on the wheel.

The warning triangle alerts approaching traffic to the stopped vehicle. Outside built-up areas it is required in the prescribed visibility conditions; motorways also have specific rules for a vehicle that cannot be moved.
The parking brake and chocks on wheels remaining on the ground help prevent accidental movement during lifting.
Firm, level ground makes lifting more stable and reduces the risk of the vehicle moving or the jack slipping.
Hydraulic jacks for heavy vehicles can have a 20-tonne capacity; check the actual rating on the jack and ensure it suits the load to be lifted.
A suitable jack can lift the relevant part even when the truck is loaded: check that its rating is sufficient for the actual load.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but the lifting point is not always the frame: use only the point specified by the vehicle manufacturer. Depending on the model it may be a designated frame or axle point; never choose an arbitrary point.
As the vehicle is lowered, the space underneath shrinks: stay clear to avoid being crushed. Do not work underneath a vehicle supported only by a jack.
A suitable, stable base under the jack spreads the load and helps prevent it sinking; the ground must still be firm and level.
Preparing the spare wheel and tools first avoids looking for them while the vehicle is raised and helps limit the time it remains lifted.
Partly loosen the nuts before lifting the wheel, while contact with the ground limits its rotation; remove them after lifting.
Preparing the spare wheel and tools before lifting avoids interrupting the work once the vehicle is raised.
After fitting the wheel, recheck nut torque after a short journey, following the manufacturer’s instructions: the check verifies that the fastening remains correct.
Gradual tightening in a crossed sequence seats the wheel evenly; the final torque must follow the manufacturer’s instructions.
If the dual-wheel assembly has a spacer, refit it correctly: it helps maintain the specified distance between the wheels.
Spacing between dual tires prevents contact while driving: friction generates heat and can damage both casings.
Complete unloading is not always necessary: the jack, lifting point and procedure must be suitable for the actual load and vehicle.
Uncoupling is not a general rule: the procedure depends on the trailer. Some manufacturers specify changing the wheel while coupled; others require uncoupling.
Even on level ground the brake alone is insufficient: chocking the other wheels helps prevent movement during lifting.
Applying the brake does not automatically make one chock sufficient: secure the wheels against movement in both directions as specified for the vehicle.
Do not assume the supplied jack cannot lift a loaded vehicle: check its rating against the actual load and follow the manual.
900 kg is not a general capacity for these jacks: truck jacks rated for many tonnes exist. Check the rating of the jack actually used.
Place the jack at the manufacturer’s specified lifting point, not just anywhere: otherwise it may slip or damage the vehicle.
A suitable wooden base can stabilize the jack; its flammability does not prohibit its use. It must be sturdy and rest on stable ground.
Prepare the spare first, so the vehicle spends less time raised while tools and the wheel are being retrieved and handled.
Prepare the wheel and tools before lifting, so the vehicle is not left on the jack unnecessarily.
There is no general requirement to use a space-saver wheel. The spare must be compatible with the vehicle and the mounting position.
The nuts must not be left loose: tighten them to the manufacturer’s specified torque, avoiding both under- and overtightening.
If the assembly specifies a spacer, refit it in the prescribed position: in some dual wheels a separator disc reduces fretting and corrosion between mating surfaces.
Dual tire sidewalls must not touch. Space is needed to prevent rubbing and allow cooling.
A safe stopping place reduces traffic risk. Whether passengers get off depends on the safety of the location and the passengers.
On the emergency lane, passengers leaving the bus could be exposed to traffic. The decision depends on the actual risks: if remaining aboard is dangerous, move them to a safe place.
The choice depends on conditions: passengers are not automatically asked to get off if doing so would expose them to greater danger.
The warning triangle alerts approaching traffic to the vehicle stopped on the carriageway. The legal obligation depends on the conditions set by the Code, including visibility and location.
The parking brake and chocks prevent the vehicle from moving while it is lifted; otherwise the jack could slip.
Level, stable ground reduces the risk of the vehicle or jack moving during lifting.
Some hydraulic jacks for heavy vehicles have a 20-tonne capacity. The actual rating depends on the model and must not be exceeded.

The quiz marks this TRUE: a bus that is not completely unloaded may be lifted only if the manufacturer’s procedure allows it and the jack and lifting point suit the actual load. Follow the manual: some manufacturers require passengers to get off first.
The quiz marks this TRUE, but the prescribed lifting point depends on the model: it may be on the frame or at a specified axle point. Use only the point and procedure given by the manufacturer.
Opening the valve lowers the vehicle and can crush anyone underneath. Never work under a vehicle supported only by a jack.
A strong, stable board under the base can spread the load and reduce sinking on soft ground. Follow the manufacturer’s procedure.
Having the spare and tools ready before lifting avoids searching for them while the vehicle is on the jack.
Loosen the nuts without removing them while the wheel is still on the ground: contact with the ground helps resist wheel rotation as force is applied.
Prepare everything needed before lifting so the job can proceed without leaving the vehicle on the jack unnecessarily.
After a short distance, check the wheel-nut torque again: insufficient fastening can allow the wheel to loosen. Follow the prescribed interval and torque.
For a cross-pattern nut assembly, tighten gradually on opposite sides so the wheel seats evenly against the hub. Follow the sequence and torque specified for the assembly.
If specified for the wheel assembly, refit the spacer in the prescribed position: some separator discs reduce fretting and corrosion between dual wheels.
The specified clearance between dual tires prevents rubbing and allows the airflow needed for cooling.

A passenger’s request alone does not make leaving onto a motorway shoulder safe: assess traffic and a protected place. Before lifting, follow the manual: some buses require everyone to get off; if safe exit cannot be arranged, seek assistance.
There is no absolute ban on getting off: at a safe location, passengers should get off if they can do so safely.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but that does not mean passengers may always remain aboard: some manufacturers require them to exit before jacking. Follow the manual and seek assistance if safe exit cannot be arranged.
Uncoupling the trailer is not obligatory to change its wheel. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions and secure the combination against movement.
Even on level ground, use wheel chocks as well as the parking brake to prevent accidental movement while lifting.
The brake does not replace chocks: block a wheel that remains on the ground at both its front and rear, following the vehicle instructions.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but jack capacity does not permit lifting with passengers aboard. Some manufacturers require everyone to exit: follow the manual and seek assistance if safe exit cannot be arranged.
900 kg is not a general maximum capacity for heavy-vehicle jacks: much higher-capacity models exist. Check the rating on the jack suitable for the vehicle.
Place the jack at the lifting points specified by the manufacturer, not just anywhere, to ensure proper support.

Wood being flammable does not in itself rule out a board: some manufacturers specify one as a stable base on soft ground. Follow the vehicle and jack instructions, however: others prohibit placing anything under the jack.
Prepare the spare wheel and tools before lifting the vehicle, so it remains raised for less time.
Prepare the tools and spare wheel before lifting the vehicle, reducing the time it stays on the jack.
There is no general requirement to use a space-saver wheel: use a replacement wheel suitable for the vehicle and specified by its manufacturer.
The nuts must secure the wheel correctly: tighten them progressively in the sequence and to the torque specified by the manufacturer, without leaving them loose.
If specified for the assembly, refit the spacer in the prescribed position: some separator discs reduce fretting and corrosion between dual wheels.
The sidewalls of dual tyres must not rub: maintain the manufacturer’s specified spacing to prevent friction and overheating.
The normal width limit includes the load and is 2.55 m. ATP vehicles for temperature-controlled perishable goods may be up to 2.60 m wide.
The normal height limit, including the load, is 4 m. Exceptions include certain urban and suburban scheduled buses on fixed routes.
The normal length limit for individual vehicles is 12 m, including coupling devices; buses and semitrailers have specific provisions.
The normal limit, including the load, is 4 m, not 5 m. Certain categories have expressly specified different limits.
Length is regulated by law: for example, the normal limit for individual vehicles is 12 m. Carrying a load does not remove the applicable limit.
The normal width including the load is 2.55 m, not 2.75 m. ATP vehicles have a specific limit of up to 2.60 m.
There is no general requirement that a trailer or semitrailer be 5 cm narrower than the towing vehicle. The relevant size limits and requirements for the combination apply.

The regulation links the 16.50 m limit to two distances measured horizontally from the fifth-wheel axis: at most 12 m to the rear and 2.04 m to any point on the front of the semitrailer. The law also provides a higher limit for particular intermodal transport, subject to its conditions.
Under the regulation’s criterion, 3 m exceeds the 2.04 m allowed toward the front of the semitrailer: if either condition is unmet, the stated limit is 15.50 m, subject to other applicable rules.
The ordinary limit is 18.75 m for both. Certain rapid-transit articulated buses have an exception on authorized reserved routes.
The ordinary 18.75 m limit applies to the combination, which must also meet prescribed measurements for the loading area and the distance between its ends.

The quiz marks this TRUE: certain specially equipped car carriers are subject to exceptional-transport rules with route and dimension conditions. In those cases the overall length, including the load, may exceed the ordinary limit within the specified allowance; this is not an automatic exemption for every empty carrier.
Air suspension does not itself raise the ordinary road-train limit to 19.35 m: the ordinary limit for the combination is 18.75 m.
There is no general ban based on 60% of the towing vehicle’s length: the dimensional limits for the trailer and the combination apply instead.
Nine metres is not a general limit: a trailer is ordinarily allowed up to 12 m, subject to other applicable dimensions.
10.75 m is not a general semi-trailer limit: the rules allow longer dimensions, taking account of the front overhang and the combination’s dimensions.
Wheelbase measures the longitudinal distance between the two axles, not the transverse distance between wheels on the same axle.
The overhangs are the parts ahead of the foremost axle and behind the rearmost axle; they extend beyond the axle support points.
Track concerns the transverse distance between wheels on the same axle, measured under technical criteria; it is not the distance between fenders.
Wheelbase is measured between axles along the vehicle; the transverse distance between wheels on one axle concerns the track.
An overhang is the part extending beyond the outermost axle at the front or rear; it is not a measure of climbable gradient.
Heavy vehicles can have parts extending beyond their axles. Drivers must account for them because the ends occupy space during manoeuvres.
The approach angle indicates how steep a ramp can be entered without the front touching the ground: a long overhang can reduce this clearance.
At a change of gradient an overhang can touch the ground. Reducing speed helps control the crossing, without increasing the available clearance.
The departure angle concerns the clearance between the rear and the ground at a change of gradient: if insufficient, the rear overhang can touch.
When passing from a descent onto level ground, the rear overhang can touch the ground. Moderate speed helps keep the crossing controlled.
In a turn the front extremity follows a wider path, so the overhang contributes to the width of space occupied by the vehicle.
The ends beyond the axles follow different paths from the wheels. Large overhangs require the driver to monitor more space when turning.
When turning, the ends can move sideways beyond the wheels’ path and reach the pavement: the entire vehicle needs sufficient clearance.
During a turn the overhang can swing sideways and strike someone nearby even if the wheels remain distant. Check the space around the vehicle.
There can also be a substantial overhang behind the rear axle, which moves sideways during a manoeuvre: the front is not the only part to watch.
A large overhang does not automatically prohibit travel on a road with speed humps. Assess the available clearance and cross the change of level at a suitable speed.
Overhangs are parts of the vehicle beyond the axles; during manoeuvres they can swing sideways and require more space, rather than making parking easier by themselves.
There is no general ten-centimetre limit on urban bus overhangs. When manoeuvring, consider the space swept by the ends near pedestrians.
An overhang is the part of the vehicle beyond an axle. Required mirrors depend on vehicle category and fields of vision, not on a general 40 cm overhang threshold.

Rear overhang is the distance from the rearmost axle to the rear extremity. There is no general 40 cm limit: for some vehicles a geometric check permits a much longer overhang, subject to the other requirements.
An interurban bus may also have parts extending beyond its axles: overhangs are not prohibited as such. Applicable dimensional limits still apply.
For a standalone two-axle motor vehicle, the stated limit is 18 tonnes under the statutory conditions; some buses have specific rules.
For three axles the stated limit is 25 tonnes; it may rise to 26 tonnes if the drive axle has twin tyres and air or equivalent suspension, subject to the other conditions.
For four axles the stated limit is 25 tonnes; it may reach 32 tonnes if the drive axle has twin tyres and air or equivalent suspension, subject to the other conditions.
The law also distinguishes limits by number of axles: for example it sets different values for standalone vehicles with two, three and four axles under the prescribed conditions.
For three or four axles, higher limits apply when the drive axle has twin tyres and air or equivalent suspension, subject to the other conditions.
For standalone two-axle motor vehicles the specific rule gives 18 tonnes, not 8 tonnes, under its conditions and subject to applicable exceptions.
For three axles the stated limit is 25 tonnes, or 26 tonnes under the special conditions, not 15 or 16 tonnes.
For four axles the stated limit is 25 tonnes, or 32 tonnes under the special conditions, not 40 or 44 tonnes.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but “type of tyres” is ambiguous: Article 62 also considers how tyres are arranged. For the higher three- or four-axle limits it requires twin tyres on the drive axle and air or equivalent suspension, among other conditions.
There is no single 15-tonne limit subject to an exception for liquids: limits for standalone vehicles depend on configuration and statutory conditions.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but “90% of the fuel contained” is ambiguous if the tank is partly filled. The technical definition uses a tank filled to at least 90% of its capacity, together with the driver and other prescribed elements.
Maximum laden mass comprises mass in running order and payload: the latter is the amount available beyond the mass in running order within the authorised mass.
Payload is the maximum useful load of the vehicle. For category N vehicles, its value appears in the third section of the registration certificate.
The maximum laden mass appears on the registration certificate: F codes distinguish the technically permissible value from the value permitted in the state of registration.
A slope does not change vehicle mass: mass in running order is defined by the vehicle configuration and included masses, not road gradient.
There is no fixed multiplier of 1.2 for mass in running order: laden mass comprises mass in running order and the permitted load, which depends on the vehicle.
Mass in running order is the mass of the vehicle ready for travel; payload is the mass that can be added within the permitted limit. They are distinct quantities.
Payload is the permitted load beyond mass in running order, not the sum of individual axle limits. Axle limits must also be respected.
Payload is the useful load permitted beyond the mass in running order, not the capacity of the tyres. Tyre capacity must also be compatible with the axle masses.

For live animal transport in a vehicle with variable-height bodywork, up to 4.30 m with its load, exceptional transport authorisation is not required if the other dimension and mass limits are met and the route is checked for the required characteristics. The ordinary height limit is 4 m.
The ordinary dimensions of work machines follow Article 61: ordinary height is 4 m, so it remains within 4.30 m. Exceptional dimensions require the special rules.
ATP vehicles may be up to 2.60 m wide; the dimensional limit covers the vehicle including its load, excluding movable mirrors.
The ordinary height limit is 4 metres, not 5.30. Under certain conditions, variable-height vehicles carrying live animals may reach 4.30 metres without exceptional transport authorization.

The ordinary height limit, including the load, is 4 metres. Under certain conditions, vehicles carrying hay bales or rolls may reach 4.30 metres without exceptional transport authorization; 5.30 metres is not the ordinary limit.
Work machines on roads normally have a 4-metre height limit. If functional needs make them exceed it, they are exceptional and subject to the relevant rules; 5.30 metres is not the ordinary limit.
ATP vehicles may be up to 2.60 metres wide. The general 2.55-metre limit is not the maximum for this category.

The ordinary height limit, including the load, is 4 metres. Certain intermodal container transports may, subject to conditions, reach 4.30 metres without exceptional authorization; 4.70 metres is not the ordinary limit.
The ordinary limit on the most heavily loaded axle is 12 tonnes regardless of vehicle type; construction vehicles have different limits and specific conditions.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but includes a boundary that differs from the law: the 12-tonne limit for two adjacent axles applies when their spacing is less than 1 m. At exactly 1 m the general axle-group ceiling is 16 tonnes; lower vehicle or document limits may still apply.
The ordinary legal limit on the most heavily loaded axle is 12 tonnes regardless of vehicle type; the rule does not set it according to the number of wheels on the axle.
The ordinary limit on the most heavily loaded axle is 12 tonnes; 14 is not the limit specified by the rule.
The special total mass limits for construction vehicles apply provided the most heavily loaded axle does not exceed 13 tonnes; the applicable circulation conditions must also be met.
For a standalone two-axle motor construction vehicle, the special laden mass limit is 20 tonnes, with no more than 13 tonnes on the most heavily loaded axle.
For a standalone three-axle motor construction vehicle, the special laden mass limit is 33 tonnes, with no more than 13 tonnes on the most heavily loaded axle.
The special limit is 40 tonnes for a standalone construction vehicle with at least four axles and two front steering axles, provided the most heavily loaded axle does not exceed 13 tonnes.
For a four-axle construction vehicle combination, the special laden mass limit is 44 tonnes, with no more than 13 tonnes on the most heavily loaded axle.

For a construction vehicle combination with at least five axles, the general special limit is 56 tonnes, with no more than 13 tonnes on the most heavily loaded axle; a specific limit applies to concrete mixers.
For a construction vehicle combination with at least five axles carrying concrete in a mixer, the special limit is 54 tonnes, with no more than 13 tonnes on the most heavily loaded axle.
For a construction vehicle the special limit on the most heavily loaded axle is 13 tonnes, not 18.
The special limit for a standalone two-axle motor construction vehicle is 20 tonnes, not 24, with no more than 13 tonnes on the most heavily loaded axle.
The special limit for a standalone three-axle motor construction vehicle is 33 tonnes, not 40, with no more than 13 tonnes on the most heavily loaded axle.
The special limit for a standalone construction vehicle with at least four axles and two front steering axles is 40 tonnes, not 50, with no more than 13 tonnes on the most heavily loaded axle.
The special limit for a four-axle construction vehicle combination is 44 tonnes, not 54, with no more than 13 tonnes on the most heavily loaded axle.
The general special limit for a construction vehicle combination with at least five axles is 56 tonnes, not 66; a specific limit applies to concrete mixers.
For a construction vehicle combination with at least five axles carrying concrete in a mixer, the special limit is 54 tonnes, not 64.
A vehicle is exceptional when its running configuration exceeds ordinary dimension or mass limits for specific functional needs. This characteristic concerns the vehicle itself.

A load can make transport exceptional even if the vehicle alone is within the limits: for example, an indivisible item can make it exceed the permitted dimensions. Other forms of exceptional transport also exist.
A load can make transport exceptional when it causes the ordinary size or mass limits to be exceeded in cases provided by law.
A forward projection of an indivisible load beyond the vehicle outline is one case of exceptional transport.
The ordinary limit for the rear projection of indivisible goods is three tenths of the vehicle length; beyond that the transport is exceptional.
Transport by a work vehicle exceeding the ordinary mass limits in Article 62 is also exceptional; specific conditions apply.
A combination with multiple trailers can be authorized as exceptional transport after technical verification: ordinary towing rules cannot simply be ignored.
A specific transit authorization is normally needed; the competent authority depends on the road network, with exceptions provided by law.
Duration and number of trips distinguish the permits: single for one trip, multiple for several trips, and periodic for a set period.
The permit must require that, in snow, ice, fog or poor visibility, the vehicle be promptly moved off the road to the nearest available area.
For single and multiple permits, when the road wear charge is due, the time and day of each trip are entered before departure; special arrangements apply to reserve vehicles.
For single and multiple permits subject to the road wear charge, the document must be returned to the issuing authority when use ends or it expires.

The quiz marks this TRUE. In the specified cases, the supplementary yellow flashing lights must be on together with the position lights and dipped headlights. The vehicle must also have hazard lights, but having them does not by itself establish a duty to use them continuously: follow the applicable circumstances and permit conditions.

For the specified vehicles carrying straw or hay and variable-height vehicles carrying live animals, exemption up to 4.30 metres also requires compliance with the other limits and verification of the route’s characteristics.
The permit may specify the route and require a technical escort according to the conditions of travel.
Exceeding ordinary mass can cause greater road wear: a charge payable to the road owner is provided for exceptional transport by mass, under the established rules.
Both limits need not be exceeded: a vehicle can be exceptional solely because of excess mass, even if its dimensions are within limits.
Radioactivity of the goods alone does not make transport exceptional: classification depends on the specified cases, such as excess size or mass.
A self-certification of loading does not replace the specific authorization normally required for exceptional transit.
Single permits are not the only type: the law also provides for multiple and periodic permits in permitted cases.
The permit must contain the instruction for snow, ice, fog or poor visibility: the vehicle must promptly be moved to an available area.
The entry rule concerns the time and day of the trip for single or multiple permits when the road wear charge is due; it does not require licence and driver qualification card details.
Where return is required, the document goes to the issuing authority when use ends or it expires.
Exceptional agricultural and operating machinery follow their own rules, distinct from the Article 10 authorization; height alone does not cover all applicable conditions.
There is no general rule requiring travel only by day: the permit may specify periods when it is invalid, which must be observed for that transport.
A difference between the goods and the registration document is not the criterion defining exceptional transport: the specified cases include excess size or mass.
Carrying fresh food on a public holiday does not by itself make transport exceptional: classification concerns the specific legal cases, such as excess size or mass.
Exceptional vehicles are not subject to a blanket ban: they may use motorways under the applicable conditions and with any required authorization.

The quiz marks this FALSE: 32 tonnes alone do not establish that the vehicle itself is exceptional. A three-axle work vehicle has a specific 33-tonne limit; carriage exceeding ordinary mass limits can be exceptional transport, and exemption from authorization depends on conditions.
Explosives are subject to dangerous-goods rules, but carrying them is not automatically exceptional transport: the applicable size, mass or load conditions matter.
Having at least five axles does not exclude the classification: a vehicle exceeding dimension limits in its running configuration for specific functional needs is exceptional.
Not all: for example, a rigid two-axle bus may reach 13.50 m without being exceptional solely because of its length.
For a rigid two-axle bus the specified length limit is 13.50 m; the general 12 m limit for other single motor vehicles does not apply.
For a rigid bus with more than two axles the specified limit is 15 m; articulated buses are a separate category.
For these scheduled services on predetermined routes a height of up to 4.30 m is permitted, above the general 4 m limit.

The quiz marks this TRUE: for certain container transports, 4.30 m is one condition for exemption from authorization, alongside other limits and route conditions. It is not an absolute height cap for every authorized exceptional transport.
The limit for a rigid two-axle bus is 13.50 m; 15 m is the specified limit for rigid buses with more than two axles.

The quiz marks this FALSE for the ordinary limit of a rigid bus with more than two axles, which is 15 m. An articulated bus is a separate category with an 18.75 m limit and can have three or more axles.
There is no single 13.50 m limit for all other vehicles: for example, the general limit for a single vehicle is 12 m, subject to the specified exceptions.
The swept path is the road space swept by the vehicle’s parts while turning, between the innermost and outermost paths.
The swept path measures space occupied while turning; it is not one of the ordinary dimensions in the harmonized registration-certificate data.
The turning test uses a circular ring with an outer radius of 12.50 m and an inner radius of 5.30 m, within which the load must also fit.
The reference ring has an outer radius of 12.50 m; the vehicle, including its load, must fit within it without entering the inner circle.
The test considers the vehicle or combination with its load: it must fit between the two stated radii without crossing either boundary.
The values are swapped: the prescribed ring has an inner radius of 5.30 m and a width of 7.20 m, with an outer radius of 12.50 m.
The swept path concerns space occupied while turning and does not always appear on the certificate: it is not among the ordinary dimensions in its harmonized data.
Length does not automatically reduce the space occupied while turning: a longer wheelbase and larger overhangs can increase the swept space.
The swept path depends on vehicle and steering geometry; it does not increase simply because mass increases.
The prescribed ring has an outer radius of 12.50 m and an inner radius of 5.30 m, giving a width of 7.20 m; the proposed values are not those in the rule.
The reference ring is not the one stated: for motor vehicles and combinations, including buses and trucks, its outer radius is 12.50 m and its inner radius is 5.30 m.
When turning, the vehicle’s parts follow different paths: the swept path covers the space between their inner and outer limits.
A self-steering rear axle helps the rear wheels follow the curve, reducing the separation between paths and therefore the swept width.
On a bend, overhangs sweep arcs outside the wheel paths: longer overhangs increase the space swept by the vehicle.
The swept path is the space covered while turning, not simply the width occupied on a straight road.
A steering rear axle can help the rear follow the bend and reduce the swept path; more steering axles do not necessarily increase it.
In a turn, different parts of the vehicle follow different paths, so the swept path can be wider than the vehicle and its load.
In the exhaust brake described by the quiz, fuel injection is cut off: the engine absorbs energy instead of receiving fuel for propulsion.
In an exhaust brake, a butterfly valve restricts the exhaust flow; the resulting back pressure resists the engine’s motion.
With the exhaust restricted, the piston pushes gases against high back pressure on the exhaust stroke; the work absorbed slows the vehicle.
Engine braking also helps slow the vehicle away from downhill sections; it is particularly useful on long descents because it reduces the load on the service brakes.
With an exhaust brake, the piston meets resistance while expelling gases against back pressure; the exhaust stroke does not become an intake stroke.
The drivetrain must remain connected to transmit engine resistance to the wheels; disengaging the clutch interrupts that connection.
Engine braking absorbs some energy without continuous use of the service brakes, limiting the heat they generate.
Engine braking uses resistance in the engine; a separate retarder can act on the drivetrain. Both help slow the vehicle without continuous reliance on the service brakes.
Electronic control can coordinate the engine brake, retarder and service brakes, distributing the braking demand among them.
Engine braking assists deceleration, but its effectiveness varies with conditions: the service brake is needed to stop the vehicle when required.
In a lower gear, at the same vehicle speed the engine turns faster and can provide greater braking resistance.
When comparing conventional engines without an auxiliary brake, the closed intake throttle of a petrol engine increases pumping losses compared with an unthrottled diesel.

The quiz marks this FALSE. Nearby questions describe combustion-engine braking; the intended meaning here is not specified. The term can also refer to electric regenerative braking: some electric vehicles recover energy while slowing.
The parking-brake control operates the spring parking brakes; it is not the engine-brake control.
In neutral, the engine is disconnected from the wheels, so its resistance cannot slow them through the gearbox. A gear must be engaged.
Engine braking slows a moving vehicle; the parking brake holds it stationary when parked, including on a slope.

In immediate danger, promptly use the service brake as the situation requires: engine brakes and retarders help control speed over time. Some systems integrate them automatically with service braking; do not wait for a separate control.
When comparing conventional engines without an auxiliary brake, the petrol engine can provide more braking: its closed throttle increases pumping losses compared with an unthrottled diesel.
The retarder and engine brake provide additional deceleration, reducing the work required of the service brakes, which remain necessary to stop the vehicle.
A hydraulic retarder dissipates energy in fluid; an electromagnetic retarder uses magnetic forces. They are two distinct auxiliary braking systems.
In the secondary type, the hydraulic retarder is located downstream of the gearbox and connected to the propeller shaft, on which it applies braking resistance.
Braking heats the oil. The heat exchanger transfers that heat to the cooling circuit to prevent overheating.
The oil fill regulates braking: at the same speed, more oil produces greater braking torque.
A lever or pedal can regulate the oil in the circuit and select different braking levels.
The stator remains fixed and produces the magnetic field; the rotor turns with the driveline and is slowed by induced currents.
In the arrangement described, the stator is fixed to the chassis and the rotor discs turn with the driveshaft.
The stator field induces currents in the rotating discs; these oppose their motion and brake the connected shaft.
Energy taken from motion becomes heat in the rotors, which ventilation dissipates into the air.
The rotor pushes oil toward the stator. Fluid resistance slows the rotor and converts energy into heat.
Energy absorbed during slowing becomes heat in the oil, which is cooled by a heat exchanger.
The control can be on the steering wheel, allowing the driver to select retardation from the driving position.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but does not define what “in series” means. Whether and how retarders are installed depends on the design and approval; a universal incompatibility between the two principles cannot be inferred.
In the arrangement described, the stator is fixed to the chassis and the discs are attached to the driveshaft, not to the steering column and gearbox input shaft.
It does not store energy on bends: coils produce a field that induces currents in the rotors, slowing them and generating heat.
The main components are a stator with coils and rotors connected to the driveline; a thermal-magnetic switch and a diffuser do not describe the device.
The retarder absorbs part of the braking without using the service brakes’ friction materials, reducing their wear and heating.
The quiz distinguishes retarders by braking principle: hydrodynamic or electromagnetic. A pneumatic control does not make the hydrodynamic braking principle pneumatic.
The oil absorbs heat during braking and is cooled in an oil-to-water heat exchanger; the metal casing alone does not do this.
In the quiz’s general comparison, the electromagnetic type is heavier; actual weight depends on the model.
In the conventional arrangement, the hydraulic retarder connects to the driveline at the gearbox output, not between the final-drive bevel gears and the half-shafts.
The retarder progressively brakes the driveline but is not intended to lock the wheels immediately; the service brake is used to stop the vehicle.
The retarder and engine brake are distinct endurance brakes and can supplement each other’s braking action.
Besides electromagnetic and oil hydrodynamic types, the Aquatarder uses water as its working fluid.
The retarder is an endurance brake: alone it cannot guarantee a stop in every situation. The service brake is needed to stop.
Dust and mud can obstruct ventilation passages, so periodic checks and cleaning are needed to allow heat to escape.
In the quiz’s general comparison, the electromagnetic type tends to heat up more and must dissipate the heat generated during braking.
In a general comparison of the two types, the electromagnetic retarder is heavier: it contains rotating metal masses and coils, while the hydraulic type uses fluid resistance.
In general, the electromagnetic type withstands lower braking loads and must dissipate the heat produced; the hydraulic type transfers heat to the cooling circuit.
The hydraulic retarder slows the transmission through fluid; it does not directly operate the wheel brake components.

Maintenance follows the manufacturer’s instructions: the hydraulic circuit uses oil and may need specific servicing, but periodic draining for cleaning with degreaser is not a prescribed general procedure.
The retarder can be used together with engine braking: both systems can contribute to slowing the vehicle.
Heat from the hydraulic retarder passes through a heat exchanger to the vehicle cooling circuit, rather than directly to the air.

The quiz marks this FALSE: the electromagnetic retarder’s electrical consumption alone does not establish that the hydraulic type is more common. The systems differ in integration, power supply and heat removal.
The retarder is an auxiliary transmission brake; it is separate from the pneumatic-hydraulic circuit operating the service brakes.

The quiz marks this FALSE: a hydraulic retarder is not easier to install on every vehicle. It may be integrated into the gearbox and cooling system, whereas an electromagnetic one needs electrical connections; installation depends on the model.
The limiter controls the fuel supply to the engine; in injection systems it can control the quantity injected to limit speed.
By controlling the fuel supplied to the engine, the limiter holds speed to the prescribed value without using the normal service brake control.

For N2 and N3 trucks covered by the rule, the general setting is 90 km/h, not 70 km/h; lower settings may be required for dangerous goods.
For N2 and N3 trucks covered by the rule, the general setting is 90 km/h, not 100 km/h.

For M3 over 10 tonnes and N3 the requirement dates back earlier. The specified exemptions still apply.
The plate and certificate document installation and allow it to be checked; inspection also covers the device’s condition and operation where these can be checked.

Driving with an altered speed limiter entails revocation of the licence; the stated suspension applies to other violations under the same provision.
The recognized workshop prepares and signs the installation certificate. It must be kept on board and shown for inspections; it is not issued by the vehicle authority.
The right main mirror gives the driver an indirect view of the road behind on the right side.

The passenger-side close-proximity mirror shows the area close to the vehicle, low down beside the door.

The left main mirror gives the driver an indirect view of the road behind on the left side.
The right main mirror covers the rear on the right; the left main mirror is used for the rear on the left.
The wide-angle mirror broadens the view of the road beside and behind the vehicle; it is not for viewing the roof.

The quiz marks this FALSE. For some heavy-vehicle categories, a Class V close-proximity mirror is required on the passenger side; one on the driver side may be optional. The configuration depends on the vehicle.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but some approved camera-monitor systems can replace mirrors under applicable requirements. An arbitrary camera is not enough: approval and required fields of vision matter.
Exterior mirrors must remain in a usable position to observe traffic behind and beside the vehicle on a motorway too; folding them would remove that field of view.

Without a rear window there is one fewer opening for a direct view to the rear; exterior mirrors help monitor the area behind.
