The quiz marks this FALSE. Wipers clear the windscreen and improve visibility, but a blade stopped in an abnormal position can obstruct it; check they work correctly.
The mere presence of a fire extinguisher does not itself restrict the view; its position matters and it must not obstruct sight.
Choosing toughened glass alone does not make a windscreen opaque: safety glazing must meet optical requirements, including light transmission.
Papers on the dashboard can reflect in the windshield and obscure the view of the road. Keeping the dashboard clear reduces these reflections.
A worn blade can leave water and streaks in the field of view. Replace it when it no longer clears the glass properly.
In darkness, interior light makes the road ahead harder to see. Keeping it off helps night vision.
Condensation on the glass obscures the view outside. Defogging the windshield and side windows before setting off keeps the field of view clear.
Seat height determines the position of the eyes relative to the windows. Adjust it to see the road well while retaining control of the controls.
Mirrors and cameras show the driver areas around the vehicle that cannot be seen directly through the windows.
These aids expand the view, but do not guarantee visibility of every area around the vehicle. A pedestrian or vehicle can remain in a blind spot.
A poorly aimed mirror or camera shows the wrong area and may leave a hazard outside the view. Check that the view is correctly directed.
Correctly adjusted mirrors show the sides better and help drivers spot pedestrians and cyclists while maneuvering, reducing the risk of hitting them.
In a left-hand-drive vehicle, the right side is far from the driver and can hide nearby road users, especially when turning. Check it carefully in the mirrors.
Sun visors can reduce glare from a low sun. Position them without unnecessarily obstructing the view.
Turning on an interior light does not always improve visibility: in darkness it can make the road ahead harder to see.
Wiper blades are replaced according to how well they clear the glass, not whenever the diesel filter is changed. These are separate maintenance tasks.
Completely covering the window eliminates the side view. A sun visor can help with sunlight while keeping the view clear.
Grease is not a windshield cleaner: it leaves a film that can reduce clarity. Clean the inside of the glass too, without leaving residue.
Mirrors and cameras reduce unseen areas, but do not guarantee complete coverage of every angle around the vehicle.
Check and adjust the mirrors from the driving position before setting off so the necessary view is available immediately. There is no need to wait for the vehicle to settle.
Adjustment aims to provide the correct field of view from the driving position. Wind is not the criterion for aiming the mirrors.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but does not explain why. Adjust mirrors from your normal driving position to see the required fields clearly, wearing glasses if needed: wearing them alone does not determine one universal mirror setting.
The tachograph card records the driver’s activities; it does not ensure automatic mirror adjustment. Check the mirror view before the journey.
Interior mirrors allow the driver to observe passengers and the door area from the cab, including during boarding and alighting.
Interior mirrors help check people on board and near the doors; exterior mirrors show people nearby outside. Checking before operating the doors helps prevent impacts or trapping.
Before moving off, the driver also checks the interior mirrors to make sure passengers have finished boarding or alighting and are safe.
A poorly aimed interior mirror can hide the door area. The driver could then close the door or move off without seeing someone still boarding or alighting.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but mirror coverage depends on the bus: an interior door mirror can also show the area immediately outside. Check people and doors using the available devices, without assuming every mirror covers the whole stop.
Interior mirrors help the driver observe the passenger compartment; exterior mirrors show other areas. The interior mirrors must also be adjusted correctly.
Some buses have interior mirrors for observing passengers, so it is not true that buses never have interior mirrors.
A trailer changes the view to the sides and rear: adjust the exterior mirrors to monitor the combination and surrounding traffic.
Before returning to the lane, make sure the rear of the trailer has also cleared the overtaken vehicle, checking the right mirrors and blind spots.
When turning, the trailer follows a tighter path than the towing vehicle. Watching it in the mirrors helps prevent it mounting the sidewalk.
When turning, the trailer follows a tighter path than the towing vehicle and can hit someone on the right. Check the mirrors and account for blind spots.
When turning, the semitrailer follows a tighter path than the tractor. Watching it in the mirrors helps prevent it mounting the sidewalk.
When turning, the semitrailer follows a tighter path than the tractor and can hit someone on the right. Check the mirrors and account for blind spots.
During the turn, the angle between the towing vehicle and trailer changes and can hide the right side of the combination from the mirrors. Allow for this blind spot.
Before returning to the lane, make sure the rear of the semitrailer has also cleared the overtaken vehicle, checking the right mirrors and blind spots.
The mirrors let the driver in the towing vehicle see the sides and rear; mirrors facing the towing vehicle are not required on the trailer.

Exceeding 15.50 metres does not in itself require a camera showing the rear of the trailer. Mirrors are used when reversing with a trailer; detection requirements depend on the rules applicable to the vehicle.
During the turn, the angle between the towing vehicle and trailer changes and mirrors can leave areas out of view. They do not always show the entire right-hand end.
Not every combination must have a special enlarged mirror approved for towing. The required devices and field of view depend on the vehicle.
Coupling a trailer does not automatically require mirrors to be replaced. Check that the available mirrors provide an adequate view and are correctly adjusted.
There is no prescribed “towing” position for every mirror. After coupling, check and adjust the view for the combination.
A trailer can be wider than the towing vehicle and restrict the view of the road behind. Check the view with the combination coupled.
The overall centre of gravity depends on the mass and position of the load: changing its type or placement can change the weight distribution.
A high centre of gravity increases rollover risk; too much weight forward or rearward can unbalance axle loads and impair handling.
Keeping the load’s centre of gravity low lowers the overall centre of gravity and reduces the tendency to roll over, all else being equal.
A lower centre of gravity reduces the vehicle’s tendency to roll over, all else being equal.
If the shoulder gives way under the wheels, the vehicle can tilt and overturn, especially near the road edge.
Curves and a high centre of gravity, for example, increase rollover risk; a level straight road is not inherently the situation most conducive to rollover.
Concentrating weight on one side unbalances the vehicle. Distribute the load evenly and close to the centre line.
The side opposite the driver is not where weight should be concentrated: balanced distribution across both sides helps stability.
A higher center of gravity makes a vehicle more prone to rollover, other conditions being equal.
A crosswind can push or destabilize a vehicle even on a straight road, not just on a bend.
On a bend, the liquid collects toward the outside and its push can carry the vehicle off the road.
When braking, inertia carries the liquid toward the front wall, where it can push the vehicle forward.
Baffles reduce liquid movement during maneuvers; their effectiveness also depends on their arrangement, and they do not eliminate all sloshing.
The openings let liquid pass between parts of the tank, while the baffles slow its movement.
At an intermediate fill level there is both a substantial mass of liquid and room for it to slosh; around half capacity this can make the tank very unstable.
Tank shape changes liquid movement and mass distribution, affecting stability on bends.
In a partially filled tank, liquid can slosh sideways; around half capacity this can greatly reduce resistance to rollover.

The quiz marks this TRUE. Liquid in a partly filled tank can surge and shift the load during manoeuvres; powders also present risks. Overall safety depends on the material, fill level, tank, controls and manoeuvre: powders are not always safer.
During acceleration, liquid moves toward the rear of the tank, transferring more load to the rear wheels.
Going downhill, liquid tends to collect toward the front of the tilted tank and can push the vehicle forward.
Going uphill, liquid tends to collect toward the rear of the tilted tank, increasing the load on the rear wheels.
On a bend, liquid moves outward, not inward; its lateral push can destabilize the vehicle.
When braking, inertia moves the liquid toward the front wall, not the rear wall.
Baffles mainly limit liquid sloshing; their primary purpose is not to reinforce the structure.
The openings are not solely for cleaning: they also let liquid pass through the baffles, which limit its movement.
An intermediate fill leaves room for liquid to slosh; around half capacity this can reduce stability even if the center of gravity is lower.
Shape also matters with a liquid load: it changes liquid movement and stability on bends.
An empty tank has no liquid mass to slosh; a partially filled tank may be more prone to rollover because the load moves.

The driver must check that the load is properly positioned and secured before setting off.

A rear projection of up to three tenths of the vehicle length is allowed only for indivisible items, subject also to overall dimension limits.

The general rule prohibits a load from projecting beyond the front of the vehicle; the allowance for indivisible items concerns the rear.

Three tenths applies to rear projection, not side projection. The ordinary side limit is 30 cm from the position lights, with further restrictions for hard-to-see loads.

Before lifting, the outriggers must bear properly on the ground to support the vehicle and reduce the risk of overturning.

Raise the tipper body carefully, checking that the material flows and the vehicle remains stable. A person can guide from a safe position, never behind the vehicle during tipping.

Unloading an entire row concentrates the weight on the other side and can unbalance the vehicle. Alternating sides keeps the load more even.
Suitable gloves protect against handling risks in summer too: their selection depends on the risks of the work, not the season.

Belts are not exempt from type approval because they are fitted to a bus: the devices are subject to approval requirements.

The exemption applies to conditions or physical impairments that specifically contraindicate belt use and are covered by the required certificate; a diagnosis alone is not enough.

On the urban buses covered by the driver’s cab specifications, the central emergency control is accessible to the driver, who can reach it quickly.

Equipment is not calculated as one small extinguisher per row. For buses with more than thirty seats the circular specifies a foam extinguisher or two CO₂ extinguishers meeting the stated specifications.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but the wording is ambiguous: two 4-kg CO₂ units may meet the historical minimum of two 2-kg units for over 30 seats if suitable and approved. The historical alternative was one 5-litre foam unit: kilograms and litres are not directly equivalent. Check applicable requirements and approved equivalents.
The extinguisher must remain in its designated location and be easy to retrieve in an emergency; winter does not justify storing it in the luggage compartment.
Periodic inspection is entrusted to competent personnel; it does not consist of discharging the extinguisher for two seconds. Work is recorded on its tag.
The six-monthly periodic check is more frequent than a twelve-month check; waiting a year does not meet that interval.
The result must be recorded on the tag attached to the extinguisher so it can be checked on board; keeping a record only at the company does not replace that entry.
The emergency stop button must be within the driver’s reach; under the seat it would not be readily accessible.

The quiz marks this FALSE: seat count and journey length alone do not establish that a doctor or paramedic must travel on board. In an accident, arrange the necessary assistance, including first aid where appropriate.
Emergency exits are not limited to doors: they can also include windows and escape hatches, depending on the vehicle’s configuration.
Clean, intact mirrors adjusted for the driver allow the available side and rear areas to be checked before setting off.
Mirrors extend the field of view, but blind spots can remain where a road user is not visible.
The driver sees some areas directly through the windows; mirrors show other side and rear areas indirectly.
Correct adjustment improves visibility, but does not necessarily eliminate every blind spot around the vehicle.
Mirrors on the two sides show different areas; working mirrors on one side do not restore the view lost on the other.

The quiz marks this FALSE: simply fitting any cameras in place of mirrors is not enough. On eligible vehicles, approved camera-monitor systems may replace specified mirrors subject to the applicable fields of view and conditions; cameras are not universally prohibited.
The manufacturer’s schedule specifies preventive maintenance and its intervals; following it helps keep the vehicle in working order.
Dirt on the windscreen can accumulate on the wiper rubber and impair wiping; keeping the glass clean helps the blades last.
Clean glass and mirrors keep both direct and reflected views clear, so they should be checked before departure.
Wear and pressure affect tyre performance; checking all wheels helps identify damage or incorrect inflation.
Check engine oil, coolant and washer fluid before setting off: they lubricate the engine, cool it and help keep the windscreen clean, respectively.
Checking brake fluid and wiper blades helps identify braking or visibility problems. For batteries with accessible electrolyte, check its level according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Buses are passenger vehicles with more than nine seats in total and require an annual inspection.
The next inspection is annual and normally falls due at the end of the same month as the previous inspection.
Working lights and indicators let the driver see and make the vehicle and its manoeuvres visible; check them before departure.
A leak from hydraulic brake lines can impair braking: look for leaks before setting off.
A dirty windscreen can interfere with the wipers; cleaning the glass and rubber helps them work properly.
The glass must provide visibility from the start: it may become dirty during the journey, but that does not remove the need to check it beforehand.
Compare the pressure with the manufacturer’s recommendation for the vehicle and load, using the owner’s manual; this is distinct from the registration document.
Gearbox and differential oil checks form part of the vehicle’s scheduled maintenance: they are not presumed to be required before every journey. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions.

It is advisable to check brake fluid and wiper blades: an abnormal level can signal a problem and worn blades reduce visibility. Follow the manufacturer’s schedule for batteries with accessible electrolyte.
Buses are passenger vehicles with more than nine seats, including the driver’s: this category requires annual inspection, not inspection every two years.
The normal deadline is the end of the month corresponding to the previous inspection, not the following month.

Driving a vehicle that has not undergone its required inspection entails a fine and suspension from circulation until inspection, subject to the prescribed exceptions; the penalty is not solely withdrawal of the registration document.

Driving a vehicle that has not undergone its required inspection entails a fine and suspension from circulation until inspection, subject to the prescribed exceptions; withdrawal of the driver’s licence is not the penalty for this offence.
Check the devices before departure and monitor them during service; a driver cannot check all of them continuously while driving.

Do not rule out checking for brake leaks because the vehicle belongs to someone else: finding a leak before departure helps avoid using a defective system. The question concerns a driver’s check, distinct from maintenance.
Class A includes vehicles with seats and space for standing passengers, with capacity up to 22 passengers excluding the driver. A capacity below 22 also falls within that limit.
Class B has no provision for standing passengers and includes vehicles with capacity up to 22 passengers excluding the driver. A capacity below 22 also falls within that limit.
Class I covers vehicles with capacity over 22 passengers excluding the driver, with standing space designed to allow passengers to move frequently.
Class III covers vehicles with capacity over 22 passengers excluding the driver, built exclusively for seated passengers.
For interurban service without standing passengers, class III is possible above 22 passengers and class B up to 22, excluding the driver.
A hired service with a driver can use class III or B buses: both are designed for seated passengers but have different capacities.
An urban service can use class I or A buses, which also provide for standing passengers; the classes differ in capacity.
A suburban service can also use class I or A buses, which provide for standing passengers; the classes differ in capacity.
A bus designed with standing spaces may be Class II or A depending on capacity and approval. Class I can also have standing spaces; the competent authority’s authorization matters for line service.
A bus designed for seated passengers can be Class III or B depending on capacity. However, nobody standing on one trip does not prove that the bus was designed without standing spaces.
The national rule imposing an exterior color on buses was repealed; urban or suburban service does not itself impose that color.
A suburban bus can also be designed for standing passengers: the permitted capacity depends on the vehicle’s characteristics.
There is no general limit of ten standing places on suburban buses: the permitted number depends on the individual vehicle and its approval.
Twenty-five percent is not a general limit on standing places on suburban buses: capacity depends on the individual vehicle and its approval.
The quiz marks this FALSE, but the class depends on designed standing spaces and authorization, not just the service name. Standing spaces alone do not establish that Class I is always excluded.
The quiz marks this FALSE, but having no passengers standing on a trip does not mean the bus was designed without standing spaces. Check its class and authorization.
In the quiz correspondence, a touring coach is associated with class III or B, designed for seated passengers; classes I and A have standing places.
Private use describes a use, not a construction class P: bus classes are I, II, III, A and B.
The quiz marks this FALSE. Hire-with-driver service normally uses Class III or B, but a Class II bus registered for line service can be authorized in specific cases; the exclusion is not universal.
A school bus is a bus intended for school transport and subject to specific requirements; that purpose does not automatically make it a special-use vehicle.
M1 identifies passenger vehicles with at most eight seats besides the driver’s seat; no standing passenger space is provided.
M2 covers passenger vehicles with more than eight seats besides the driver’s and a maximum mass up to and including 5 tonnes.
M3 covers passenger vehicles with more than eight seats besides the driver’s and a maximum mass over 5 tonnes.
Category M groups motor vehicles for passengers; the regulation covers vehicles with at least four wheels.
Category M covers motor vehicles designed and constructed primarily to carry passengers and their luggage.
The description corresponds to M2. M1 instead has at most eight seats besides the driver’s.
The upper limit for M2 is 5 tonnes, not 10; above 5 tonnes, a vehicle with more than eight seats besides the driver’s is M3.
With more than eight seats besides the driver’s, a maximum mass up to 5 tonnes identifies M2; M3 requires a mass over 5 tonnes.
There is no M4 category in this classification: the vehicle described is M2.
M identifies motor vehicles for passengers; trailers and semi-trailers belong to category O.
N1 covers motor vehicles for goods with a maximum mass up to and including 3.5 tonnes.
N2 covers motor vehicles for goods with a maximum mass over 3.5 and up to and including 12 tonnes.
N3 covers motor vehicles for goods with a maximum mass over 12 tonnes.
Category N covers motor vehicles for carrying goods; the classification used by the quiz concerns vehicles with at least four wheels.
N identifies motor vehicles designed and constructed primarily to carry goods; trailers belong to category O.
The N1 upper limit is 3.5 tonnes, not 5: a vehicle with a maximum mass over 3.5 and up to 12 tonnes belongs to N2.
N2 covers over 3.5 and up to 12 tonnes. Above 12 tonnes the vehicle is N3, so the stated range does not define N2.
N3 covers goods vehicles with a maximum mass over 12 tonnes, not those up to 10 tonnes.
NP is not an international category for own-account transport: goods motor vehicles are divided into N1, N2 and N3 by maximum mass.
N covers motor vehicles for goods; trailers and semi-trailers belong to category O.
NT is not an international category for transport for others: goods motor vehicles are divided into N1, N2 and N3 by maximum mass.
O1 is the class of trailers with a maximum mass up to and including 0.75 tonnes; above that threshold O2 begins.
O2 starts above 0.75 tonnes and goes up to and including 3.5 tonnes; above that is O3.
O3 starts above 3.5 tonnes and goes up to and including 10 tonnes; above that is O4.
O4 starts above 10 tonnes maximum mass; exactly 10 tonnes is still O3.
O is the category for towed vehicles, including semi-trailers; the subcategories depend on maximum mass.

The quiz marks this FALSE. In Italy a qualifying carrello appendice is treated as an integral part of its towing vehicle; that national treatment alone does not prove a blanket exclusion from EU category O1.
The lower O2 threshold is above 0.75 tonnes and the upper limit is 3.5 tonnes inclusive. Two tonnes is not the boundary defining the category.
O3 covers trailers with maximum mass over 3.5 and up to 10 tonnes; above 10 tonnes is O4. Brakes and suspension do not change these thresholds.
O4 is defined by a maximum mass over 10 tonnes, not by the ability to travel off road.
O identifies trailers divided by maximum mass; it does not indicate that a vehicle comes from outside the EU.
Trailer categories run from O1 to O4 according to maximum mass. There is no O5 category for automatic coupling.
The suffix G is added to category M or N when the vehicle meets the technical requirements for off-road vehicles.
G identifies the off-road subcategory of an M or N vehicle meeting the technical requirements, not its military use.
In a jaw coupling, the jaw on the powered vehicle receives the eye on the trailer drawbar, connecting the two vehicles.
On a turntable-steered trailer, the drawbar is fixed to the rotating frame connected to the turntable on the trailer; this allows the front axle to turn.
On a turntable-steered trailer, the drawbar acts on the rotating front axle frame, allowing the trailer to follow the bend.
The towing eye is the end of the drawbar that enters the powered vehicle’s coupling jaw and is held by the coupling device.
Periodic lubrication of coupling parts subject to friction limits wear and helps movement. Follow the manufacturer’s lubrication points and intervals, including for low-maintenance components.
The crossed connection between the two turntables coordinates steering of the trailer axles through a turn.
Corrected steering helps the trailer follow the towing vehicle’s path more closely, so the combination sweeps a narrower path in a turn.
In the pneumatic system described by the quiz, the control applies the trailer brakes ahead of the towing vehicle’s to keep the combination stretched out.
Overrun brakes are intended for light trailers: above 3,500 kg the higher categories require continuous or semi-continuous brakes.
The breakaway cable applies the trailer brake if it separates from the towing vehicle, stopping it without the normal connection.
The cable connects the emergency device to the towing vehicle: if the trailer separates, tension on the cable applies its brake.
The electrical connection supplies the trailer lights, which must operate together with those of the towing vehicle.
The jockey wheel supports the drawbar during coupling; before setting off it must be raised and secured so it cannot touch the road.
At the set pressure, the regulator releases excess air and stops supply; it resumes when pressure falls.
If the connections break and the supply line loses pressure, the trailer device uses its own air reserve to brake automatically.
In the dual-chamber actuator, a spring supplies the parking force; compressed air overcomes the spring to release the brake.
A mechanical device can compress and hold the spring, releasing the brake when air pressure is unavailable.
The quiz marks this TRUE. On some trailers the identification number can be stamped on the drawbar, but the location depends on the model: check the manufacturer’s instructions.
The trailer has its own air reserve: braking does not depend on a single tank on the towing vehicle.
The control line carries the braking command: it is not always pressurized while driving without braking. The automatic line supplies the reservoir.
The automatic line supplies the reservoir and is normally pressurized even without pressing the brake; the service command passes through the control line.
In a road train the drawbar trailer connects to the towing vehicle’s hitch; a fifth wheel on the towing vehicle is typical of a semi-trailer coupling.
A ball hitch is common for light towing, not the typical coupling for heavy trailers. The coupling must nevertheless be approved and suitable for the load.
An overrun brake uses the trailer’s thrust on the coupling; it can have a mechanical or hydraulic transmission and does not require an air-hydraulic system on the semi-trailer.
The PTFE lining reduces friction on the plate and can eliminate the need to grease that surface; maintain the other parts according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
In pneumatic connections, the coupling halves carry compressed air for brake supply and control, not oil.
The stated pressure is too high: the trailer’s pneumatic connection uses pressures of a few bar, not 25 bar.
There is no general 60 cm limit for a drawbar: its length depends on its construction and must allow proper coupling and manoeuvring.
It depends on the drawbar: a hinged drawbar can move vertically and does not bear a vertical load as a rigid one can.
Lubricate towing couplings according to the device instructions and its operating conditions; do not necessarily wait for the vehicle inspection.
The safety valve stays closed in normal operation and limits excessive pressure when needed; if it were always open, air would escape.
At normal operating pressure the regulator stops the charging phase; the safety valve instead protects against excessive pressure.
At start-up the compressor must be able to charge the system. The regulator exhaust operates at the cut-out pressure, not merely because the engine has started.
The red coupling identifies the supply, or automatic, line; the control, or graduated, line is identified by yellow.
Disconnecting the supply line causes a pressure drop that automatically brakes the trailer. Reservoir air is used to apply the brakes; it does not immediately empty through the disconnected hoses.
A disconnected trailer is braked automatically, but a dedicated release device can release the brakes for maneuvering. First secure it against uncontrolled movement.

A broken control line does not necessarily brake the trailer immediately by itself. In the system described, applying the towing vehicle's brake reduces supply-line pressure and triggers automatic trailer braking.
Pressing the pedal operates the duplex valve, which meters pressure to the two service-brake circuits.
The duplex valve meters the service brake through two separate circuits. If one fails, the other can still provide emergency braking, though with reduced effectiveness.
Releasing the pedal opens the duplex valve's exhaust, reducing pressure in the brake lines and releasing the brakes.
In the system studied, the duplex valve has separate sections for the front and rear brake circuits. This separation lets the intact circuit work if the other fails.
In the towing vehicle's system, the duplex valve sends commands to the triple-control trailer valve, whose output reaches the modulated diverter before the trailer lines.
The duplex valve controls the service brake by pedal. The parking brake is operated separately through the hand control and spring brakes.
The pedal operates the duplex valve for service braking; the hand control operates the spring brakes for parking.
The duplex valve does not store air: it meters air from the reservoirs to the brake circuits. It also has exhaust valves to reduce pressure when the pedal is released.
The duplex valve's exhaust valves also work in normal operation: they open when the pedal is released to reduce circuit pressure.

The duplex valve meters the towing vehicle's service braking; it does not manage a broken trailer control line. In the system described, protection acts on the supply line when the towing vehicle's brake is applied.
The duplex valve controls the towing vehicle's service circuits. If the automatic supply line breaks, the pressure drop activates the trailer's emergency valve, which uses reservoir air to brake.
The trailer does not have a second pedal-operated duplex valve: its brake valve receives the control-line signal and meters reservoir air to the brakes.
The trailer control valve receives signals from both service circuits and the hand control. It therefore also modulates trailer braking for emergency and parking functions.
The triple-control trailer valve is on the towing vehicle equipped to tow: it receives the towing vehicle's commands and sends a signal toward the trailer brake system.
In the system studied, five pipes connect the trailer control valve to the two duplex sections, the hand control, the reservoir and the modulated diverter.
The trailer control valve receives separate signals from the front and rear sections of the duplex valve. If one section fails, the other can still command trailer braking.
In the system studied, a single pipe carries the control valve's output air to the modulated diverter; the other connections provide supply and control signals.
If the control line breaks, applying the tractor brakes causes the modulated diverter valve to reduce supply-line pressure proportionally, bringing on the trailer brakes.
If the control line fails, applying the tractor brakes causes the modulated diverter valve to reduce supply-line pressure proportionally, so the trailer reacts as if the supply line had failed.
If the control line fails, applying the tractor brakes causes the modulated diverter valve to reduce supply-line pressure proportionally and trigger automatic trailer braking.
The modulated diverter valve is on the towing vehicle and controls the lines leading to the trailer.
In this system the modulated diverter valve receives its signal from the triple-control valve, so it is downstream of it.
Two lines run from the modulated diverter valve to the couplings: the supply line feeds the trailer and the control line commands its brakes.
The modulated diverter valve manages the brake lines to the trailer; a vehicle not equipped to tow does not need this connection.
The trailer relay emergency valve is fixed to the trailer frame and manages its air supply and braking.
The trailer relay emergency valve receives both the supply line and the control line from the towing vehicle.
The trailer relay emergency valve connects the supply line to the trailer reservoir and sends air to the brake actuators when required.
If the trailer becomes detached, the supply line loses pressure and the trailer relay emergency valve sends reservoir air to the trailer brakes.
In this system the manual control releases the brakes of the detached trailer by exhausting air from the brake actuators.
The check valve retains air in the reservoir; the inlet valve sends it to the brakes and the exhaust valve allows them to release.
The inlet valve does not necessarily stay open throughout braking: in the WABCO example it closes at equilibrium during partial braking, while it remains open during full braking.
If the control line fails, the modulated diverter valve protects the trailer: when the tractor is braked, it proportionally reduces supply-line pressure and activates the trailer brakes.
If the supply line loses pressure, the relay emergency valve on the trailer responds; the resulting automatic braking is not caused by the triple-control valve.
The triple-control valve allows braking when one towing-vehicle brake circuit fails; the modulated diverter valve responds to control-line failure.
The modulated diverter valve is on the towing vehicle, downstream of the triple-control valve; the relay emergency valve is on the trailer.
When one service-brake circuit on the towing vehicle fails, the triple-control valve maintains the trailer braking command.
The modulated diverter valve responds to control-line failure; when one towing-vehicle service-brake circuit fails, the triple-control valve maintains the command.

In the illustrated WABCO system, loss of the supply line triggers automatic trailer braking using air from the trailer reservoir. Supply and control are separate lines; this alone does not determine control-line pressure.
When the supply line loses pressure, the relay emergency valve uses air from the trailer reservoir to brake it; the triple-control valve does not cause this automatic braking.
The load-sensing valve adjusts brake pressure to the load and can be fitted to either the towing vehicle or the trailer.
In the lever-operated type, the load-sensing valve is fixed to the frame and linked to the axle: the change in distance indicates the load.
By varying pressure according to axle load, the load-sensing valve adjusts braking force between unladen and laden conditions.
On the powered vehicle, the regulator generally acts on the rear brake circuit, adjusting pressure to the load on the axle.
The quiz marks this TRUE. In one conventional layout the load-sensitive modulator supplies the brakes on both axles; arrangements can vary by trailer.
The regulator changes brake pressure according to the axle load, adapting braking force to the load condition.
The regulator senses changes in load through its suspension linkage and automatically adjusts braking pressure.
In the mechanical system, the distance between axle and chassis changes with load; the linkage operates the regulator, which adjusts brake pressure.
When the vehicle is unladen, the regulator reduces brake pressure compared with the fully laden condition, reducing the risk of wheel lock.
The regulator can also be fitted to a trailer, where it adjusts braking pressure to the load.
The regulator acts automatically according to the load; the driver does not need to activate it before departure.
In the system described, the regulator is fixed to the chassis and connected to the axle by a linkage; it is not fixed directly to the axle.
The regulator meters braking according to load; automatic braking when the supply line loses pressure is a function of the trailer braking device.
The regulator adjusts pressure to the load, but cannot replace the trailer’s air reserve if the reservoir fails.
The semi-trailer kingpin enters the tractor’s fifth wheel, which locks it and allows the combination to articulate.
The fifth wheel with its dovetail entry is fixed to a subframe attached to the tractor, distributing stresses across the chassis.
Moving the fifth wheel changes where the semi-trailer rests on the tractor and therefore the distribution of load between the vehicles and their axles.
The fifth wheel can tilt relative to the tractor, allowing the semi-trailer to follow small changes in the road’s slope.
The jaw holds the kingpin in the fifth wheel and the locking mechanism keeps the grip closed under the stresses of travel.
The kingpin coupled to the fifth wheel transmits traction from the tractor to the semi-trailer; the fifth-wheel plate supports the vertical load.
A damaged or worn kingpin must be replaced: repair welding can alter its strength and wear characteristics.
The corrected-track trailer uses two circular turntables linked by a figure-eight cable, which coordinates axle steering.
The trailer relay emergency valve controls the semi-trailer brakes along with the tractor’s brakes and applies them automatically if the air supply is lost.
The road tractor couples to the semi-trailer by a fifth wheel and kingpin; a coupling jaw and drawbar are used to couple a trailer.
The semi-trailer rests on the fifth wheel and transfers a substantial part of its mass to the tractor, not a minimal part.
The powered vehicle and trailer are connected by a coupling jaw and drawbar; a fifth wheel and kingpin connect a road tractor to a semi-trailer.
The fifth-wheel lead is a technical value recorded on the registration document; its position affects load distribution.
The kingpin must be properly retained in the fifth wheel: excessive play causes shocks and instability and is not needed for turning.
On couplings requiring grease, the kingpin and fifth-wheel plate must be lubricated as instructed: grease reduces wear on contacting surfaces.

The fifth-wheel position determines how the load is distributed between axles and is not changed at will according to the road. Even with a sliding fifth wheel, the position must follow the vehicle’s limits and instructions.
Load placement changes the vertical force on the hitch: poor distribution can make the combination sway and become unstable.
With an overrun brake, the towing vehicle slows before the trailer’s thrust applies its brakes, so the trailer brakes with a short delay.
Trailers up to 3.5 tonnes normally use overrun brakes: when the towing vehicle slows, the trailer’s thrust operates the drawbar control and the wheel brakes.
An overrun brake can transmit the force produced by compression of the drawbar device hydraulically to the wheels.
An overrun brake can use mechanical transmission: compression at the drawbar moves linkages and cables that apply the wheel brakes.

Trailers of limited mass normally use an overrun brake; in the mechanical version, thrust on the drawbar applies the brakes through linkages. A relay emergency valve, which controls braking in a pneumatic system, is therefore unnecessary.

Trailers of limited mass normally use an overrun brake; in the mechanical version, thrust on the drawbar applies the brakes through linkages. A modulator that adjusts pneumatic pressure according to the load is therefore unnecessary.
The system can be mechanical: in an overrun brake, thrust on the drawbar can operate the wheel brakes through levers and linkages.
The system is not limited to mechanical transmission: an overrun brake can also transmit force hydraulically to the wheels.
After coupling, raise the jockey wheel and secure it in its travel position rather than leaving it on the ground.
Manual uncoupling does not replace the parking brake: apply it and secure the trailer before leaving it. The breakaway device serves a different purpose.
The crankshaft is a key component: through the connecting rods it converts the pistons’ reciprocating motion into usable rotation.
The air filter traps incoming dust and particles, protecting both gasoline and diesel engines.
In four-stroke engines of both types, valves control the incoming charge and the exit of combustion gases.
The toothed belt or chain synchronizes the camshaft with the crankshaft; the cams open the valves at the right time.
Automatic control adjusts spark timing in a gasoline engine and injection timing in a diesel to operating conditions.
The muffler reduces exhaust noise: an expansion chamber lets the gases expand and reduces sound pulses.
The piston moves back and forth; the crankshaft rotates, converting that reciprocating motion into rotation through the connecting rod.
There is no universal 20,000 km interval: replace the timing belt according to the vehicle manufacturer’s schedule.
They are separate components: the crankshaft converts piston motion into rotation; the driveshaft carries torque between drivetrain components.
A diesel engine can have a turbocharger: the turbine uses exhaust gases to drive a compressor that compresses the intake air.
A diesel engine also needs an oil lubrication system to protect moving parts; diesel fuel does not replace it.
Using gas does not always mean more engine maintenance: needs depend on the model and its maintenance schedule, with specific checks also required for the gas system.
In both, fuel burns inside the engine; the method of ignition differs.
In a diesel engine, injected fuel burns in hot compressed air inside the cylinder.
Internal combustion engines can be two-stroke or four-stroke: the number of piston strokes per cycle differs.
In a piston engine, the cylinder houses the piston and bounds the space where compression and combustion occur.
Hot combustion gases expand and push the piston, producing mechanical work.
A spark-ignition engine can use petrol or, with a suitable fuel system, methane-rich natural gas.
In common reciprocating engines, the piston moves in the cylinder and is pushed by combustion gases.
In a four-stroke engine, intake, compression, combustion with the power stroke, and exhaust follow in sequence.
The cams actuate the valves at the intended time; springs close them.
In a conventional four-stroke engine, the valve gear includes at least one intake and one exhaust valve per cylinder.
The throttle regulates intake airflow in response to the accelerator demand, affecting power.
If synchronization is lost, pistons and valves can collide in some engines and suffer serious damage.
The chain synchronizes the crankshaft and camshaft so the valves operate at the right time relative to the pistons.

In premixed or port-injection systems, the cylinder draws in air and fuel. The quiz marks this VERO, but in direct injection the fuel enters the cylinder directly, so the mixture need not be drawn in already prepared.
In a spark-ignition engine, the mixture burns inside the cylinder and the gases push the piston.
The Otto cycle is associated with spark ignition: a spark ignites the compressed mixture.
Not all have injectors: a carburettor can prepare and supply the air-fuel mixture.
A spark plug ignites the mixture in a spark-ignition engine; in a diesel engine the fuel ignites in hot compressed air.
The connecting rod joins the piston to the crankshaft, not the camshaft, and transmits motion.
The piston moves back and forth in the cylinder; the mechanism transmits this motion to the rotating crankshaft.
The useful process goes the other way: combustion produces hot gases that move the piston and generate work.
A spark initiates ignition of the mixture; in diesel compression ignition, heat from compressed air starts it.
An even number is not required: single-cylinder engines also exist.
Internal combustion produces exhaust gases and noise: the silencer reduces exhaust noise.
A spark-ignition engine is also an internal combustion engine: combustion occurs inside both engines.
Diesel engines are also internal combustion engines: fuel burns inside the cylinder, but is ignited by the heat of compressed air.
Engine knock results from abnormal combustion of the mixture, with rapid pressure oscillations; it does not mean the piston strikes the cylinder head on every revolution.
The belt synchronizes the crankshaft and valve timing; if it breaks, the engine can stop or be damaged. In some engines it also drives the water pump, but not always.

The quiz marks this FALSO, but the theoretical comparison needs a basis: at the same compression ratio the ideal Otto cycle is more efficient. A diesel can use a higher ratio and achieve higher practical efficiency.
Diesels generally reach lower maximum speeds: mixture formation and combustion take time, and less time is available as speed increases.
The governor automatically adjusts the amount of fuel injected to control engine speed and prevent overspeeding.
A diesel does not limit its own speed by throttling air as a traditional petrol engine does: a governor must control the fuel.
A spark-ignition engine can generally run at higher speeds: in a diesel, preparing and burning the mixture takes time.
In a diesel, injected fuel ignites in the hot compressed air without an ignition spark.
The principle remains autoignition in compressed air, but the chamber differs: direct injection delivers fuel into the main chamber; indirect injection starts combustion in a prechamber.
The timing system must keep the crankshaft and camshaft synchronized. Some diesels use gears for this connection instead of a belt or chain.
A glow plug is an electric heater supplied at low voltage; it heats the chamber to help a cold start.
When comparing engines, diesel combustion is generally slower: injected fuel must mix with air as it burns.

Advancing injection can give diesel fuel more time to ignite and burn as engine speed rises. The quiz marks this VERO, but actual timing depends on calibration, speed and load; it does not necessarily increase in every case.
The quiz marks this VERO, but immediate switch-off is not universal: some systems keep the glow plugs active after starting, while the engine warms up.
Glow plugs are fitted in the cylinder head to heat the chamber; the dashboard may have an indicator, but not the plugs themselves.
The valves are not all intake valves: exhaust valves are also needed to release burnt gases. A common arrangement uses two for each function.
Narrowing the pipe does not repair a faulty silencer: the exhaust system needs inspection and repair. A restriction increases backpressure.
Glow plugs help cold-start diesels by heating the chamber. In ordinary spark-ignition engines, a spark ignites the mixture instead.
There is no general rule that keeps them on until 80 °C: operation depends on the system and can include post-glow after starting.
A glow plug helps heat a cold diesel; a spark plug instead ignites the mixture in a spark-ignition engine. They are not equivalent replacements.
The diesel cycle uses compression ignition: injected fuel ignites in air heated by compression.
A diesel generally has higher efficiency, not much lower: its higher compression ratio helps it make better use of the fuel’s energy.
The pedal affects the throttle opening and thus the intake air. In electronic systems, the control unit operates the valve using pedal position among its inputs.
In a spark-ignition engine, ignition is commanded by the spark plug, whose spark starts combustion of the air-fuel mixture.
A spark-ignition engine can use natural gas or LPG when fitted with a suitable fuel system: a spark still ignites the mixture.
The spark plug produces the spark that ignites the air-fuel mixture in the cylinder: this is the principle of spark ignition.

Combustion takes time. As engine speed increases, the spark is generally advanced relative to the piston position so combustion occurs at the useful time. The setting also depends on engine conditions.
Injectors supply fuel; spark plugs produce the spark. In fuel-injected spark-ignition engines they have different functions and work together.
The tank stores gasoline. The mixture with air forms in the intake system or cylinder, not in the tank.
As engine speed increases, spark advance generally increases, rather than decreases: combustion takes time while the engine turns. The setting also depends on other conditions.
A natural-gas engine still produces exhaust emissions, and a catalyst helps reduce them. The fuel does not automatically make it unnecessary.
An LPG engine still produces exhaust emissions, and a catalyst helps reduce them. LPG does not automatically make it unnecessary.
In a natural-gas engine the mixture burns inside the engine and the combustion gases produce work, so it is an internal combustion engine.

The quiz treats natural gas as less polluting: in some tests it produced fewer non-methane hydrocarbons than gasoline and fewer nitrogen oxides than diesel. Results depend on the vehicles, driving cycle and pollutant; unburned methane also matters.
In an LPG engine the mixture burns inside the engine and the combustion gases produce work, so it is an internal combustion engine.

The quiz treats LPG as less polluting: in one test it produced fewer nitrogen oxides than gasoline; in another comparison, propane nitrogen oxide emissions were estimated to be lower than those of diesel. Results depend on the vehicles, driving cycle and pollutant; emissions can be comparable with modern control systems.

Exhaust pipes collect gases expelled by the engine and carry them outside the vehicle.

The governor controls engine speed by adjusting the fuel quantity to keep operation within the intended limits. It may be mechanical or electronic.

In electronically controlled unit injectors, an electronically controlled valve regulates injection timing and quantity while the integrated pump generates pressure.
An incorrect spray mixes fuel and air less effectively and worsens combustion. Injectors must therefore deliver and atomize fuel as designed.
An altered spray makes combustion less effective and can increase fuel consumption because some fuel is used less efficiently.

Diesel injection can also be electronically controlled: the control unit manages the injectors and fuel quantity.
Unit injectors can have electronic injection control, even though the pumping action is mechanically driven by the valve train.

Coasting downhill with the engine off is not a procedure for cleaning or adjusting injectors. The fault must be identified and addressed with suitable equipment.
The injection system meters the fuel in response to the driver’s request and engine conditions, not through a dashboard knob.
Holding the accelerator fully down in neutral is not a procedure for cleaning or adjusting injectors. The fault must be diagnosed and addressed with suitable tools.
The inline pump meters and pressurizes diesel fuel, sending it through high-pressure lines to the injectors.

Compressed natural gas has a lower energy density by volume than gasoline, so a full tank of the same volume does not guarantee greater range.
Natural gas, mostly methane, mixes rapidly with air. Emissions also depend on the engine and its calibration; they are not necessarily higher because of poor mixing.
Use a replacement of the specified type and current rating: a different rating can cause unnecessary blowing or inadequate circuit protection.
Fuses are normally grouped in boxes; the vehicle manual shows where to find and access them.
On common blade fuses, the color and number identify the current rating. Fuses with the same rating can therefore share the same color and number.
A fuse protects the circuit by interrupting current when an overcurrent melts its internal element.
The internal metal element is designed to melt under overcurrent, opening the circuit.
The owner’s manual shows where the boxes are and helps identify the fuse for the circuit concerned.
On common blade fuses, the insulating part’s color helps identify the current rating; also check the marked value.
The number on the fuse indicates its current rating and helps select a replacement with the same specifications.
Rated current is expressed in amperes, whose symbol is A; the number identifies the fuse’s current rating.
Different circuits have dedicated fuses, so a fault can interrupt the affected circuit without cutting power to all the others.
Fuse protection is common: circuits are divided and protected by fuses selected for their respective loads.
Accessible fuses can be replaced using the manual and a replacement with matching specifications. If the fault recurs, have the system checked.
A lower current rating is not the required substitute: use the fuse type and rating specified for the circuit.
Not all fuses are replaced at every periodic inspection: locate and replace the blown fuse, and investigate the cause if the problem recurs.
A fuse is an electrical protection device: it opens a circuit under overcurrent; it does not control oil pressure.

The quiz marks this FALSO: on common automotive fuses the number used to select protection gives the current rating in amperes. A fuse also has a voltage rating, which can be marked; it cannot always be ruled out.

The quiz marks this FALSO: when selecting a fuse, check its current rating in amperes (A). Fuses also have a voltage rating, and V is the correct symbol for volts; the quiz answer does not invalidate that unit.
The color indicates the fuse’s current rating, not that replacement is reserved for a workshop. Follow the vehicle instructions and use a matching replacement.
A fuse that blows repeatedly suggests a possible fault: have the circuit checked and use the specified rating, rather than choosing a lower one.
Replacing a fuse with wire would remove overcurrent protection. If the fuse blows repeatedly, have the circuit checked.
Before replacing a fuse, switch off the ignition and electrical equipment, then use a replacement with matching specifications.
Heavy vehicles also use fuses with different current ratings, selected for the circuits they protect.
An ordinary blade fuse breaks the circuit under excess current and has no polarity. Use the specified type and current rating.
Diesel vehicles also have electrical circuits protected by fuses. The absence of spark ignition does not eliminate the electrical system.
In some layouts the accessory belt drives both the alternator and coolant pump, circulating coolant while the engine turns.
The belt transfers engine movement to the alternator pulley, allowing it to generate electricity.
The alternator initially generates alternating voltage; a rectifier converts it for the vehicle electrical system.
The red charging light signals a charging system problem, possibly an alternator fault. The light alone does not identify the exact cause.
A loose belt can slip and fail to drive the alternator properly, causing insufficient charging. It is one possible cause.
The alternator produces alternating voltage, while the battery charges with direct current: the rectifier converts it.
With the engine running, the charging light normally goes out. If it stays on, a possible charging problem requires investigation; the light alone does not certify every component.
The alternator’s diode rectifier converts alternating voltage into direct voltage for the electrical system and charging.
The battery has a state of charge: the alternator generates energy for the system and recharges the battery; it does not store energy like a battery.

The quiz marks this FALSO, but diesel engines without an alternator exist, for example with mechanical starting. In road vehicles equipped with a charging system, the alternator supplies the electrical system and recharges the battery.
The alternator and battery have complementary roles: the former powers electrical loads and charges the latter, which stores energy for starting, for example.
The proposed division is wrong: with the engine running, the alternator powers electrical loads, including lights, and charges the battery. The battery also supplies energy for starting.
In the quiz the charging fault light is red, not orange. It can indicate a problem with the alternator or another charging system component.
An alternator fault does not necessarily stop the engine immediately: the battery can temporarily power the system, but discharges if not recharged.
The alternator powers the system and charges the battery simultaneously: alternating current describes the kind of current generated, not alternating recipients.
No button is needed to select between engine and battery: the charging system powers electrical loads and charges the battery, regulating output according to conditions.
In the quiz system, the engine drives the alternator by belt: when the engine stops it generates no current and loads draw on the battery.
In the quiz vehicles, both gasoline and diesel engines use an electric starter to turn the engine initially so it can start.
The starter is an electric motor: it receives energy from the battery and turns the combustion engine through the pinion.
A discharged battery may not supply the current needed by the starter. Faulty connections or components can also prevent starting.

The pinion must mesh with the flywheel ring gear to turn the engine. If damaged, it may fail to engage properly, leaving the starter spinning without cranking. The quiz also mentions its thrust bearing; that specific cause is not confirmed by the checked source.
The starter is electric and receives current from the battery; diesel fuel instead feeds combustion in the diesel engine.
The starter motor is electric: the relay engages the pinion and closes the circuit supplying it. A hand crank does not operate this motor.
A vehicle with an automatic gearbox can also have a starter motor to start the engine; the gearbox type does not eliminate it.
The starter turns the engine for starting and disengages afterward. It is not run backward to brake.
With the engine running, the alternator supplies electrical loads and maintains the battery charge.
The battery supplies direct current: during discharge it flows in one direction through the external circuit.
The service battery supplies low-voltage direct current; the alternator produces alternating current, which is then rectified.
On batteries with accessible cells, check the level and add distilled water if necessary, following the manufacturer’s instructions.
Sealed batteries do not need routine topping up. Keeping them clean and dry and protecting the terminals from corrosion helps maintain them; use the product specified by the manufacturer.
A clean, dry battery and protected terminals limit leakage currents and corrosion. Use the product specified by the manufacturer on the terminals, such as petroleum jelly if prescribed.
Battery mass increases vehicle weight: for the same route and conditions, it can increase the energy needed to move the vehicle, reducing its range.
Heavy vehicles commonly have a 24 V service system, separate from any high-voltage traction circuit.
The battery supplies direct current, not alternating current. The alternator produces alternating current, which is rectified for the electrical system.
If the alternator is not charging, electrical loads consume the battery’s remaining charge: it does not necessarily discharge instantly.
Do not add antifreeze to a battery. For batteries that can be topped up, use distilled water as directed by the manufacturer.
There is no requirement to use water above 25 °C. For a battery that can be topped up, use distilled water and follow the level instructions.

The quiz marks this FALSO: an engine still being warm does not by itself establish a general prohibition. For a refillable battery, follow the manufacturer’s instructions with the engine off and safe access; sealed batteries are not topped up.
Connecting the terminals directly causes a short circuit and can produce sparks; it does not replace alternator charging.
The battery also supplies electrical loads and accessories, in addition to the engine starting system.
The battery can supply electrical loads with the engine stopped; it does not automatically disconnect whenever the engine stops.
The battery stores chemical energy and supplies direct current, not alternating current.
In a spark-ignition gasoline engine, a spark ignites the compressed air-fuel mixture in the cylinder.
In a diesel engine, injected fuel ignites from the heat of compressed air, not from a spark.
A diesel engine ignites fuel using hot compressed air: it does not require two spark plugs per cylinder.

In a diesel, fuel ignites in hot compressed air; glow plugs help cold starting. Spark-ignition engines use spark plugs. Their functions differ, and the statement does not establish a general rule that one must withstand more heat.
The engine-driven alternator converts mechanical energy into alternating electrical energy; a rectifier converts it for the electrical system.
The light may normally illuminate when the ignition is switched on before starting; if it stays on while driving, it indicates a possible charging problem. Stop safely and follow the vehicle manual.
The drivetrain carries mechanical power from the engine to the driven wheels, allowing them to move the vehicle.
The clutch connects the engine to the gearbox; the gearbox changes the ratio, and the bevel gears and differential transmit motion toward the wheels.
In a rear-engine, rear-wheel-drive layout the engine and gearbox are near the wheels, so the long longitudinal shaft connecting units at opposite ends is unnecessary.
In heavy vehicles the connection can be divided into sections with joints and intermediate supports, transmitting motion despite changes in alignment.
With a front engine and rear-wheel drive, the conventional layout uses a longitudinal shaft to carry motion from the gearbox to the rear axle.
The drivetrain transfers power to the wheels. Positioning and communication systems are used to determine and communicate location.
GPS provides positioning; the drivetrain is the mechanical assembly that carries power to the wheels.
Leaf springs, the steering wheel and the speed limiter serve suspension, steering and speed-limiting functions. The drivetrain instead includes components such as the gearbox and differential.
An electric motor must also transmit power to the wheels through suitable mechanical components, although it does not necessarily need a multi-speed gearbox.

In a conventional mechanically linked permanent all-wheel-drive layout, a center differential distributes drive between axles and front and rear differentials allow the wheels on each axle to turn at different speeds. Other all-wheel-drive architectures can differ.
Disengaging the clutch breaks the connection to the gearbox, allowing the engine to keep turning without driving the transmission.
The drivetrain connects the engine to the driven wheels and transfers the power needed for propulsion.
The gearbox adapts the ratio between engine and wheels to driving conditions, but does not always keep the engine near its maximum-power speed.
Many electric vehicles use a single ratio, while combustion-engine vehicles normally use several. There are exceptions.
The clutch connects or separates the engine and gearbox; the gearbox selects different ratios between rotational speeds.
The clutch allows the engine to be connected progressively to the gearbox or separated from it, for example when changing gear.
With a conventional pedal, releasing it engages the clutch and connects the engine to the gearbox.
It is the other way around: with a conventional pedal the clutch is engaged when the pedal is released and disengaged when it is pressed.
In the conventional layout the clutch is between the engine and gearbox, not between the gearbox and propeller shaft.
These components carry motion from the engine to the wheels: the clutch connects, the gearbox changes the ratio, and the shaft and differential transmit motion to the axle.
Clutch friction allows the engine and gearbox to be connected gradually, avoiding a sudden engagement when moving off.
In a plate clutch the friction surfaces transmit torque when pressed together and can slip during gradual engagement.
Wear of the friction surfaces changes the adjustment. Self-adjusting systems compensate for it; manually adjusted systems must be checked and adjusted according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
A leak from an engine or gearbox seal can contaminate the disc: oil reduces friction and can cause slipping.
If the friction material is excessively worn, the clutch may no longer transmit all the torque and can slip.
A leak in the hydraulic control can contaminate the lining: oil reduces friction and the disc may slip.
The pressure plate spring presses on the disc. If damaged, it can provide too little clamping force and cause slipping.
Continuous slipping produces excess heat: overheating can damage the lining and pressure plate.
A multi-disc clutch can run in an oil bath: multiple friction surfaces transmit torque in a compact space.
In vehicle transmissions, a single-disc clutch is commonly dry: its surfaces operate without an oil bath.
The driven disc of a dry single-disc clutch has friction linings on both sides. They are clamped between the flywheel and pressure plate to transmit torque.
Some vehicles have multi-disc clutches: the multiple friction surfaces transmit torque in a compact space.
In manually operated heavy vehicles, the pedal can operate an air-assisted clutch servo, reducing the effort required from the driver.
A hydraulic control transmits pedal movement through a master cylinder and fluid to a clutch actuator, making operation easier.

The quiz marks this TRUE: an automatic transmission uses a torque converter and automatic selection instead of a driver-operated clutch pedal and manual shifting. It can still contain mechanical gears.
The quiz marks this TRUE for the absence of a conventional clutch pedal, but some automatic torque-converter transmissions have an internal mechanical lock-up clutch.
With a starting gear selected, the automatic system controls clutch engagement using the accelerator input among other signals, without requiring a clutch pedal.
A rigid gear connection cannot replace progressive engagement: when starting, the clutch lets the engine and transmission gradually reach the same speed.
The clutch connects and disconnects the engine and gearbox input; the driveline continues through the differential to the driven wheels.
The driven disc of a conventional dry clutch has friction linings; it is not simply bare steel.
In an automated clutch, an actuator and control unit manage engagement; the driver does not replace the pedal with a simple switch.
In the conventional layout, the clutch is between the engine and gearbox input, not between the gearbox and differential.
Avoiding gear changes does not eliminate the cause of slipping. Have the clutch and its control checked, because continued slipping causes overheating.
Chalk or sand will not repair a slipping clutch. Friction surfaces must stay clean and the cause of the slipping must be found and corrected.
Resting a foot on the pedal can keep the release bearing loaded and accelerate its wear. Release the pedal after changing gear.
In a traditional automatic transmission, the torque converter transmits torque during takeoff and planetary gears provide the ratios; it can still contain internal clutches.
Four-wheel drive concerns the distribution of torque to the wheels; it does not by itself eliminate the need for an engagement device between engine and gearbox.
Steering axles direct the vehicle; their number does not determine the number of transmission clutches.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but moisture and freezing can lock the disc to the flywheel in particular conditions: a GM bulletin documents this for certain models. It is not necessarily common to all heavy vehicles.
A stiff pedal requires diagnosis of the control and clutch components. Removing a spring is not a correct adjustment and can compromise clamping force.
The clutch does not require a dedicated fan: heat produced mainly during slipping dissipates through its components.

Keeping the clutch depressed downhill removes engine braking and reduces control. In a modern vehicle, staying in an appropriate gear with the accelerator released generally uses less fuel than coasting in neutral.
The clutch need not be held down to cool it: when fully engaged, heat from slipping is practically absent. Pressing the pedal downhill also removes engine braking.
A multi-plate clutch is selected according to the torque to be transmitted and the design, not because there are more than four gears.
Press the pedal to disengage the clutch and release it gradually to reconnect the transmission smoothly; releasing it abruptly can make the start jerky.
Each gear selects a different ratio between engine and gearbox output; downstream, the drivetrain carries motion to the driven wheels.
First is a reduction gear: the engine turns more than once for each output revolution. This reduction increases the torque available for starting.
The synchronizer uses friction to bring the gear and shaft speeds together before engagement, making shifting easier and quieter.
A two-range reduction unit can provide two ratios for each gear in the main gearbox, doubling the number of combinations.
Extra ranges provide more ratios to choose from, helping the driver adapt available traction to changes in load and gradient.

The quiz marks this TRUE: a conventional gearbox selects distinct useful ratios to vary speed and torque. This does not establish a universal physical impossibility of duplicate ratios in every design.
More ratios in heavy vehicles help select suitable traction for different loads and gradients; for example, some truck transmissions have 16 gears.
The reduction unit does not reduce the number of available gears: adding a second range can multiply the ratios available from the main gearbox.
The gearbox changes the ratio between the engine and transmission output. The ratio between the drive shaft and axle shafts concerns the final drive and differential.
In the conventional layout the clutch is between engine and gearbox: it connects or disconnects the engine from the gearbox input.
There is no general limit of six gears: some heavy-vehicle transmissions have many more, for example sixteen.
First gear reduces rotational speed: the output turns more slowly than the engine, not faster.
Vehicles used for exceptional loads can also have a gearbox: they need ratios suited to moving very heavy loads.
Selecting a lower gear increases torque at the wheels, useful when a heavy load requires more tractive force.
The gearbox’s different gear pairs produce different ratios between engine speed and output shaft speed.
Changing ratio changes the torque available at the wheels: a lower gear offers greater tractive force for the same engine torque.
A low gear multiplies engine torque more and provides greater force to start the vehicle, at the expense of speed at the same engine rpm.
A greater reduction multiplies the torque delivered to the wheels: at the same engine torque, available tractive force increases.
The quiz marks this TRUE. In some heavy-vehicle manual gearboxes, pneumatic assistance helps gear selection and reduces effort; the linkage and layout depend on the design.
Gearbox oil reduces friction and wear. In splash lubrication some gears dip into the oil and distribute it as they rotate.
Insufficient oil can leave gears and bearings poorly lubricated and cause noise. It is one possible cause, not a definite diagnosis.
A worn or damaged bearing can make noise as the gearbox turns; other faults can also cause noise.
Some heavy vehicle gearboxes have many ratios: for example, 12-speed gearboxes exist.
Some automatic transmissions maintain torque delivery during a gear change, making movement more uniform.
Oil lubricates the gearbox components. Replace it at the intervals specified for that gearbox and its use.
Check the gearbox oil level periodically as the manufacturer specifies, to maintain adequate lubrication.
A planetary gear set is a system of gears; in some transmissions it provides different ranges of ratios.
In meshing gears, rotational speed is inversely proportional to tooth count: the smaller driven gear turns faster.
The larger driven gear has more teeth and turns more slowly than the smaller gear driving it: the ratio reduces speed.
Two meshing gears with the same number of teeth have equal rotational speed in magnitude: the ratio is unity.
A secondary retarder can be mounted on the output side of the gearbox and act on the driveline to slow the vehicle.

The gearbox changes the speed and torque ratio, but a separate final reduction also lies between it and the wheels. Overdrive can make gearbox output turn faster than the engine without proving the wheels do so.
Heavy vehicle transmissions are not normally limited to two ratios: configurations with many gears exist, for example twelve.
At the same engine torque, a lower gear multiplies torque at the wheels more; a higher gear gives less.
Low gears multiply torque more and therefore, at the same engine torque, provide greater tractive force at the wheels.
On an uphill gradient with a heavy load, a low gear may be needed for more tractive force; the choice depends on conditions and is not always the highest gear.
To start uphill with a loaded vehicle, select a sufficiently low gear to multiply the torque needed to move off.
A quiet gearbox can still use gears: synchronizers help engagement but do not replace the gear wheels that provide the ratios.
There is no general limit of five gears: automatic transmissions for heavy vehicles can have twelve ratios.
In a synchronized manual gearbox, use the clutch as instructed by the manufacturer; omitting it is not a fuel-saving rule. Some automated transmissions follow different procedures.
At the same vehicle speed, shifting down makes the engine turn faster, not slower.
At the same vehicle speed, shifting up reduces engine speed rather than increasing it.
To increase engine braking, use a lower gear appropriate to the speed, rather than a high gear.
The tachometer shows engine rotational speed; it does not directly show the drive wheels’ revolutions.
The turbocharger is driven by engine exhaust gases: its operation does not begin only above third gear.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but does not define the cooling arrangement. Some gearboxes can cool oil indirectly through engine coolant; the sources do not confirm a specific combined installation on a construction vehicle.
The gearbox changes the ratio between engine and transmission. In gear, output speed varies with engine speed; it is not kept constant independently of it.
On a descent, keep a suitable gear engaged to use engine braking. Selecting neutral breaks that connection and is not required.
All-wheel drive can send driving force to all wheels rather than only the front or rear wheels. Actual distribution depends on the system.
With front-wheel drive, driving force reaches the wheels on the front axles; the rear wheels are not driven.
With rear-wheel drive, driving force reaches the wheels on the rear axles; the front wheels are not driven.
Heavy vehicles commonly drive the rear axles rather than the front axles. The actual configuration depends on the vehicle.
An automatic gearbox selects ratios; all-wheel drive describes which wheels can receive driving force. One does not imply the other.
Rear-wheel drive identifies the driven wheels, not the engine position: the engine can also be at the rear.
The pinion meshes with the crown wheel and transfers motion through their teeth. Together they form the final-drive gear pair.
The bevel gear pair provides final reduction: the crown wheel turns more slowly than the pinion. This adds to the ratio change produced by the gearbox.
In the axle described by the quiz, the longitudinal pinion meshes with the crown wheel and directs motion toward the transverse half-shafts, changing direction by 90°.
With a front engine and rear-wheel drive, the longitudinal shaft carries motion to the axle, where the bevel gear pair directs it toward the rear half-shafts.
The axle ratio expresses the final-drive reduction and is related to the ratio of crown-wheel teeth to pinion teeth.
The axle bevel gear pair reduces speed rather than increasing it: the crown wheel turns more slowly than the pinion.
In the axle described by the quiz, the bevel gear pair turns the motion through 90°, from the longitudinal shaft toward the half-shafts, not 60°.
The pinion and crown wheel form the final drive and mesh with each other; they are not engaged like a gear using a dashboard control.
The pinion transmits motion to the crown wheel through meshing teeth, not through a friction disc.
The synchronizer brings the parts to be coupled to compatible speeds before engagement, making gear changes easier.
In a bend the outer wheel travels farther and must turn faster. The differential allows the two driven wheels to rotate at different speeds.
Changing ratio adjusts wheel torque and speed: a low gear increases available driving force. The gearbox does not create power from nothing.
In a bend the wheels travel different distances. The differential lets them turn at different speeds, avoiding the scrubbing caused by a rigid connection.
A heavy vehicle faces widely varying loads and resistance. More ratios allow a better choice of driving force and engine speed under different conditions.
In the type of gearbox described, the splitter control near the knob selects a slow or fast ratio, providing more closely spaced ratios. Control layouts vary between gearboxes.
An open differential allows different wheel speeds but does not guarantee optimal traction on slippery ground: one wheel may spin. A differential lock can improve traction.
On a bend, the outer wheel travels farther and rotates faster than the inner one. The differential allows this difference; it does not transfer speed from the outer wheel to the inner one.
The synchronizer brings the selected gear and its gearbox shaft to the same speed, making engagement easier. It does not equalize crankshaft and driveshaft speeds.
The synchronizer matches speeds inside the gearbox to facilitate shifting; the clutch connects and disconnects the engine and transmission. Synchronization does not make the clutch unnecessary.
The flywheel is attached to the crankshaft; its inertia smooths variations in rotation. It provides a clutch surface and a ring gear for the starter motor.
The flywheel stores energy and smooths changes in crankshaft speed; it does not automatically increase engine speed when effort rises on a hill.

The quiz marks this TRUE: a conventional driven axle uses a differential to let its wheels turn at different speeds in bends. Some independently driven wheel-motor systems need no mechanical differential.
In a drive axle, the differential transmits motion to both sides through two half-shafts, one on each side.
