The differential distributes motion between the two sides of the drive axle and allows them to turn at different speeds, as needed on a bend.
The differential gears are lubricated with oil. Change it according to the manufacturer’s intervals and specifications.
On a bend, the wheels on the same axle travel different distances; the differential lets them rotate at different speeds while transmitting motion.
The driveshaft carries motion to the axle; it does not prevent the differential from moving. Joints allow operation even when the connected components are not aligned.
An axle can both steer and drive the wheels; it can then have a differential to distribute motion to them.
Off-road vehicles can also have differentials, sometimes lockable to improve traction. Rough terrain does not rule out their use.
Dual wheels are paired on the same side of an axle; they do not require a differential for each wheel. One differential can serve both sides of the axle.
Construction vehicles can also have differentials; locking systems are available for difficult terrain.

The bevel gear pair and differential have different jobs: the gear pair transmits and reduces the drive to the axle, while the differential permits different wheel speeds. They are not interchangeable.
An automatic gearbox does not require the differential to be inside it. The layout depends on the vehicle and may place the differential separately in the axle.
The clutch connects and disconnects the engine and gearbox, controlling the flow of motion; it is therefore part of the transmission.
A dry single-disc clutch uses one friction disc operating without an oil bath; it is one possible design.
In automated manual transmissions, an actuator controls the clutch and can engage it without the driver operating a pedal.
In some vehicles, electronics command an actuator that controls the clutch instead of leaving direct control to the driver.

There are friction clutches and systems using fluids, electrohydraulic controls or electromagnetic controls. The classification can refer either to how motion is transmitted or to how the clutch is actuated.
There are single-disc and multi-disc clutches; the latter add friction surfaces to transmit torque.
More discs provide more friction surfaces and can increase the torque that can be transmitted, making this design suitable for demanding applications.
A clutch can be controlled automatically: an actuator engages and disengages it under the transmission system’s control.
In a dry clutch, the friction surfaces operate without an oil bath; in an oil-bath clutch, the plates are immersed in lubricant, which helps cool them.
The control can transmit pedal force through a hydraulic circuit; in heavy vehicles it can also have pneumatic assistance.
An automatic transmission does not necessarily require a single-plate clutch: transmissions also exist with a torque converter or a multi-plate clutch.
The clutch is part of the transmission: it connects and disconnects the engine and gearbox, and is not part of the suspension.
Automatically operated clutches exist: for example, an electronic control unit can regulate clutch operation without a pedal.
Heavy vehicles can also use multi-plate clutches: examples exist for construction vehicles and mobile cranes.
Disengaging the clutch breaks the connection between engine and transmission; engaging it restores that connection.
When moving off, gradually engaging the clutch progressively transmits torque from the engine through the transmission to the driving wheels, avoiding a jerk.
With a gear selected and the clutch disengaged, the engine is separated from the transmission and can keep running while the vehicle is stationary.
As speed falls, centrifugal force decreases and the springs draw the weights inward: the clutch disengages below its disengagement threshold, which can differ from its engagement threshold.
In a hydraulic control, the pedal creates pressure in the fluid, which acts on the release cylinder; the system can make operation easier.
Disengaging the clutch interrupts torque transmission from the engine, making a gear change easier; the clutch is then engaged again.
Progressive engagement allows the transmission to take up motion from the engine gradually, making the start smoother.
In a centrifugal clutch, increasing speed moves the weights outward: their contact automatically engages the clutch.
When the pedal is not needed, take your foot off it: resting it there can cause premature wear or unintended disengagement.
An electronic control unit can automatically manage the clutch actuator according to driving conditions and the driver’s inputs.
Automatic electromagnetic clutches exist: an electric current creates a magnetic field that enables connection and torque transmission.
In a centrifugal clutch, the weights move outward as speed rises and return inward as it falls, enabling engagement and disengagement.
As speed rises, centrifugal force increases: the weights move outward and can engage the clutch.
Even with a loaded vehicle, the clutch allows torque to be transmitted gradually when moving off, making the start smoother.
While driving, do not rest your foot on the pedal: unintended pressure can cause premature wear or disengage the clutch.
As speed rises, centrifugal force moves the weights outward, not inward.
When speed falls, centrifugal force decreases and the springs return the weights inward, not outward.
When speed falls, the springs can return the weights inward: they do not necessarily remain stationary.
The clutch connects and disconnects the engine and transmission; steering controls the vehicle’s direction.
In a centrifugal clutch, increasing speed moves the weights outward; once they overcome the springs, they engage the clutch.
Payload depends on the permitted masses and the vehicle’s mass; the clutch control type alone does not always make it lower.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but does not define “telescopic levers”. In one documented centrifugal clutch, weights move with speed and overcome springs to engage it; this example does not rule out every other mechanism.
In a centrifugal clutch, disengagement depends on speed falling and the springs returning the weights, not on movement of universal joints.
Automatic engagement is not exclusively hydraulic: rotating centrifugal weights can also engage the clutch.
Hydraulic control transmits pedal movement to disengage the clutch; it is not a device intended to improve cornering stability.
Hydraulic control transmits pressure through liquid in the circuit, not through air pressure.
The clutch connects and separates the engine and transmission, not the injection pump; it permits gradual engagement.
Disengaging the clutch interrupts the connection to the transmission, making gear changes easier even while moving.
In hydraulic control, pressure is generated by the pedal-operated cylinder in a hydraulic circuit; it is not engine oil pressure.
Pressing the pedal disengages the clutch; with the pedal released, the clutch is normally engaged and transmits torque.
With the pedal fully pressed, the clutch is disengaged; when released, it is normally engaged and transmits torque.
Having no pedal does not imply direct drive: an automated gearbox can control the clutch automatically and have several gears.
The pressure plate presses the clutch disc against the flywheel, allowing torque to be transmitted.
The pressure plate belongs to the clutch, which transmits engine torque to the gearbox input shaft.
The hydraulic control transmits pressure from the master cylinder to the slave cylinder. Suitable control ratios can reduce the force needed at the pedal while allowing for the required travel.
An automatic clutch engages and disengages without requiring a driver-operated clutch pedal.
Not all motor vehicles have a clutch pedal: systems with an automatic clutch can operate without one.
The pressure plate is part of the clutch: it presses the disc against the flywheel to transmit torque; it is not part of the differential.
The pressure plate belongs to the clutch and presses its disc against the flywheel; it is not a drum brake component.
When the clutch is engaged, the pressure plate presses the disc against the flywheel: contact allows torque to be transmitted.
The pressure plate belongs to the clutch and thus the drivetrain, not the suspension.
The pressure plate belongs to the clutch and transmits torque; it is not a braking component.
The quiz marks this FALSE, but the sources do not define “variable discs”. Single-plate and multi-plate clutches exist; these examples alone do not prove every other type impossible.
For vehicle multi-disc clutches, the distinction is between dry operation and an oil bath: the liquid used in a wet clutch is oil, not water.
Wet multi-plate clutches exist, so they are not necessarily dry.
A multi-plate clutch can also work with a manual gearbox, as on some motorcycles.
Having no clutch pedal does not eliminate the gearbox: an automatic control can operate the clutch of an automated gearbox.
With an automated clutch, the control operates the clutch without the driver pressing a pedal; the pedal is not locked down.
With an automated clutch, the control operates the clutch without the driver pressing a pedal; the pedal is not locked up.
A clutch can be operated automatically with a gearbox: the absence of a pedal does not mean there is no gearbox.
Automatic clutch control can be used with an automated gearbox; it does not eliminate the gearbox.
The clutch connects the engine to the transmission and allows gradual engagement, so torque reaches the drive wheels progressively.
Pressing the pedal moves the release bearing through the control mechanism; the bearing acts on the mechanism to disengage the clutch.
The disc’s friction material wears during engagement and the disc may need replacing.
Frequent starts and prolonged slipping increase friction lining wear, so driving style matters.
An excessive load places greater stress on the clutch, especially when starting, and can accelerate wear.
Some controls require pedal play or travel to be checked and adjusted according to the manufacturer’s instructions; others self-adjust.
With a conventional control, releasing the pedal allows the spring to clamp the disc and engage the clutch; pressing it disengages the clutch.
The disc hub is splined to the gearbox input shaft and remains connected to it even when the disc separates from the flywheel.
In a hydraulic control the pedal operates a master cylinder; pressure sent to the slave cylinder moves the release bearing and disengages the clutch.
The control can use compressed air, including to assist a hydraulic circuit, to help operate the release mechanism.
A cable and fork can mechanically transmit pedal movement to the release bearing.
With the pedal released, the pressure plate presses the disc against the flywheel, allowing torque to be transmitted.
If the lining is too worn, the clutch may no longer transmit the required torque and the disc slips against the flywheel.
Releasing the pedal gradually lets the clutch engage progressively and makes starting smoother.
In heavy vehicles, hydraulic control can be combined with a servo that assists clutch actuation and reduces pedal effort.
Pneumatic-hydraulic control is also suitable for commercial vehicles: compressed air can assist the hydraulic clutch control.

The quiz marks this FALSE: pneumatic-hydraulic clutch actuation alone does not establish a universal first-gear parking rule. Apply the parking brake and follow the vehicle instructions for gears and chocks.
During normal driving in gear, the clutch is engaged and transmits torque from the flywheel; it separates temporarily when disengaged.
The driver can operate the pedal: the hydraulic control transmits the action and compressed air provides assistance.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but the scope of a worm-gear mechanism is not established. A conventional pedal can operate the release bearing through linkage or hydraulics; that does not prove every other arrangement impossible.
The disc hub is connected to the gearbox input shaft, not its output shaft.
The disc hub is connected to the gearbox input shaft, not an auxiliary shaft.
The pedal operates the clutch release mechanism, not the differential gears.
The friction material of a dry clutch must be kept free of oil and grease: contamination can cause slipping.
The friction material does not require periodic cleaning with petrol; if worn or contaminated, the disc and the cause of the fault should be assessed.
The friction surface of a dry disc is not periodically greased: grease can cause slipping. Lubricating the hub during installation is a separate operation.
The springs supply the force that clamps the disc: periodically loosening them is not a maintenance procedure and would reduce clamping force.
Changing brake fluid maintains the braking system; it is not a general rule for maintaining the clutch. Follow the vehicle’s instructions for any hydraulic clutch control too.
Engine oil lubricates the engine; changing it does not replace clutch-specific checks and repairs.
The dipstick checks engine oil, not clutch condition. Check the clutch control according to the vehicle instructions.
Friction material wears in use; excessive wear can cause slipping.
Automatic actuation does not eliminate component wear: checks and repairs depend on the system and manufacturer’s instructions.
Self-adjustment compensates for wear but does not eliminate it: a self-adjusting clutch may still need inspection or repair.
An automatic clutch controls transmission engagement; it does not by itself make a vehicle more prone to rollover. On bends, speed and load stability are among the factors that matter.
When moving off, release the pedal gradually to engage the clutch without sudden jerks.
The oil film separates moving surfaces and carries away heat; insufficient lubrication can cause seizure.
In a wet-sump system the pump draws oil from the sump and sends it under pressure through passages to the parts requiring lubrication.
The oil film reduces direct contact between moving surfaces and therefore limits wear from rubbing.
A thin oil film separates moving surfaces, reducing direct contact and friction.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but does not define “natural circulation”. In forced lubrication a pump feeds oil to bearings; other lubrication methods exist, but cannot automatically be equated with the quiz term.
The injection pump belongs to the fuel supply; the oil pump is a separate component of the lubrication circuit.
Lubrication reduces friction between moving parts by means of an oil film; its purpose is not to increase friction.
High acidity does not prevent deposits. Cleanliness also depends on detergent and dispersant additives and the oil’s resistance to degradation.
The oil pressure warning light comes on when pressure is too low: oil may not adequately reach the parts that need lubrication.
A faulty pump may fail to deliver oil through the circuit at the required pressure, causing the warning light to come on.
A broken pipe can leak oil; a blockage on the suction side can reduce delivery. Either can impair pressure and lubrication.
If there is too little oil in the sump, the pump may not draw in enough to maintain pressure in the circuit.
Worn piston rings control the oil on the cylinder walls less effectively, so more oil can reach the combustion chamber and be consumed.
The filter traps impurities in the circulating oil, limiting the abrasive particles that reach lubricated surfaces.
Viscosity describes the oil’s resistance to flow. It changes with temperature and normally decreases as the oil warms.
After switching off the engine, wait for the oil to drain back into the sump for a reliable reading. Follow the manufacturer’s waiting time.
On level ground, the oil in the sump is correctly positioned relative to the level marks, avoiding a reading distorted by a slope.
The oil pressure light does not identify the type of oil added: it indicates insufficient pressure in the circuit.
The light indicates insufficient pressure, not necessarily a low oil level: a faulty pump can also cause it.
There is no need to run the engine for 15 minutes. Switch it off and wait for the oil to return to the sump before checking, following the manual.
The check is not limited to a workshop: in vehicles with a dipstick, the driver can check the level by following the manual.
Park the vehicle on level ground: raising the front tilts the oil in the sump and can distort the reading.
Antifreeze belongs in the cooling system, not the oil sump. Use the engine oil specified by the manufacturer.
The sump collects the oil, the filter traps impurities, and the indicator allows pressure to be monitored: all are associated with lubrication.
Both gasoline and diesel engines have moving parts that need lubrication to reduce friction and wear.
The oil film separates surfaces moving relative to each other, reducing direct contact, friction and wear.
The pump draws oil from the sump and sends it through the circuit to engine parts; a gear pump is one design used.
With insufficient pressure the lubricating film can fail and metal surfaces can be damaged. Stop safely and switch off the engine.
Oil degrades with use and must be changed according to the vehicle’s maintenance schedule.
Oil carries heat away from the parts it lubricates, helping to cool them as well as reducing friction.
With use, oil accumulates contaminants and additives are depleted: change it according to the manufacturer’s schedule.
Transmission oil also ages: its additives can degrade and reduce lubrication. Replace it when specified by the manufacturer.
For topping up, use oil that meets the required specifications: oil with different characteristics may not provide the intended protection.
The level can fall during use. Checking it regularly and topping up with the specified oil when needed helps keep it between the prescribed marks.
The oil film and protective additives help shield metal surfaces from agents that cause corrosion.
Multigrade oil is formulated to flow when cold and maintain suitable viscosity when hot; its viscosity still changes with temperature.
The gauge shows oil pressure; the red light warns of potentially insufficient pressure. They are monitoring signals, not a complete diagnosis.
Light smoke with a blue tint can accompany oil consumption when, for example, the piston rings do not seal. Color alone cannot identify the cause with certainty.
The red light warns that oil pressure may be too low for proper lubrication. Stop and switch off the engine; the cause must be checked.
The dipstick has MIN and MAX marks. The reading should be between them, following the manufacturer’s procedure.
The filter traps contaminants. Replacing it with the oil avoids leaving a filter loaded with impurities in service. Follow the manufacturer’s intervals.
Choose the specification required by the manufacturer for that engine; do not automatically interchange oils intended for different uses. Some oils meet both diesel and gasoline specifications.
Oil degrades and collects contaminants in use; the manufacturer’s time and distance intervals determine when to replace it.
Substances can be added to the base oil to improve functions such as oxidation resistance and wear protection.
Oils can be formulated with mineral or synthetic base oils; the choice for an engine depends on the required specifications.
Oxidation in service can increase viscosity, the oil’s resistance to flow, changing its lubrication behavior.
In use, oil reacts with oxygen and degrades. Antioxidants slow this process but do not eliminate it.
Oxidation can produce organic acids in oil; their accumulation contributes to lubricant deterioration.
Circulating oil absorbs heat from hot areas and carries it elsewhere, helping cool components.
The system delivers oil between surfaces in relative motion: the film separates them and limits direct contact.
The lubricating film limits contact between moving surfaces and thus reduces wear.
The oil film separates surfaces sliding against each other, reducing friction compared with direct contact.
The pump circulates pressurized oil through the system to supply the points requiring lubrication.
A faulty pump can compromise oil pressure. The light or gauge signals the problem but does not identify its cause on its own.
A faulty relief valve or a clogged filter can contribute to low pressure; both are possible causes to check.
If there is too little oil, the pump may not supply the circuit properly and pressure can fall. Check the level as directed in the manual.

The quiz marks this TRUE: delivery through the consortium network is one route for used mineral oil. It is not the only one: it can also go to an authorized waste handler outside consortium management; the law also allows transfer to businesses in other EU states.
Viscosity alone is not enough: a diesel engine also needs oil meeting the performance specifications and grade indicated by its manufacturer.
Viscosity alone is not enough: use oil that also meets the manufacturer’s specifications for that diesel engine. Some oils meet both diesel and gasoline specifications.
The gauge shows oil pressure, not the amount in the sump. Check the level with the dipstick or the vehicle’s specified system.
The oil pressure light warns of insufficient pressure: it can come on even if the sump is not empty. If the engine is running, stop and switch it off.
The oil pressure light warns of insufficient pressure, not a correct temperature. If it comes on while driving, stop and switch off the engine.
The pressure light signals a problem needing immediate attention, not an oil change due in 5,000 km. Stop, switch off the engine and check the level.
Black smoke can result from excess fuel or insufficient air; it does not prove oil is burning. Worn pistons or rings can instead produce blue smoke.
The filter cleans oil in the lubrication circuit; a blockage is not indicated by reddish exhaust smoke. Replace it according to the maintenance schedule.
Used oil must be replaced with new oil specified by the manufacturer. Filtering it through a cloth and returning it to the sump is not an oil change.
High oil consumption does not prove excessive cylinder pressure: worn piston rings, for example, can cause it. The cause needs diagnosis.
Gearbox oil may also require replacement according to the manufacturer’s schedule. Transmission components heat up in operation.
During use, oil can oxidize and become contaminated, for example by soot or fuel. Increased salinity is not the main change described.
The oil pressure light warns of insufficient pressure, not a temperature above 100°C. If it comes on while driving, stop and switch off the engine.
Do not add vegetable oil: use engine oil with the viscosity and specifications prescribed by the manufacturer for the operating conditions.
Do not add gasoline to oil, even a little: fuel contaminates it and can reduce its viscosity. Choose the prescribed grade for cold conditions.
The pump must pressurize oil soon after starting, without waiting for the coolant to reach 65°C. Check pressure immediately.
There is no general rule that oil passes through the water radiator at 120°C. A heat exchanger can cool oil while keeping it separate from coolant.
The quiz marks this FALSO: the sump collects oil returning from the engine; in some engines the oil cooler is separate. Other designs, however, integrate a cooler into the sump.
The lubrication circuit carries oil to moving parts to reduce friction and help cool them. It does not unblock clogged injectors.
If the level is low, top up with the specified oil, observing the indicated level. Topping up does not replace the scheduled oil change.
Do not add diesel fuel to oil: fuel contaminates it and can reduce its viscosity. Use oil of the required grade and specification.
There is no universal two-month interval. Oil changes depend on the engine and its operating conditions: follow the manufacturer’s schedule.
Dark color alone does not determine when to change oil. Follow the prescribed intervals and, where applicable, oil analysis recommendations.
Replace the oil filter at the scheduled intervals without waiting for the red light. The pressure light signals a condition requiring immediate attention.
The gearbox and differential have their own maintenance schedules: their oils need not be changed at every engine oil change. Follow the vehicle’s intervals.
Collect used oil and take it to an authorized collection facility for management or recovery; do not burn it outdoors. It can contain contaminants.

The quiz marks this FALSO: the engine-oil circuit mainly lubricates engine parts, while the fuel circuit supplies the pump. Design matters, however: some injection pumps use engine oil, while others are lubricated by fuel.
The pump is driven mechanically by the engine, for example through gears connected to the crankshaft; it is not necessarily driven by the flywheel.
Not all belts are lubricated: oil contamination can damage belts designed to run dry. Special belts designed to run in oil also exist.
There is no required set of three filters of these types. The oil filter traps impurities and its arrangement depends on the engine; activated carbon is used, for example, in cabin air filters.
The gauge indicates pressure, not level. Check the level with the dipstick or, where fitted, the vehicle’s electronic indicator.
Wear of the gears increases internal leakage in the pump and tends to lower oil pressure, not raise it.
The filter traps impurities in the oil and is selected to meet the engine specifications. There is no winter versus summer filter distinction.
Used oil is waste that must be collected and disposed of properly: diluting it does not permit discharge into the sewer.
Coolant passes through the block jackets and cylinder head, absorbing heat from the hot engine parts.
Hot coolant passes through the radiator, where it gives heat to the outside air, and then circulates back through the engine.
In the radiator, heat passes from the coolant to the air flowing across its surfaces, making it a liquid-to-air heat exchanger.
Suitable coolant must resist freezing and boiling during use and protect the system components from corrosion.
If the thermostat does not open properly, coolant flow to the radiator can be restricted and the engine can overheat.
The system removes heat produced by the engine and helps maintain an operating temperature that protects components from overheating damage.
The radiator transfers heat from the coolant to the air, helping keep engine temperature suitable for operation.
In a closed, pressurized system water can exceed 100°C without boiling: pressure raises its boiling point.
In cold climates coolant with adequate antifreeze protection is needed: water alone can freeze and damage the system.
Normally an appropriate mixture of water and coolant additive is used, not distilled water alone: the additive also protects against freezing and corrosion.
In liquid cooling, heat passes to coolant circulating through passages; fins on the cylinder head are typical of air cooling.
Coolant needs a low freezing point and a high boiling point to remain liquid over its operating range.
Even in a closed system, the level must be checked according to the manufacturer’s instructions: leaks or other problems can lower it.

The absolute prohibition is wrong: some manufacturers allow water alone in an emergency to reach a service center. The specified coolant must then be restored; water alone does not provide the same protection.
Do not open the cap immediately: the hot system is pressurized and steam and scalding liquid can escape. Wait for the engine to cool.
The fan increases airflow through the radiator to remove heat, especially at low speed or when stationary; it does not prevent freezing.
Pouring very cold water over a hot engine can cause thermal shock damage. Let it cool without opening the pressurized system while hot.
The red warning light indicates excessive coolant temperature and draws attention to possible overheating.
A thermostat stuck closed obstructs coolant flow to the radiator and can cause overheating.
If the electric fan fails, less air flows through the radiator, especially at low speed or when stationary.
When a belt drives the fan, a loose or broken belt can prevent it working properly and reduce cooling.
An internal blockage restricts coolant flow, while external dirt restricts airflow. Both hinder heat removal.
The hot system is pressurized: opening the cap can release steam and hot liquid and cause burns. Wait for it to cool.
Engine heat is removed either by air or by circulating liquid that transfers heat to the air in the radiator.
Insufficient lubrication increases friction between parts and the heat produced, so it can contribute to overheating.
Insufficient coolant impairs heat transfer from the engine to the radiator and can cause overheating.
Do not open the cap immediately: hot pressurized liquid and steam can cause burns. Wait for the system to cool.
The temperature warning light comes on to signal overheating; it does not go out to indicate excessively hot coolant.

Large trucks commonly use liquid cooling: coolant absorbs engine heat and releases it through the radiator. A fan moves air through the radiator, but that does not make the engine directly air-cooled.
Driving is not the only possible cause: a faulty thermostat or low coolant level can also cause overheating.
Leaving the hood partly open does not fix the fault. Stop safely, allow the engine to cool and identify the cause of overheating.
No fixed speed of 40 km/h solves every overheating problem: stop safely and check the cause.
Clutch play is not the relevant cooling check. Check, for example, the coolant level and fan operation instead.
Do not put ice into the hot system: opening the cap can cause burns. Let it cool and check the coolant specified by the manufacturer.
Thinner oil is not a general remedy for overheating. Find the cause and use oil approved by the manufacturer.
Cooling removes heat produced by combustion, keeping engine parts within suitable operating temperatures.
In a liquid-cooled system, the centrifugal pump circulates coolant, the radiator transfers heat to the air, and the fan assists airflow.
Deposits in the tubes can restrict coolant flow through the radiator and reduce heat removal.

The quiz marks this VERO: in one system a belt drives the fan through an electromagnetic clutch, engaged by a thermal switch when needed. An electric fan can also mean a fan driven by an electric motor, which is a different arrangement.
The thermostat regulates the route to the radiator: coolant bypasses it when the engine is cold, and the passage opens at operating temperature.
Removing the thermostat is not a sufficient repair: it regulates temperature, and a faulty component should be checked and replaced according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
The main danger of overheating is engine damage: continued operation at excessive temperature can damage components.
The main danger of overheating is engine damage, not simply increased fuel consumption.
Overheating can damage the engine. Switching off the air conditioner can reduce the heat load, but that is not the main effect of the fault.
The dashboard normally indicates coolant temperature, sometimes with a warning light for excessive temperature; a radiator pressure gauge cannot be assumed to be fitted.
There is no universal limit of 80°C: normal temperature depends on the engine and can exceed that value. Follow the range indicated by the manufacturer.
The engine must reach its intended operating temperature: keeping it cold all the time does not help fuel economy. The thermostat assists warm-up and regulates temperature.
Coolant carries engine heat to the radiator; air passing through it disperses the heat, aided by the fan when needed.
The radiator transfers heat carried by water-based coolant to the air without mixing the two fluids.
Adding cool coolant too quickly to a very hot engine can damage it. Wait for it to cool and follow the manual: opening the hot system also risks burns from pressurized coolant and steam.
Coolant is not normally replaced with plain water in summer: the prescribed mixture also protects against corrosion and boiling.
The engine radiator releases heat to the outside air. A separate heater heat exchanger fed by hot coolant heats the cabin.
Do not replace coolant with ethyl alcohol: use the manufacturer’s prescribed mixture, with freeze protection suited to the expected temperatures.
The fan increases airflow through the radiator, helping transfer heat from the liquid to the air.
In an automatically controlled system, the fan stops when the temperature falls to the set value because the same cooling is no longer needed.
In an automatically controlled system, a temperature sensor calls for the fan when coolant gets hot enough. The extra airflow through the radiator helps remove heat.
A centrifugal pump uses an impeller to move liquid around the circuit, carrying heat from the engine to the radiator.

In an urgent situation, if coolant is unavailable, some manufacturers permit temporary use of water to reach a service facility. It is not a permanent fill: water alone risks freezing, corrosion and overheating; the prescribed coolant must be restored.
The coolant mixture lowers the freezing point and raises the boiling point compared with water; actual values depend on the mixture and pressure.
The gauge shows coolant temperature and the warning light signals excessive temperature. These are useful indications but do not replace checks for faults.
The thermostat regulates coolant flow to the radiator: it helps initial warm-up and helps maintain operating temperature.
The fan is not limited to stationary operation: it can also run while driving when cooling requires it.
The fan is normally controlled automatically according to cooling needs, rather than by a driver-operated switch.
The fan starting does not necessarily switch off the compressor at the same time. In severe conditions the system may nevertheless control the air conditioner to protect the engine.
The fan can come on even below 0°C: its control depends on the system and cooling needs, not just on the outside temperature.
Exceeding 80 km/h does not always prevent the fan from coming on: control depends on the system and coolant temperature as well as vehicle speed.
A long descent does not require the fan to be switched off: its control depends on cooling needs.
The thermostat automatically regulates coolant flow to the radiator according to temperature; it is not operated by a dashboard switch.
The tire’s contact patch with the road develops the forces needed to steer, accelerate and brake.
The tire deforms and cushions road irregularities, contributing to the vehicle’s springing along with the suspension.
Driving force passes to the road through the tire’s contact patch; the wheel slips if available grip is exceeded.
Braking force passes to the road through the tire’s contact patch, within the available grip limit.

The quiz marks this VERO: the tire carries the load through a deformable contact patch, spreading contact over the road. This can reduce concentrated loading, but it does not guarantee the pavement cannot be damaged; heavy loads also wear it.
Lateral forces developed in the contact patch allow the vehicle to follow the intended direction until available grip is exceeded.
Tread grooves collect and move water away from the contact patch, helping maintain contact with a wet road.
A tire must be able to deform: its elasticity helps absorb irregularities and maintain road contact.
Tires do not need to be warmed before setting off. Instead, check their pressure cold according to the vehicle’s instructions.
A pressure warning indicates low pressure, not that a tire needs replacing. Wear and damage must be checked directly.
A softer compound does not require the shock absorbers to be stiffened. Replacement tires must match the vehicle’s specifications.
Wear reduces groove depth and can impair wet grip, increasing the risk of aquaplaning.
The stated gradient does not itself require reinforced tires: the choice must meet the vehicle’s specifications and required load capacity.
Approved retreaded tires suitable for the vehicle can also be used on motorways; retreading does not entail a general ban.
In a disc wheel, the disc connects the wheel to the hub and the rim supports the tire.
The rim designation identifies its dimensions and construction, helping select a compatible tire.
In the rim designation, the width is the distance between the flanges, not the tire width.
A letter in the designation, such as J, identifies the rim flange profile type.
The rim designation includes the nominal diameter where the tire bead fits; the diameters must be compatible.
The ET marking indicates offset: the distance between the rim’s center plane and the disc’s mounting face at the hub.
The date code on the tire sidewall indicates its week and year of manufacture, not an expiry date.
The rim code describes the rim. The date code on the tire sidewall gives the week and year of manufacture, not the exact day.
The rim code identifies rim characteristics, not a tire inspection date; wear and damage must be checked regularly.
The rim code describes the rim, not the tire’s expiry year. The sidewall code indicates when the tire was made.
The rim code describes the rim, including its dimensions and profile; it does not identify the material of the tire fitted to it.
The wheel normally consists of a rim and disc; the rim supports the tire. An inner tube, when present, is separate from the wheel.
The rim designation gives its dimensions and profile; by itself it does not certify suitability for off-road use.
The marking uses technical rim designations, such as dimensions and profile; it does not change with the vehicle holder’s language.
In a tube-type assembly the inner tube holds the air; tubeless assemblies without a tube also exist.
A tubeless tire holds air using a low-permeability inner rubber liner instead of a separate tube.
In a tubeless assembly the valve is fitted to the rim because there is no inner tube to attach it to.
In a tube-type assembly the valve belongs to the inner tube and passes through the rim hole for inflation.
In a puncture, a tubeless tire generally loses air more slowly: air escapes through the hole, while from a punctured tube it can also pass between the tube and tire and escape through the rim.
When a tube is fitted inside a tubeless tire, air can remain between the tube and tire during mounting. The assembly requires a compatibility check and the precautions specified by the manufacturer.
The carcass supports the structure, the beads secure the tire to the rim, and the tread is the surface that rolls on the road.
The beads are the tire edges that rest on the rim seats and hold the tire in position.
On a tubeless tire the beads must seal against the rim seats; together with the inner liner they help retain air.
In radial truck tires the carcass may consist of plies of rubber-coated steel cords; other tires may use textile fibers.
Tread block design and rubber compound affect rolling noise; tire condition and wear also have an effect.
Heavy vehicles can also use tubeless tires, which retain air without a separate inner tube.
A tubeless tire is not inherently more dangerous: after a penetrating puncture it can lose air more gradually. A damaged tubeless tire still needs attention.
A tubeless assembly does not require an inner tube: the tire and its seal against the rim retain air, with a valve on the rim.
The comparison is reversed: a tubeless tire struck by a penetrating object generally loses air more gradually than a tire with a punctured tube.
A tubeless assembly has an inflation valve fitted to the rim; it is the separate inner tube that is absent.
Center wear does not simply depend on having an inner tube: among other causes, it can be associated with excessive pressure for the load.

The quiz marks this FALSO: the registration document normally records approved tyre specifications, such as size and codes, rather than necessarily showing the tread pattern. This does not rule out special annotations on individual documents.

The quiz marks this FALSE. For heavy vehicles Michelin includes the tread in its description of the same type on an axle and recommends identical patterns, but elsewhere allows different patterns under certain conditions. An older ministerial inspection procedure required the same pattern on each axle; the scope of the current rule remains unclear.
The beads rest on the rim; the tread contacts the road and contributes to grip.
The tread grooves in the road contact area help channel water away, not small cuts on the sidewalls.
Sidewalls must flex under load and absorb irregularities; they are not rigid.
In a cross-ply carcass, the cords in the layers run diagonally and cross each other.
In a radial tire the carcass cords run from bead to bead, roughly at right angles to the direction of travel.
The distinction depends on carcass cord orientation: radial or diagonal and crossed.
The radial carcass lets the sidewalls flex more readily than cross-ply construction.
In a bend the radial belt stabilizes the tread; cross-ply construction can deform more and lose some road contact.
The construction types are radial and cross-ply; “staggered plies” does not describe a carcass type here.
Carcass construction is classified as radial or cross-ply, not longitudinal.
The distinction concerns the arrangement of carcass cords, not the number or material of the plies.
In a bend the belt stabilizes a radial tread; a cross-ply tread can deform and lose some contact rather than generally retaining more.
The reverse is true: radial sidewalls are generally more flexible than cross-ply sidewalls.
The tread touches the road: its compound and pattern contribute to grip.
Grooves channel water away from the contact area, helping the tire maintain grip on wet roads.
Wear indicators are small raised bars in the main grooves: they signal wear when the tread reaches their level.
Compound flexibility changes with temperature: some compounds become stiffer in the cold.
Manufacturers and tire types use different patterns to balance grip, wear and noise.
Front and rear axle patterns may differ, provided the tires suit their positions and the vehicle.

The quiz marks this VERO, but 1.6 mm over the whole surface is a more conservative condition, not the minimum required everywhere. For Italian autoveicoli (such as cars and trucks), trolleybuses and trailers, the rule requires at least 1.6 mm in the main grooves in the central zone covering approximately three quarters of the tread; the pattern must remain visible across the full width and circumference.

The quiz marks this FALSO: the rule does not specify an exact 80% of the surface. For Italian autoveicoli (such as cars and trucks), trolleybuses and trailers it requires at least 1.6 mm in the main grooves in the central zone covering approximately three quarters of the tread. Coverage of 80% is not itself unlawful: all main grooves and pattern visibility must be checked.
Radial and cross-ply describe carcass arrangement; they do not require the radial tread to be wider.
Dual mounting does not remove tread requirements: on motor vehicles the main grooves must retain the prescribed minimum depth.
Tread blocks are elastic: they deform and compress as they enter the contact patch, then regain their shape.
The tread is a rubber compound; nylon may instead appear in reinforcement layers separate from the tread.
The tread must be able to deform: its compound balances grip and wear resistance rather than maximizing rigidity.
There is no general 3 mm limit on block height: tread depth depends on the tire’s design and use.

For autoveicoli (the Italian category including cars and trucks), trolleybuses and trailers, the minimum is 1.6 mm in the main grooves in the central area, not 2.5 mm over the entire surface. The pattern must remain visible across the full width and circumference.
The sidewall must flex under load while providing enough lateral stability: moderate flexibility balances these functions.
The sidewall has a rubber covering that protects the casing, whose rubber-coated plies provide structural reinforcement.
The side surface also exchanges heat with the air, helping cool the tire as it moves.
An overly flexible sidewall deforms more under cornering forces, increasing slip angle and reducing steering precision.
Damage reaching the plies compromises the casing structure; an intact-looking outer rubber surface is not enough.
The sidewall needs some flexibility to deform under load while providing lateral stability; very high rigidity is not a general requirement.
Greater lateral stiffness limits deformation in corners and tends to reduce slip angle; excessive flexibility tends to increase it.
Dual tires need adequate spacing so their sidewalls do not rub; coating them with aluminum alloy is not the solution.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but a structural sidewall repair can be possible under specific conditions: a certificate alone does not make every cord injury repairable. Specialist inspection and assessment are needed; the question does not clarify the Italian rules for damage already repaired.
The 1.6 mm value concerns the main tread-groove depth for autoveicoli (the Italian category including cars and trucks), trolleybuses and trailers, not sidewall thickness.
The index is a code for the maximum mass a single tire can carry at the associated speed, under the manufacturer’s specified conditions.
154 is a load index in the table: it is a code corresponding to a mass, not the mass itself.
Tires suitable for single and dual fitment can have two indices: the second gives the capacity of each tire in a dual fitment.
The sidewall shows the index as a numerical code in the service description; a table links it to the permitted mass.
15400 is not an index in the table: an index is a numerical code such as 154, not a five-digit mass.
Dual fitment is indicated by its load index, often after the single-fitment index and separated by a slash, not by the suffix TWIN.
The index is a numerical code looked up in the load table, not a mass in kilograms followed by KG.
Load capacity must also be known for dual fitment: the marking can include the index for that fitment.
The speed symbol identifies the maximum speed associated with the tire’s load capacity under the specified conditions.
J is one of the speed category symbols; the table assigns a reference speed to each symbol.
The speed symbol is among the sidewall markings, alongside the load index in the service description.
The symbol refers to the maximum speed of its category under the specified conditions; the stated capacity assumes a suitable, properly maintained tire.
The symbol indicates a category maximum speed, not a minimum speed to maintain.
Dual fitment does not double the indicated speed: the symbol retains its category value, while the load may have a specific dual-fitment index.
The load index is a numerical code corresponding to a load capacity; speed is indicated by a separate symbol, not by km/h after the index.
A speed category symbol is also marked for dual fitment; the load indices distinguish the fitting conditions.
The TUBELESS marking identifies a tyre designed for use without an inner tube.
M+S identifies a snow tyre: it is designed to improve traction in snow compared with a normal tyre.
The sidewall can indicate the type: for example, TUBE TYPE identifies a tyre designed for use with an inner tube.
The manufacturing code gives the week and year: in the four-digit code the first two digits give the week and the last two the year.
TWI can appear on the sidewall to help locate the tread wear indicators.
TWI marks where to find the indicators on the tread that show wear in the grooves.
In the usual marking the nominal rim diameter is generally given in inches, not millimetres.
In the usual marking the nominal section width is generally given in millimetres, not inches.
M+S identifies a snow tyre, not a requirement concerning towing a trailer.
International approval is shown by a circled E and the country number, not by MCTC; Italy’s number is 3.
TWI locates the tread wear indicators, not the inflation valve.
TWI refers to tread wear indicators; it does not indicate dual fitment.
The manufacturer’s trade name or brand is among the sidewall markings, so the brand can be identified.
The registration document records permitted sizes, including any alternatives: compare these details with the tyre markings.
Tyres normally fitted to the same axle must be of the same type, rather than being chosen independently for each side.
Different axles may have different types, provided those on the same axle are the same type; normally fitted tyres must still have the same structure.
Rim diameter alone does not determine rolling circumference: a different sidewall height can compensate for the difference in rim size.

The quiz marks this TRUE. For alternative tyres, a 1996 ministry circular called for checking that the vehicle’s maximum dimensions remained unchanged and that wider tyres did not extend beyond the body. Choose permitted sizes and check the applicable requirements: this source does not establish a universal rule for every part of the rim and every original outline.
Fitted sizes must match those authorized for the vehicle and recorded in its registration documents; a different size requires the applicable approval procedure.
There is not necessarily only one type: alternative sizes and different types on different axles may be permitted, subject to fitment requirements.
The registration document records specifications such as permitted sizes, not a required tyre brand; the brand appears on the sidewall.
Tyres normally fitted on the same axle must be the same type, not different types.
TRACT is not a code identifying every drive-axle tyre. For example, Michelin uses D for a tread pattern designed for the stresses on drive axles, which transmit engine and braking torque.
Rotation can even out wear; maintenance frequency depends on the vehicle, tire position and use. The quiz marks the claim of a requirement within 20,000 km false.

The registration document lists permitted tire specifications, not a general starting date. Tires meeting those specifications, including speed rating, may be used year-round; winter equipment requirements depend on road orders.
Tread grooves channel water away from the contact patch, helping the tire maintain grip on wet roads.
When water cannot escape quickly enough, it forms a film beneath the tire. The tire loses contact with the road and therefore loses grip.
On the water film, tires lose the contact needed to transmit lateral forces, so the vehicle may not respond to steering.
At higher speeds the tire has less time to clear water from the contact patch, increasing the risk of a separating film forming.
Shallower grooves can clear less water, making it easier for the tire to ride up on a water film when other conditions are equal.

Other conditions being equal, lower inflation pressure can reduce contact pressure at the center of the tread. Water can enter beneath the tire more easily, so hydroplaning can begin at a lower speed. Use the pressure prescribed for the vehicle and load.
Slow down gradually by easing off the accelerator until the tires regain contact. Sudden maneuvers can worsen the loss of control.
Dual wheels do not eliminate aquaplaning: their tires can also lose road contact if water cannot escape quickly enough.
Four millimeters of tread does not guarantee immunity. Speed, water depth, pressure and road surface also matter.
Trailer tires can also ride up on a water film and lose grip. Aquaplaning depends on tire-road contact, not on whether the wheels are driven.
Accelerating increases the risk. Instead, ease off the accelerator and slow gradually until grip returns.
Hard braking is a sudden maneuver on tires that have lost contact. Instead, ease off the accelerator gradually and let the vehicle slow until grip returns.
Turning sharply to full lock does not restore contact and can cause a sudden change of direction when grip returns. Slow gradually while keeping the steering pointed in the direction of travel.
ABS limits wheel lock during braking, but it cannot prevent a water film forming or create contact when the tire is separated from the road.
In a dual-wheel configuration, two tires sit side by side at each end of the axle to share the load and contribute to traction.
A pair with similar wear has more closely matched diameters. A larger tire can carry an excessive share of the load.
Both dual tires should be kept at the same pressure appropriate for the load so that the pair works properly.
The inner wheel’s valve is less accessible. A suitable extension makes checking and inflating easier without dismantling the pair.

The clearance between the tires must prevent their sidewalls touching under load. On demountable rim assemblies a spacer band separates the rims; other wheel designs obtain clearance through their geometry.
A pressure loss in the inner tire of a dual pair can be hard to spot. A pressure warning device helps detect it so action can be taken.
Dual wheels are normally used on rear load-bearing or drive axles, while the steering axle generally has single wheels.
The two tires are separate and each must be checked and inflated. Dual fitment does not imply connected inner tubes or a single valve.
Dual fitment does not automatically reduce grip: side-by-side tires contribute to traction. Actual performance also depends on the tires and road conditions.
The spacer keeps dual wheels apart so the tire sidewalls do not touch as they flex under load.
Exceeding 7 tonnes does not by itself require dual wheels on the last axle. The choice of single or dual fitment depends on vehicle approval and tire load capacity.
Dual wheels alone do not create an ABS requirement. Braking requirements depend on the vehicle category and its type approval.
Rubber forms the casing, while plies and reinforcements support its structure. Mounted on the rim and inflated, the tire carries the load through pressurized air.
The number 22.5 is the nominal diameter in inches of the rim on which the tire fits; it is not the tire width.
Pressure that is too high for the load concentrates more pressure at the center of the contact patch and can accelerate wear there.
Inspection covers the tread and sidewalls: uneven wear, age-related cracking, cuts or bulges can reveal problems that need assessment.
A heavily worn tread disperses less water: a film can form between tire and road, causing loss of contact and grip.
If the grooves cannot clear the water, the tire can lift off the road. Wear, high speed, deep water and insufficient pressure increase the risk.

The size must be permitted for the vehicle, and the load and speed indices must meet the requirements. For commercial vehicles, under the prescribed marking rules, they may be higher than those on the registration document; some winter tires may have a lower speed code under specified conditions.
For motor vehicles, the minimum is 1.6 mm in the main grooves, not 1.2 mm over the whole surface. The tread pattern must still be visible across the width and around the circumference.
152 and 148 are load indices for single and dual fitment respectively. The nominal width is 315 mm and 80 is the percentage ratio of sidewall height to width.
The order is reversed: 152 is the load index for single fitment and 148 for dual fitment.
R indicates radial construction; 22.5 is the nominal rim diameter in inches, not a radius in centimeters.
Check pressure when the tires are cold and compare it with the prescribed value: temperature and pressure rise during driving.

The quiz marks this FALSE. Underinflation can increase hydroplaning risk, but some manufacturers say overinflation can increase it too. Speed, water and tread also matter: check the prescribed pressure when the tyres are cold.
The first index, 154, applies to single fitment; the second, 149, to dual fitment. M is the speed category symbol.
The registration document lists permitted tire characteristics, including the speed code. Some winter tires may have a lower code under specified conditions.
The aspect ratio compares section height with width: for example, 80 means the height is 80% of the nominal width.
A directional tire must be mounted so that it rotates in the direction of the sidewall arrow when moving forward.

M+S identifies a tread designed to improve performance in mud and fresh or melting snow. The marking alone does not establish a pass in the snow test associated with the 3PMSF Alpine symbol, or set a minimum operating temperature.

There is no separate 1.4 mm limit for three centimeters at the edges. On motor vehicles the main grooves in the central area must be at least 1.6 mm deep; the pattern must be visible across the full width.
For motor vehicles the specified minimum is 1.6 mm in the main grooves, not 2 mm over the entire surface. The pattern must remain visible across the width and around the circumference.
R indicates radial construction and M is the speed code. They do not indicate use on a trailer or mountain roads.
The order is the other way around: the first load index is for single fitment and the second for dual fitment.
A spare wheel is not generally required: fitted tyres or equivalent systems are compulsory, not an additional wheel.
Even a heavy vehicle can lose contact with the road if water builds up beneath its tyres. Weight does not eliminate the risk of aquaplaning.
M & S identifies a tyre intended to improve traction in mud and snow, not its country of manufacture.
Radial tyres have more flexible sidewalls, which work more independently from the tread than in cross-ply construction.
Tubeless means the tyre is designed to retain air without an inner tube.
Dual tyres should be matched and arranged evenly on both sides: compatible sizes and the same tread pattern on the axle help distribute the load and maintain consistent handling.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but does not say what kind of resistance it means. Radial tyres have plies running across the tyre and a belt stabilizing the tread; bias-ply tyres have crossed plies. Resistance depends on the damage, design and use: for example, Michelin describes radial tyres as more resistant to damage and heat than bias tyres.
A construction vehicle does not by definition require radial tyres: choose tyres approved and suitable for the vehicle and its use.
Pressure is not automatically higher because a tyre is tubeless. Use the pressure specified for the tyre, load and operating conditions.
Tubeless describes the absence of an inner tube and does not imply poorer road holding. Grip depends on the tyre’s characteristics and condition, including its pressure.
Rub marks on the inner sidewalls should not be dismissed as harmless wear: contact caused by underinflation or incorrect fitting can damage dual tyres and needs checking.
Correct pressure allows the tyre to absorb road irregularities as intended. Excessive pressure can make the ride harsher.
Pressure affects the contact area and the tyre’s behaviour: keeping it correct helps road holding.
Underinflation changes the tyre’s behaviour and can reduce vehicle stability. Maintain the pressure specified for the load.
Choose the pressure according to the load and the manufacturer’s instructions: an underinflated tyre deforms excessively under load.
Incorrect pressure increases wear and can damage the structure. Maintaining the specified pressure helps extend tyre life.
Correct pressure helps the tread maintain its intended contact patch with the road. Incorrect pressure changes its shape and contact distribution.
The specified pressure supports comfort and efficiency; it does not necessarily increase fuel consumption. Underinflation increases rolling resistance and therefore fuel use.
Do not let half a bar out of the tyres for a descent. Maintain the prescribed cold pressure for the load and use.
Correct pressure matters all year, not only in summer: incorrect pressure impairs tyre performance and life.
Find the operating pressure in the vehicle or tyre manufacturer’s instructions for the load. A sidewall value may be a maximum, not the pressure specified for that vehicle.
Pressure must also be correct at partial load: use the value specified for the actual load and operating conditions.
The correct pressure comes from the manufacturer’s instructions for the vehicle, tyres and load; it need not be entered on the registration certificate.
Check pressure when the tyre is cold because driving heats it and raises the pressure, changing the reading relative to the specified value.
With excessive inflation, contact tends to concentrate in the centre of the tread, which can become hotter than the edges during driving.
With insufficient pressure, the shoulders work and flex more, so they can be hotter than the center after driving. Temperature also depends on use.
Low pressure changes the shape of the contact patch: the shoulders work more than the center, and the load is not distributed correctly across the tread.
When underinflated, the center works less than the shoulders: contact and pressure are not distributed as they are at the appropriate pressure.
Excess pressure changes the contact patch: the center remains in closer contact than the shoulders, changing the load distribution.
Overinflation concentrates contact toward the center and reduces the relative contact at the shoulders.
Underinflation changes the contact patch and tire deformation, impairing grip and handling.
Excess pressure changes the contact patch and can reduce grip: the tire does not work on the road as intended.
When underinflated, the casing flexes excessively on each revolution; this deformation generates heat and can overheat the tire.
Excess deformation and altered contact promote premature, uneven wear, often more noticeable at the shoulders.
With low pressure the shoulders work harder than the center and tend to wear faster.
The more compliant casing flexes more on each revolution, dissipating more energy and increasing rolling resistance.
Low pressure increases deformation and rolling resistance, so more energy is needed to move the vehicle and fuel consumption rises.
The air supports the casing less, so it flexes more than intended under load on each revolution.

The quiz marks this VERO: underinflation changes tyre stiffness and can affect body motion. At the same cornering force it can increase roll; it is not established that both roll and pitch always increase. Check cold tyre pressure against the specified value.
Greater deformation and an altered contact patch impair the tire’s response, reducing the vehicle’s road holding.
An underinflated tire deforms more and responds less effectively to forces, compromising vehicle stability.
At the same load, increasing pressure tends to increase the effective rolling radius slightly, and therefore the corresponding diameter.
With more pressure the tire resists deformation under load more strongly: it becomes stiffer.
An overinflated tire is stiffer and absorbs road irregularities less, making the ride harsher.
The center is not typically the hottest part: with insufficient pressure the shoulders work harder and can become hotter. Driving style also matters.
The opposite is true: when underinflated, the shoulders remain in contact and work relatively harder than the center.
The center remains in contact: overinflation reduces the relative contact at the shoulders.
Excess pressure makes the tire stiffer and the ride harsher, reducing comfort.
The reference is cold pressure: driving warms the tire and raises pressure, affecting comparison with the specified value.
Excess pressure makes the tire stiffer and less compliant under load, not more flexible.
At the same load, increasing pressure makes the tire flatten less: its rolling radius tends to increase, not decrease.
Cold weather does not remove the risks of overinflation: excessive pressure can make a tire more vulnerable to impacts and affect vehicle handling.
Do not deflate the rear tires by half a bar for a descent: insufficient pressure can impair stability and grip. Use the pressure specified for the load.
Air suspension does not require a fixed reduction in tire pressure. Follow the value specified for the tires, load and use.
Air suspension does not replace tire checks: pressure must still be checked periodically on these vehicles.
Overinflation tends to concentrate the load at the center of the tread; it does not automatically mean that the edges will be hotter after a trip.
Underinflation tends to make the tread shoulders work and wear more, rather than the center.
Overinflation tends to concentrate load and therefore wear at the center of the tread, rather than at the edges.
Lowering pressure below the recommended value is not a way to make parking easier: it can increase steering effort and impair handling.
On snow, do not assume an underinflated tire has more grip: insufficient pressure affects handling. Maintain the pressure specified for the conditions of use.
Excessive pressure can make the ride harsher and reduce comfort; comfort does not necessarily remain unchanged.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but a saving is possible under some conditions. In a truck study higher pressures reduced rolling resistance and a model estimated lower fuel use; the test reference pressure was not identified as the manufacturer’s recommended pressure. Use the pressure specified for the vehicle and load.
Excessive pressure does not guarantee a shorter stopping distance: it can reduce grip. Maintain the prescribed pressure for proper braking.
Regular pressure checks are essential: incorrect pressure can damage the tire and worsen grip and wear.
For heavy-vehicle tires, use the tire manufacturer’s guidance appropriate to the load and configuration, while also observing the vehicle and wheel requirements.
The spare tire can also lose pressure while unused. Check it along with the fitted tires so it is ready when needed.
An unbalanced wheel can cause vibration and uneven tread wear. Balancing corrects the imbalance of the wheel and tire assembly.
Incorrect toe or camber changes contact with the road and can cause uneven tread wear.
Incorrect steering adjustment can alter wheel alignment and cause uneven wear. Have the alignment checked and corrected.

The quiz marks this TRUE: a sidewall cut can damage the structure and requires specialist assessment; some tyres must be replaced. Certain commercial tyres may be structurally repaired within specific limits after inspection. A cut is not automatically repairable, and the technical guide does not establish an Italian legal exemption.
Check the reference pressure when cold: driving heats the tire and raises its pressure, so a hot reading cannot be directly compared with the cold value.
Pressure normally rises during driving. Deflating a hot tire to its cold specification can leave it underinflated once it cools.
The driver does not freely choose pressure based on asphalt temperature: follow the specified cold values for the vehicle, tires and load.
Incorrect toe can make the tread scrub and wear unevenly. An alignment check identifies and corrects the fault.
Load distribution affects how each tire works and can contribute to uneven wear; consider it alongside pressure and alignment.
Heat changes pressure; it does not keep it correct. Check it regularly with cold tires, including in summer.
Pressure that is too low reduces the tire’s lateral stiffness, so its slip angle can increase for the same lateral force.
Uneven deposits of mud, tar or gravel add mass to one part of the wheel and can upset its balance.
Uneven mass creates forces as the wheel turns, so it may bounce or wobble sideways.
Vibrations from an unbalanced wheel can reach the steering and make driving less smooth.
A workshop uses a balancing machine to locate the imbalance and applies weights to compensate for uneven mass distribution.
Imbalance makes the wheel bounce and can wear the tread unevenly, producing more worn spots.
An unbalanced wheel can oscillate, disturbing the vehicle’s ride and control as well as causing vibration.
There is no dedicated red warning light for wheel imbalance. It often appears as vibration and needs checking. A pressure warning concerns inflation instead.
Camber is an alignment angle; it does not compensate for uneven mass distribution. An unbalanced wheel needs balancing.
Toe concerns the direction of the wheels, not their mass distribution. An imbalance requires balancing.
An inner tube holds air; it does not correct the wheel’s mass distribution. Bouncing caused by imbalance requires balancing.
Increasing pressure by 0.2 bar does not remove a mass imbalance. Set the prescribed pressure and balance the wheel.
Reducing pressure by 0.4 bar does not remove a mass imbalance. Set the prescribed pressure and balance the wheel.
A damaged tire can impair control. Slow down gradually and stop in a safe place as soon as possible.

The quiz marks this VERO, but the consulted sources do not establish a general link between toe-in and inner-edge wear. Excessive toe-in generally tends to wear the outside, while toe-out or negative camber can contribute to inside wear. Causes can combine, so the alignment and suspension need checking.
On a long trip, a check can reveal a tire that is abnormally hot compared with the others. Overheating can indicate a problem requiring inspection.
The bar is a unit used for inflation pressure; a gauge can also show other units such as PSI.
Do not change a wheel wherever the vehicle happens to be. First reach a safe place if possible and protect passengers according to the conditions.
Greater wear on one side is not exclusively due to balance: an alignment problem, such as toe or camber, can also cause it.
Stops are not just for the tires: they also let the driver rest. Driving breaks are required for transport covered by the relevant rules.
Pressure is commonly shown in bar or other units such as PSI. The atmosphere is a pressure unit, but is not the one generally used for the indication considered here.

The quiz marks this false, but its wording is imprecise: a maximum pressure may appear on the sidewall. If it means the recommended pressure for the vehicle, look in the manufacturer’s information rather than infer it from the sidewall limit.
Alternative sizes listed on the registration document are specified for the vehicle. Other applicable characteristics and requirements must also be respected.
A tire dealer’s recommendation alone does not make an alternative size permissible: check that it is recognized for the vehicle and meets applicable requirements.
Firm, level ground reduces the risk of the jack failing; the triangle warns approaching traffic when the law requires it.
A position away from traffic reduces exposure to vehicles; the parking brake helps prevent movement while lifting.
Chocks secure the wheels remaining on the ground and help prevent the vehicle from moving while raised.
First loosen the nuts without removing them while the wheel is still on the ground; then raise the vehicle and finish removing the wheel.
Heavy-vehicle wheels are difficult to handle and the work carries risks: competence, training and suitable equipment are needed.
First secure the nuts temporarily; once the wheel rests on the ground, tighten them progressively to the specified torque.
Dual wheels do not always require a workshop for replacement, but competent personnel, suitable equipment and the specific procedure are needed.
The sequence concerns securing the wheel to the hub: follow the vehicle or wheel manufacturer’s procedure, not the tire maker’s.

The quiz marks this FALSE. To check wheel-nut tightening, use a calibrated torque wrench and follow the manufacturer’s specified torque and procedure. However, “dynamometer” is a broad term covering instruments that measure force or torque; the question does not specify which instrument it means.
Replacing a complete wheel does not require fitting it deflated: check the spare’s pressure according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Changing a complete wheel is different from mounting a tire on a rim: a valve leak test is not required for every wheel change.
There is no fixed half-bar increase for every spare: the correct pressure depends on the wheel and the applicable instructions.
In the cold, winter compounds stay flexible and can improve grip even on cold roads without snow; about 7 °C is a guideline, not a guarantee in every condition.
The compound and tread pattern are designed for cold weather: sipes create edges that help grip snow.
Fitting them on all wheels helps balance grip between axles, including when braking and cornering.
Sipes are thin cuts in the tread: they create extra gripping edges on snowy surfaces.
Winter compound is formulated to stay flexible in the cold, allowing the tread to maintain contact with the road.
In cold weather, summer or conventional tire compounds can stiffen, reducing grip even before snow falls.
Some winter models have holes for studs, which increase grip on ice; their use depends on the applicable rules.
The Italian mandatory snow-chain sign also permits suitable snow tires: the two types of equipment are alternatives.
There is no universal 20°C threshold at which winter tyres suddenly lose grip: performance varies with the tyre and conditions. In warm weather they may wear more quickly.
Chains can also be used on winter tires, provided they fit the wheel and vehicle and are installed according to instructions.
They are useful beyond deep snow: winter compound stays flexible in the cold and can help even on cold roads without snow.
Not all winter tires can take studs, but some models are designed to accept them.
They should not be limited to the drive axle: fitting them on all wheels helps keep the vehicle’s handling balanced.
ESP helps control stability, but does not prohibit winter tires: the two perform complementary functions.
Fitting winter tires alone does not require special vehicle approval: the tires must be approved and meet the parameters permitted for the vehicle.

If chains are used to meet a winter equipment requirement, unapproved chains do not count as compliant equipment and a penalty for lacking the required equipment may apply. Suitable winter tires can satisfy the requirement as an alternative.
Chains must comply with applicable standards and fit the tire dimensions; install them according to the instructions.
On snow-free asphalt, chains can damage tires and the road: remove them when the surface is clear.

Anti-skid devices must be fitted at least to the wheels of the driven axles, also following the vehicle and device instructions. On a four-wheel-drive vehicle, fitting them only to the rear wheels is therefore not enough.
Do not compensate for using chains on asphalt by adding 1 bar. Use the manufacturer’s specified pressures and remove the chains on a clear surface.
Winter tires do not automatically impose lower road speed limits. The speed allowed by the particular tire and all applicable limits must still be respected.
In friction brakes, pads or shoes oppose motion and convert kinetic energy into heat.
Air brakes need time for air to reach and pressurize the actuators: this lag makes their response slower than hydraulic brakes.
Secondary braking allows the vehicle to stop if the service brake fails, using the secondary brake or the part of the service brake that remains effective.
A heavy vehicle can use compressed air to operate its brakes, or air to control a hydraulic circuit: both are possible designs.
If the trailer uncouples and its air connection breaks, the emergency system automatically applies the trailer brakes.
The compressor does not supply the tanks continuously: the governor stops delivery at maximum pressure and resumes it when pressure falls.
The safety valve is set above normal maximum pressure, not between minimum and maximum: it protects against abnormal overpressure.
Service, secondary and parking braking functions are required. Secondary braking is not always the handbrake: the intact part of the service brake can provide it.
ABS also operates on snow, modulating braking to limit wheel lock. It cannot create more grip than the surface provides.
An air-over-hydraulic system can use compressed air to operate a booster that acts on the brake fluid. It does not always require a compressed nitrogen tank.
ABS modulates pressure to limit locking, preserving some lateral tire force and helping maintain direction and stability.

ABS adjusts braking pressure to limit wheel lock. Compared with braking with locked wheels, it can shorten the distance, with an even greater benefit on some low-grip surfaces. The result depends on the surface and vehicle, however, so a shorter distance is not guaranteed.
The governor controls air production and prevents normal pressure exceeding the preset maximum, resuming charging when it falls.
The check valve lets air flow to the tanks but prevents its return, preserving pressure when the supply side is vented.
When the set maximum is reached, the exhaust valve releases excess air to limit supply pressure; the check valve retains the air in the tanks.
The safety valve acts when a fault causes abnormal pressure, releasing air to protect the system.
The disc is fixed to the hub and rotates with the wheel; the pads clamp it to brake through friction.
In the caliper, hydraulic pressure acts through pistons to press the friction pads against the disc.
The master cylinder pressurizes the fluid, which acts on the caliper pistons and presses the pads against the disc.
The quiz marks this TRUE. ABS limits sustained wheel lock and helps preserve steering, but grip and stopping distance depend on the surface: some tests found longer stops on loose gravel.
In a wedge drum brake, the brake chamber pushes a rod and wedge between the shoes, forcing them apart against the inside of the drum.
The friction lining covers the brake shoes and contacts the inside of the drum during braking.
A ventilated disc has air passages that help dissipate heat generated during braking.
The governor controls reservoir charging through the compressor; it is not directly connected to the timing chain.
The governor controls the supply pressure in the reservoirs. The pedal-operated valve meters the air sent to the brake actuators.
In a hydraulic disc brake, fluid pressure acts on the caliper pistons. In an air brake, air instead operates a chamber and a mechanism that clamps the pads.
ABS modulates braking to resist wheel lock; it does not replace the secondary braking function needed if the service brake fails.
In a drum brake, the shoes expand against the inside of the drum. A disc clamped by pads belongs to a disc brake.
The designs differ: drum-brake shoes press outward, while disc-brake pads clamp the disc in a caliper.
Both types need not be fitted to every wheel: heavy vehicles can use disc or drum service brakes.
The governor controls charging within the pressures specified for the system; it does not always maintain more than 18 bar. Settings depend on the vehicle.
