The quiz marks this FALSE, but designs exist for brake drums with openings and fins to aid cooling. The question does not clarify exactly what it means by “self-ventilated”.
A retarder is an additional brake that reduces the work of the service brakes; it does not prevent the use of drum brakes.
An electromagnetic retarder acts on the transmission alongside the service brakes, so it can coexist with disc brakes.
In heavy vehicles, compressed air powers actuators that produce the force needed for braking; this is a common solution for large commercial vehicles.
In an air-over-hydraulic system, air operates a device that generates pressure in the fluid circuit, so both circuits are present.
In a spring brake actuator, air keeps the spring compressed when the brake is released. Venting the parking chamber lets the spring expand and apply the brake.
In a spring brake actuator, the spring mechanically supplies the force holding the vehicle; air keeps it compressed when the brake is released.
Service, secondary and parking braking are three required functions: normal slowing and stopping, stopping after a failure, and holding the vehicle stationary. They may share components.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but the residual braking of a split-circuit system helps bring the vehicle to a stop; it does not make driving to a workshop with a broken brake line safe, even slowly. Stop safely and seek assistance.
Secondary braking is intended to stop the vehicle if the service brake fails; it is not defined as a device activated by the driver becoming ill.
Secondary braking stops the vehicle if the service brake fails; parking braking holds it stationary. They are distinct functions, although they may share components.
The automatic supply line feeds the trailer and is pressurized in normal operation. A pressure drop triggers automatic trailer braking.
The service line sends the braking command to the trailer. Its pressure rises when the brake is applied; it is not always pressurized.
Air-over-hydraulic systems exist: compressed air operates a converter that pressurizes the brake fluid.
A broken pipe compromises braking. Stop as soon as it is safe, rather than necessarily at the exact point of failure, and have the faulty vehicle checked.
The spring section of the combined brake chamber holds the vehicle. The parking control releases the air holding the spring compressed, allowing the spring to apply the brake.
Moisture in compressed air can condense and collect at the bottom of the tanks.
Drain the condensation as specified for maintenance: water can freeze and interfere with brake operation.
The tanks must maintain the specified operating pressure. Too little air can make service braking insufficient and activate the low-pressure warning.
The hand valve exhausts air from the spring section of the combined chambers. The spring applies the brake; air releases it.
In systems with spring brakes, loss of pressure releases the springs, which apply the brakes. The vehicle does not simply remain unbraked.
Water is a contaminant, not a useful way to increase pressure. It can freeze or damage components and must be drained.

The quiz marks this FALSE. The parking brake normally holds the vehicle stationary, but for certain configurations the regulation requires that it can also be applied while moving. Follow the vehicle’s emergency instructions.
Brake tank pressure must be checked against the specified values for the braking system; it does not have to equal the air suspension pressure.
In friction brakes, the energy of motion is converted mainly into heat at the braking surfaces, slowing the vehicle.
The service brake acts on all wheels and distributes its action among the axles to brake the vehicle in a balanced way.
Friction brakes slow the vehicle by pressing pads or shoes against discs or drums, dissipating energy as heat.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but maximum braking force does not always equal the adhesive weight: it also depends on the grip coefficient and dynamic wheel load. Equality is a special case, not a general rule.
ABS regulates brake pressure to limit wheel lock and seek effective use of available grip. The force achieved and stopping distance depend on the surface and system.
Avoiding wheel lock helps preserve directional control and use the available grip during braking.
Load distribution changes the weight on the wheels and axles, affecting available grip and the distribution of braking.
ABS does not double braking force. It modulates pressure to prevent wheel lock and use the available grip.
Locking every wheel does not guarantee the shortest distance. Regulating braking can make better use of grip and preserve steering control; the result depends on the surface.
Weight distribution does affect braking: it changes the load on each axle and therefore the grip each can use.
Maximum braking force is not fixed at half the weight on the braked wheels: it also depends on the tire-road coefficient of adhesion.
Excessive heating reduces brake effectiveness and can cause brake fade.
A mass over 7.5 tonnes does not mean that brakes are water-cooled: the brake components dissipate the heat produced by friction.
The service brake acts on all wheels, so the second rear axle also contributes to braking.
Service, secondary and parking brakes have different functions: slowing the moving vehicle, stopping it after a failure, and holding it stationary. They may share components.
The vehicle must be held stationary by purely mechanical action, even if another form of energy is used to apply the brake.
The service brake acts on all wheels, distributing braking across the axles.
The driver must be able to adjust braking force as needed, rather than having only fully applied or released brakes.
The service brake control must be accessible from the driving position without releasing the steering wheel, allowing the driver to steer while braking.
Secondary braking must also be adjustable, so the driver can control the stop if the service brake fails.
Secondary braking must be adjustable: it does not normally consist of applying the parking brake fully. It can also be provided by the working part of the service brake.
The parking brake holds the vehicle stationary by a mechanical device; the brake booster assists service braking.
The service brake must be adjustable, not required to operate in pulses: the driver adjusts the force with the control.
The parking brake control must be independent of the service brake control, although some components may be shared.
The quiz marks this FALSE: not all autoveicoli must carry wheel chocks. Chocks help prevent accidental rolling; rules require their use for heavy vehicles parked on steep gradients.
The compressor produces compressed air, and reservoirs store it as a reserve for the brake circuits.

The quiz marks this TRUE: reservoirs and protected circuits must retain enough pressure for braking. The compressor cycles, however, and in some systems a discharge segment vents when cut-out pressure is reached. Without the layout, “always pressurized” cannot be assumed for every segment.
In an air-over-hydraulic brake, the converter uses compressed-air force to create pressure in the hydraulic fluid that operates the brakes.
Separate circuits serve the front and rear wheels and, where present, the trailer supply; this limits the effects of a leak in one section.
The load-sensing device adjusts pressure to the rear brakes for the load: an unladen vehicle needs less force than a fully laden one.

The quiz marks this TRUE. On vehicles fitted with spring parking brakes, sufficient air is normally needed to release them; without pressure they may remain applied. The vehicle may nevertheless be physically movable: do not force it to move; stop safely and seek assistance.
Before setting off, check the pressure gauges: the reservoirs must contain enough air for the brakes to operate.
The protection valve preserves pressure in intact sections if one leaks; the working section can provide secondary braking with reduced effectiveness.
The protection valve separates the two service circuits and also protects the trailer supply, when present, from a leak in another circuit.
The remaining braking function is there to stop after a failure; it does not restore full performance, so the fault must be repaired before a new journey.
In the arrangement considered, brake sections have separate reserves; other tanks can supply auxiliary equipment and air suspension.
Compressed air can deposit moisture in the tank: a drain valve allows accumulated condensation to be removed.
In a drum brake, shoes press against the drum; in a disc brake, pads clamp the disc. Both create friction at the wheels.
The load-sensing regulator adjusts brake pressure to the axle load, so braking force follows the load conditions.
The antifreeze device reduces ice formation from moisture in pneumatic components; it does not correct supposedly low cold-air pressure.
Air-over-hydraulic brakes can also be used on passenger vehicles: air operates the hydraulic part. Safety depends on meeting the applicable requirements.
Load-dependent control adjusts pressure; ABS addresses the risk of wheel lock. A heavy load does not mean ABS is switched off.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but does not specify what it means by “automatic brake”. One example is a trailer automatic brake, which can apply if the lines separate; the sources consulted do not establish that every truck has an automatic brake.
Separate circuits retain some braking if one fails, but they do not guarantee full braking at every wheel. A defective vehicle must not be used normally.
In an air-over-hydraulic system, air acts on the converter, which pressurizes the fluid going to the brakes. The direction of transmission is the reverse of the statement.
The type of actuation does not impose that division: air-over-hydraulic drum brakes and pneumatic disc brakes both exist.
The compressor is normally driven by the vehicle engine through gears or a belt, not by the starter motor used to start the engine.
When the brake is released, air from the chambers is vented to the atmosphere through pneumatic valves, not through the engine exhaust.
An air brake system can have ABS: it adjusts brake pressure to limit wheel lock.
The converter fluid transmits pressure to the hydraulic brakes; this does not require a dedicated radiator. The layout depends on the vehicle design.
The engine drives the compressor and pressure is regulated automatically; the driver does not have to start it with a button before setting off.
Pneumatic braking uses compressed air produced by the compressor. Even in heavy vehicles it is not inherently replaced by compressed nitrogen.
The quiz marks this TRUE. In one illustrated common layout the parking brake acts on the rear wheels and the service brake also acts on the front; other configurations may differ.

The quiz marks this TRUE: in a common spring brake, venting the release chamber lets the spring apply the brake mechanically. Not all air-brake systems use this design: DD3 uses an air-applied brake with a mechanical lock.

The quiz marks this TRUE: in spring parking brakes, sufficient air in the release chamber compresses the spring and releases the brake. Other systems differ: DD3 may also require a full service-brake application to unlock the mechanism.
A graduated parking brake can contribute to secondary braking because the driver can vary its action while stopping.
In a spring brake, air compresses the spring and keeps the brake released. When the air is exhausted, the spring applies the brake.
Secondary braking must be graduated. A parking control that cannot be graduated cannot provide that controlled braking function.
The control is not necessarily a pedal: it can also be a valve operated by hand by the driver.
In a spring brake, the spring holds the brake applied; air compresses it to release the brake. Losing pressure therefore does not simply make the brake inactive.
In the pneumatic layout with a load regulator, the brake command reaches the regulator before the rear brake chambers, so pressure is adjusted to the load.
The dual valve operated by the pedal supplies the two service circuits separately. This separation preserves braking in the intact circuit if the other fails.
In a dual-circuit system each circuit has its own reservoir and separate pipes; the common control allows some braking to remain if one circuit fails.
The foot valve meters pressure to the brake circuits: pressing the pedal harder increases the braking demand.

The quiz marks this TRUE: a simple dual valve can supply two service circuits in a coordinated way. Actuator pressure can nevertheless vary with load regulation, and some valves proportion their outlets differently; it is not always equal.
Duplex refers to the two circuits controlled by the valve, not two separate controls: the service brake is operated by the pedal.
The valve meters air from the reservoirs to the braking circuits; it does not fill the reservoirs alternately.
The valve meters the braking requested by the pedal; it does not automatically double pressure when a loaded vehicle travels downhill.

The quiz marks this FALSE: the basic role of a dual valve is to control both circuits, not always to impose different pressures. Some valves can nevertheless proportion their outlets differently, and load regulation can change downstream pressure.
Separate circuits allow the circuit still working to provide emergency braking if the other loses pressure.
In the conventional layout the load-sensing valve acts on the line to the rear brakes, adjusting the pressure requested by the brake control to the load.
With less load on the rear axle, the valve reduces pressure to its brakes relative to the demand, adapting braking force to the available load.
By reducing pressure at lower loads, the valve limits the tendency of the wheels to lock; it does not provide the same instantaneous control as ABS.
With mechanical suspension the valve can be fixed to the frame and linked to the axle: their relative movement signals changes in load.
With air suspension, bellows pressure can provide the valve with a load signal without manual driver control.
Adjustment is automatic: load is sensed, for example, from suspension movement or bellows pressure, not by an activation button.
The valve adjusts pressure to load and can coexist with ABS, which responds to wheel-lock risk.
In the mechanical type described, the valve is fixed to the frame; a linkage reaches the axle to sense suspension movement.

The quiz marks this FALSE. Load regulation can use mechanical or pneumatic sensing; some trailer air-brake designs also use hydraulic suspension pressure as the load signal. The brake remains pneumatic, and this example does not establish that the design is used on the motor vehicles in the question.
The valve regulates pressure according to load; it is not a friction braking component that needs air cooling.
The quiz marks this TRUE. An air dryer can be placed between the compressor and reservoirs to treat the air; an antifreeze device reduces ice formation. Its position depends on the system layout.
The dryer removes moisture from the air; the antifreeze device reduces the risk of water forming ice in the circuit, including the pipes.
Moisture in the circuit can freeze and obstruct valves. The dryer removes it and the antifreeze device reduces the risk of ice forming.
The dryer can incorporate the regulator that controls supply pressure in the same unit.
Besides removing moisture, the dryer can separate contaminants such as oil from compressed air.
The risk is water freezing in the circuit, not air freezing in the reservoirs; the antifreeze device reduces ice formation.
The dryer treats air after compression, before the reservoirs; it does not control the humidity of the air drawn into the compressor.
The dryer operates automatically in the compressed-air supply circuit; the driver does not have to start it by hand.
The dryer removes moisture and can separate oil aerosols; it does not add lubricant to the air going to the valves.
One dryer can treat air upstream of several reservoirs; there need not be one dryer per reservoir.
The governor controls air production between cut-in and cut-out thresholds, replenishing pressure when it falls.
At the upper threshold the governor unloads the compressor, limiting supply pressure; a safety valve protects against excess pressure.
The governor considered here has a safety valve that operates if pressure becomes excessive.
At the upper threshold the governor unloads the compressor; when pressure falls to the lower threshold, loading resumes.
At cut-out pressure the governor can vent air to the atmosphere; venting stops when pressure falls to the cut-in threshold.
Supply pressure varies between cut-in and cut-out thresholds; it is not held fixed at 15 bar.
The governor controls reservoir supply pressure; the brake control modulates the pressure sent to the brakes during braking.
The brake governor controls the system supply pressure; it does not directly control air suspension pressure.
Air suspension does not replace the governor: the brake supply still needs pressure control.
The governor acts automatically according to air pressure, without a hand control operated by the driver.
In a drum brake, shoes lined with friction material press against the drum to slow the wheel.
In a disc brake, pads lined with friction material press against the disc to slow the wheel.
Heavy vehicle service brakes use friction: for example, pads press on a disc or shoes on a drum.
Friction produces heat; prolonged or excessive use can overheat brakes and reduce their effectiveness.
In friction brakes, energy of motion is converted into heat that must be dissipated into the surroundings.
In a conventional disc brake the pads act on the disc; shoes are associated with the drum.
Shoes and pads belong to different types of brake: shoes act on a drum and pads on a disc.
The typical problem is overheating from friction; ventilation helps dissipate heat.
Heavy vehicle service brakes normally use friction, with discs or drums; an electromagnetic retarder, if fitted, is a separate device.
Exceeding 7.5 tonnes does not require liquid-cooled brakes: air-cooled disc brakes exist for heavy vehicles.
Vehicles over 3.5 tonnes can also have ventilated discs; ventilation helps dissipate heat.
In an air-over-hydraulic brake, compressed air acts on a device that generates hydraulic force; fluid then transmits that force to the brakes.
The compressor charges the air tanks; the control then sends air to the converters, which operate the hydraulic circuit.
When the brake is pressed, the valve meters air from the tanks to the converters, which generate hydraulic pressure for the brakes.
In a drum brake with a double-piston wheel cylinder, fluid pressure pushes the two pistons outward, pressing the shoes against the drum.
The converter uses the force of compressed air to pressurize fluid, which transmits the action to the brakes.
Brake fluid is practically incompressible, so it transmits pressure through the hydraulic circuit. Vapour bubbles, by contrast, are compressible.
The fluid must be changed according to the manufacturer’s instructions: glycol-based fluid absorbs moisture, which lowers its boiling point.
The level must be checked and topped up with the specified fluid if necessary. A low level also calls for checks for leaks and wear.
A heavy truck can use this system: air operates a hydraulic circuit that transmits pressure to the brakes; it is not ruled out for being too elastic.
No mixture is prepared: air acts on the converter, which pressurizes fluid in the separate hydraulic circuit.
No mixer is needed. The converter transfers the force of the air to the fluid, which remains in the hydraulic circuit.
Bypassing the converters does not turn the system into fully pneumatic brakes: they produce the hydraulic pressure for the brakes. A leak requires repair.
The direction is the reverse: the converter uses air pressure to generate pressure in the brake fluid.
The converter is downstream of the tank and control valve: it receives metered air and operates the hydraulic circuit. It is not between compressor and tank.
The fluid transmits pressure to the brakes; it does not lubricate friction surfaces. Oil on the linings impairs their operation.
Air-over-hydraulic brakes do not rule out towing: a suitably equipped vehicle can also supply the trailer’s air brakes.
The compressor is normally driven mechanically by the engine, directly or by belt; it supplies air for the system.
The compressor draws in filtered air, compresses it and feeds the tanks, where it is stored for the system.
Compression generates heat and moving parts need lubrication, so the compressor needs cooling and lubrication.
The compressor does not burn fuel: it is normally driven by the engine and compresses air for the tanks.
The compressor is not an engine fuelled by a mixture: it is driven by the vehicle engine and compresses air.
The compressor produces compressed air and is driven by the engine. Engine braking instead slows the vehicle using engine resistance, not by reversing the compressor.
Moisture in the air can freeze in pipes and valves, obstructing airflow and the operation of the controls.
ABS monitors wheel rotation and modulates braking pressure when a wheel is about to lock, helping maintain steering control.
Moisture in compressed air can condense in the tanks and freeze. Periodic draining removes condensate and reduces this risk.
If pressure has fallen while parked, the compressor must recharge the tanks. Before moving off, wait until pressure is within the operating range.
ABS helps prevent wheel lock by modulating braking; it cannot restore insufficient air pressure needed to operate the brakes.
Disc brakes are also used on commercial vehicles, buses and trailers, not just passenger cars.
Disc brakes are used on trucks, buses and trailers too: heating does not prevent their use on commercial vehicles.
The secondary brake on buses is designed to be operated by the driver from the driving seat. An emergency brake available to passengers, as on trains, is not required on all buses.
The hammer breaks the glass of an emergency exit so occupants can escape; it does not operate the brakes.
The service brake circuits have separate pressure indications, sometimes with two needles on one gauge, so the reserve in each circuit can be checked.
A red warning light alerts the driver when available pressure falls below the required level, indicating an insufficient braking reserve.
The pedal operates the brake valve, which meters air to the brake actuators; the driver can vary the applied pressure.
The governor controls the compressor at the specified pressure limits, keeping reservoir pressure within the operating range.
Pressing the pedal harder makes the valve increase pressure to the brake actuators and thus braking force, within the system’s limits.

The multi-way valve protects the air reserves. For example, an integrated check valve prevents air in the reservoirs from flowing back toward the broken supply pipe, preserving pressure in the service reservoirs.
Reservoir supply pressure remains in the normal operating range even when fully loaded; braking pressure can instead be adjusted for the load.
Even when unladen, the reservoirs must remain in the normal pressure range; any load adjustment concerns braking, not lowering the air reserve.
A leak in one section does not necessarily bring the autoveicolo (such as a bus or truck) to an immediate stop: the unaffected parts allow residual braking when the driver applies the service brake.
Reservoirs supply the system’s circuits, rather than one reservoir being assigned to each wheel; air is then distributed to the brake actuators.
The service brake is controlled by the pedal, which operates the brake valve; it is not regulated by a dashboard hand control.
Continuous and graduated describe characteristics of braking, not two modes selected according to the force needed. Service braking force is controlled with the pedal.
The mechanical coupling joins the vehicles; the pneumatic connection serves the trailer brakes and the electrical connection serves equipment such as lights and signals.
The two-line connection uses flexible hoses and approved coupling heads: one line supplies the trailer and the other controls braking.
The dedicated electrical connection supplies the trailer ABS and carries its warning signal; the air lines alone cannot perform this function.
The colors distinguish the lines: red for supply and yellow for control, helping prevent the connections being confused.
Protective gloves during coupling protect the hands against mechanical hazards when handling the connections between towing vehicle and trailer.
The pneumatic connection uses flexible hoses with distinct coupling heads: red for supply and yellow for control, not two green couplings on rigid pipes.
Air must physically pass through the flexible lines connecting towing vehicle and trailer; a wireless connection cannot carry it.
The braking connection between towing vehicle and trailer uses pneumatic lines, not a hydraulic line. The electrical connection for the system uses cables and connectors; it is not wireless.
A two-line air connection uses a service line and a supply/emergency line, each with its coupling, not four lines.
The couplings can be disconnected: connecting the lines is part of coupling the trailer and does not require a workshop each time.
A lot of steam may come from coolant entering the cylinders, for example through a damaged head gasket. Steam alone does not identify the fault with certainty.
A damaged head gasket can let coolant into the oil circuit, forming an emulsion that reaches the sump.
The red light can signal a serious cooling problem: stop safely and switch off the engine to avoid further overheating and damage.
The red light can indicate low oil pressure. Running the engine further can damage it: stop safely and switch it off immediately.
The light can signal low oil pressure: stop and switch off immediately. Check the level and top up only if low, with oil of the prescribed specification; seek assistance if the light remains on.
The light can indicate low pressure: switch off the engine and check the level. If low, top up with oil of the prescribed specification; seek assistance if the light remains on.
The lubrication light warns of a possible pressure problem; it does not give a thousand-kilometre deadline for the filter. Stop and switch off the engine.
The lubrication light can indicate low pressure; it does not automatically mean the oil is due for replacement. Stop and switch off the engine.
Steam from the exhaust does not prove the radiator is overfilled: it can indicate coolant entering the cylinders. Draining coolant will not fix that leak.
Coolant in the sump indicates a passage between the cooling and lubrication systems, for example through the head gasket; a simple external radiator leak does not explain this mixing.
Accelerating does not resolve a cooling warning and can worsen overheating. Stop safely and switch off the engine when the warning instructs you to.
Too little air relative to fuel can cause incomplete combustion and black smoke. A clogged air filter is one possible cause.
Too much diesel relative to the available air can cause incomplete combustion and black smoke.
Black smoke is associated with incomplete combustion: for example, it can result from too much fuel or too little air.
Black smoke does not establish low compression with certainty: air or fuel supply problems can also cause it. The actual cause must be investigated.
Black exhaust smoke is associated with incomplete combustion; it does not prove an engine fire has started.
Black smoke is associated with incomplete combustion; burning oil is commonly associated with bluish smoke. Colour alone cannot identify the fault with certainty.
Black smoke calls for checks of combustion and fuel supply, not higher-octane diesel. Octane measures resistance to self-ignition and is mainly associated with gasoline.
In some engines burning oil can produce white smoke, but other causes, such as injection problems, are also possible. Colour alone does not identify the fault.
A clogged air filter restricts available air and can contribute to incomplete combustion and smoky exhaust.
A faulty injector can disrupt injection and combustion, causing exhaust smoke.
If too much fuel is injected relative to available air, combustion can be incomplete and produce smoke.

The quiz marks this FALSO, but the sources consulted do not establish whether petrol used instead of diesel can cause white smoke. White smoke has several possible causes and does not by itself identify the fuel; a suspected misfuel needs a separate check.

The quiz marks this FALSE, but white smoke alone neither measures diesel consumption nor rules out excessive consumption. It can have other causes, such as a cold engine or air in the fuel system; consumption must be measured and the fault diagnosed separately.
The oil filter belongs to the lubrication system. A clogged air filter can restrict combustion air and cause smoke.
The regulator limits pressure produced by the compressor; a fault can allow pressure to rise above the intended level.

The quiz marks this TRUE. In some integrated units the protection valve includes a limiter: if it fails to limit properly, pressure in its regulated circuit may exceed the intended value. The affected circuit depends on the system; an excessive reading requires diagnosis without assuming which component has failed.
The pressure gauge shows the air pressure in the tanks, allowing an above-normal value to be identified.
The compressor fills the tanks with compressed air; a malfunction can prevent it maintaining the required pressure.
The tank stores compressed air, not diesel. Contamination can impair the system rather than guarantee a shorter stopping distance.
The retarder assists braking but does not replace the service brake. Abnormal pressure requires a safe stop and a fault inspection.
Repeatedly pressing the pedal uses up available air; the compressor recharges the tanks. If pressure is insufficient, stop safely and have the fault checked.
Do not disconnect the suspension to compensate for low pressure: stop safely and have the system checked. The circuits are protected by the protection valve.
Tank pressure is read on the pressure gauge; a thermometer shows temperature, not air pressure.
The hazard warning tell-tale is red; it indicates that the flashing hazard signal is active.
The red coolant temperature warning light signals an abnormal engine temperature condition.
The red warning light indicates insufficient engine oil pressure, which is needed for lubrication.
The red warning light draws attention to an unfastened seat belt.
The red warning light shows that the parking brake is engaged and should be released before moving off.
The direction-indicator tell-tale is green, not red; it flashes when the indicators operate.
The dipped-beam tell-tale is green, not red.
The high-beam tell-tale is blue, not red.
The front fog-lamp tell-tale is green, not red.

The quiz marks this FALSE. The windscreen symbol with arrows identifies the defrosting or defogging control; the rear-window symbol refers to the back window. Check the indicator colour for the vehicle and applicable regulation.
The straight horizontal lines identify the main-beam headlights; the symbol identifies their control.
The symbol with straight horizontal lines denotes the main beams: their tell-tale is blue.
The symbol denotes the main beams, whose tell-tale is blue, not green.
The symbol with straight horizontal lines denotes the main beams; the dipped-beam symbol has downward-sloping lines.
The horizontal lines identify high beams, not the rear fog light, which has a different symbol.
The symbol with horizontal rays concerns high beams being on; it is not a reminder to switch off the position lights.
The downward-sloping rays identify the dipped headlights and their control.
The dipped-beam indicator, recognizable by the downward-sloping rays, is green.
The dipped-beam indicator is green; the blue one indicates high beams, shown with horizontal rays.
The sloping rays identify dipped headlights. The rear fog light uses a distinct symbol and a yellow indicator.
The sloping rays identify dipped headlights; high beams have horizontal rays.
The symbol with sloping rays identifies dipped headlights, not position lights.
The two opposing arrows identify the direction indicator control, used to signal the chosen direction.
The opposing arrows identify the direction indicators, whose indicator light is green.
The arrows identify the direction indicators: their indicator light is green, not yellow.
The opposing arrows indicate the direction indicators, not the position light control.
The double triangle identifies the hazard warning light control, which makes the direction indicators flash simultaneously.
The double triangle controls the hazard warning signal, which flashes the direction indicators together.
The double triangle identifies the hazard warning signal, for which a red indicator is provided.
The double triangle controls the hazard lights, which warn others of a temporary danger, for example in an emergency.
The double triangle controls the hazard lights. The portable warning sign is a separate device placed on the road.
The double triangle concerns the hazard lights; it is not the parking brake indicator.
The double triangle identifies the manual hazard light control; automatic activation after a collision is possible on some vehicles, but the symbol does not guarantee it.
The hazard light operating indicator flashes; it is not a steady red light.
The drawing of a windscreen and blade identifies the windscreen wiper control, which cleans the outside surface of the windscreen.
The drawing identifies the windscreen wiper control: the symbol table provides for a control, not an operating indicator, for this function.
The drawing identifies the windscreen wiper control; it is not the amber indicator described in the question.
The windscreen and blade identify the wiper; the fog lamp has a different headlamp symbol.
The horn-shaped figure identifies the audible warning device control, which sounds an audible warning.
The stylized horn identifies the horn control: it operates the horn rather than warning of a fault.
The stylized horn identifies the horn control, not an amber warning light.
The stylized horn identifies the horn control, not a red warning light.
The fuel pump identifies the reserve warning light: it warns that the tank level is low and refuelling is needed.
The pump identifies the amber low-fuel warning light, prompting you to refuel.
The pump indicates reserve fuel, not a fault in the fuel supply system.
The pump identifies the amber low-fuel warning light, not a flashing red light.
The pump identifies the amber low-fuel warning light, not a green light.
The thermometer above waves identifies the high coolant temperature warning: the engine risks overheating.
The thermometer above waves identifies the red high coolant temperature warning light.
The light warns of possible overheating that can damage the engine: stop as soon as it is safe and switch the engine off.
The red light with the thermometer above waves warns that coolant temperature is too high, not too low.
In the quiz, the thermometer above waves identifies the red high coolant temperature warning light, not an amber light.
Overheating can damage the engine: do not continue for 50 km; stop as soon as it is safe and switch the engine off.
With the engine running, the battery light signals a charging problem: the battery is not charging properly.
The battery with plus and minus signs identifies the red charging-system warning light.
The battery with plus and minus signs identifies the red charging-system warning light, not a blue light.
The light signals a charging problem with the engine running; it does not mean the battery is necessarily already completely flat.
The oil can with a drop identifies the warning for insufficient oil pressure in the engine lubrication circuit.
The oil can with a drop identifies the red warning light for insufficient engine oil pressure.
The oil-can light signals insufficient oil pressure, not an excessive oil level. Pressure and level are separate checks.
The oil-can light signals insufficient oil pressure, not a critical oil temperature.
The person with a belt identifies the seat-belt reminder: it signals that the driver’s or a passenger’s belt is unfastened.
The person with a belt identifies the red reminder to fasten the seat belt.
The light reminds an occupant to fasten an unfastened belt; it does not itself indicate a belt fault.
The figure indicates the seat belt: its warning light is red, not green.
The stylized windscreen with upward arrows identifies the control for defogging or defrosting the windscreen.
The windscreen with upward arrows identifies the defogging system: its indicator is amber.
The symbol identifies windscreen defogging, whose indicator is amber, not red.
The windscreen defogging indicator shows that the system is switched on, not that it has failed.
The symbol with horizontal beams pointing right identifies the rear fog lamp control.
The symbol identifies the rear fog lamp: its on indicator is amber.
The symbol with horizontal beams pointing right identifies the rear fog lamp; the front fog lamp symbol has sloping beams pointing left.
The symbol identifies the rear fog lamp, whose indicator is amber; the front fog lamp indicator is green.
The symbol with sloping beams pointing left identifies the front fog lamps, whose indicator is green.
The symbol identifies the front fog lamps; the rear fog lamp has horizontal beams pointing right.
The symbol identifies the front fog lamps, whose indicator is green, not red.
The warning light concerns coolant temperature. A faulty sensor or indicator can produce an incorrect warning even without actual overheating.
Too little coolant can reduce the removal of heat from the engine and cause the overheating signaled by the light.
A faulty coolant pump can stop coolant circulation and cause the overheating signaled by the light.
If the belt drives the coolant pump, a broken belt can stop circulation and cause the overheating signaled by the light.
A thermostat stuck closed can prevent coolant from reaching the radiator, causing the overheating signaled by the light.
A faulty fan reduces radiator cooling, especially at low speed or when stationary, and can cause overheating that lights the warning.
The symbol concerns engine coolant temperature, not brake temperature.
The light indicates coolant temperature, not the vehicle load directly. Overheating can result, for example, from low coolant or a faulty pump.

The quiz marks FALSO: constant speed alone does not identify a fault. The lamp warns of high coolant temperature; demanding conditions or a cooling-system fault can still cause overheating during a constant-speed trip.
The symbol indicates engine coolant temperature, not a lack of gearbox oil.

The quiz marks FALSO: the lamp indicates high coolant temperature; it does not directly measure antifreeze condition. However, depleted corrosion protection can allow deposits that restrict circulation and contribute to overheating. Check the cooling system and follow coolant replacement intervals.
The light concerns engine cooling; it is not the passenger compartment air-conditioning fault light.

The quiz marks VERO. The figure indicates battery charging, not ignition directly. One possible indirect link is an ignition fault that stalls the engine: in a vehicle whose lamp stays on with the ignition on and engine stopped, the lamp may then light. This is an inference from examples involving different vehicles, not a diagnosis; if it stays on with the engine running, check the charging system.
With the engine running, the battery symbol warns of a charging problem: one possible cause is that the alternator no longer supplies current to the battery.
The belt drives the alternator. If it breaks, the alternator can stop charging and the battery warning light can come on.
The alternator supplies the electrical system and charges the battery while the engine runs. If a fault stops its output, the battery is not recharged.
The battery symbol refers to the charging system: if it stays on with the engine running, the battery may not be charging properly.
The battery warning concerns charging, not an individual headlamp bulb. A failed bulb is not in itself a charging-system fault.
The light indicates a charging-system problem; simply using several electrical devices at once is not in itself a system fault.
The light signals a charging problem that needs checking. Switching the engine off for an hour does not repair the fault and is not a procedure prescribed by the light.
The light concerns the charging system; it does not measure outside temperature. Have the system checked instead of automatically attributing the warning to cold.
Spark plugs ignite the mixture; charging depends on the alternator and its circuit. Fouled plugs are not in themselves an alternator fault.
The battery symbol indicates a charging fault, not the pressure of the liquid inside the battery.
The light indicates a charging problem to have checked as soon as possible; it does not mean stopping immediately in every circumstance. Follow the vehicle instructions and stop safely if necessary.
The light indicates a charging problem; it does not prove the battery is already completely discharged. Its remaining charge must be checked.
The oil can and drop is the oil-pressure warning: with the engine running it indicates insufficient pressure in the lubrication circuit.
The oil pump generates pressure in the circuit. If the gear pump malfunctions, pressure can fall and turn on the warning light.
With too little oil, the pump may not supply the circuit properly and pressure can fall. The light measures pressure, not oil level directly.
The light indicates low pressure. Stop safely, switch off the engine and check the level with the dipstick according to the manual; a fault can exist even if the level is correct.

The quiz marks this FALSE: the pictured lamp warns of an oil-pressure problem, not the oil-change date. Overdue changes can nevertheless contribute to deposits and, in some circumstances, pressure problems. If it lights while driving, stop safely and switch off the engine as instructed by the manual.
Do not rev the engine to try to extinguish the light: insufficient pressure can damage it. Stop safely, switch it off and check the level.
There is no permitted 200 km distance with the oil-pressure light on. Stop safely and switch off the engine: continuing can damage it.

The quiz marks this TRUE. A power-steering problem can cause excessive steering response, but that alone does not establish tyre-related oversteer in a turn. The question does not clarify the precise connection with incorrect adjustment.

The quiz marks this TRUE. A faulty power-steering adjustment can cause an abnormal steering response and should be checked; that alone does not establish tyre-related understeer in a turn. The sources consulted do not clarify the precise connection asserted in the question.
Power steering adds assistance to steering, reducing the force required from the driver even in heavy vehicles.
In conventional hydraulic power steering, an engine-driven pump requires power. Other systems may use an electric pump or motor.
Power steering adds force to the steering mechanism, so the driver needs less effort at the wheel.
Steering assistance can help the driver control direction after sudden deflation, but it cannot restore tire grip or guarantee control.
Power steering adds force to the driver’s input: lighter steering makes a quick maneuver easier, especially in heavy vehicles.
Power steering assists the vehicle’s steering even with a trailer attached: the trailer does not itself switch off the assistance.
Power steering lightens the control, making steering easier; it is not a device that slows steering down.
The engine drives the pump, which supplies assistance; steering firmly does not require the driver to accelerate.
Power steering helps turn the wheels, but using it downhill does not itself heat the tires.
Electrohydraulic systems exist in which an electric motor drives the hydraulic pump.
A working system assists steering on hairpin bends too: a descent and repeated bends are not in themselves a fault.
Power steering assists the control and reduces, rather than increases, the effort required from the driver.

The quiz marks this FALSE: power steering normally reduces steering effort; grip depends on the tyres and road. A fault can nevertheless impair control, for example through excessive response or wandering, and needs inspection and repair.
A leak can lower the fluid level and reduce hydraulic assistance, making the wheel harder to turn, especially at low speed.
The power steering circuit uses its own fluid: a leak can reduce assistance and is not compensated by a transfer of brake fluid.
Incorrect gear mesh or adjustment can cause excessive play or stiff steering.
Loss of lubricant leaves the steering gear components less protected and can lead to wear and operating problems.
Winter tires in warm weather can change tire behavior, but are not themselves a fault in the mechanical steering components.
The limiter acts on vehicle speed; incorrect calibration is not a mechanical defect in the steering gear or linkage.
With understeer the vehicle turns less than the steering input calls for, tending toward the outside of the bend.
With understeer the directional response is less than requested, so the path widens compared with the intended path.
During oversteer, the vehicle turns more than expected and the rear may move outward, tightening its path.
During oversteer, the vehicle turns more than the driver intends; the rear may slide outward.
Poor load distribution changes axle loads and available grip, potentially shifting cornering behavior toward understeer or oversteer.
In either case the vehicle follows a different path from the one intended; uncorrected loss of grip can lead to loss of control.
Understeer widens the path. With oversteer, the vehicle instead tends to turn more than requested.
Understeer normally widens the path because the front loses grip; a spin is associated with the rear sliding in oversteer.
Underinflated front tires can reduce front directional control and encourage understeer, rather than the stated oversteer.
An excessively tight path indicates oversteer. Hard acceleration is not the general correction: release the accelerator and look and steer toward the desired path.
During understeer, the vehicle tends to follow a wider path than intended; a tighter path is instead oversteer.
Two front steering axles do not guarantee neutral handling: these vehicles can also oversteer or understeer, depending on conditions and tire response.
A tighter path than intended indicates oversteer; with understeer the vehicle tends to take a wider bend.
The suspension connects the wheels to the vehicle structure, allowing relative movement and damping oscillations.
Springs and shock absorbers reduce impacts and oscillations transmitted to the structure, so their condition affects passenger comfort.
Excessive loading strains the suspension beyond its capacity. Respect the vehicle and axle load limits.
Poorly distributed cargo can overload an axle and the suspension supporting it, increasing the risk of damage.
There is no general extra 20% capacity for the suspension. Vehicle and axle mass limits must be respected; weighing deductions do not increase suspension capacity.
The suspension supports and guides wheel movement relative to the structure; adjustments do not mean the entire system can be switched off at will.
Shock absorbers control suspension oscillations, limiting wheel bounce and helping keep the wheels in contact with the road.
By controlling oscillations, the suspension helps keep vertical wheel loads more uniform and maintain road contact.
The suspension helps stabilize vehicle attitude by limiting body oscillations; it does not keep the body motionless in every situation.
Shock absorbers resist body oscillations, including sideways roll and pitch under braking or acceleration.
The suspension allows the wheels to follow uneven surfaces, reducing impacts and oscillations transmitted to the structure.
The suspension helps maintain road contact, but it is not the antilock device: ABS, where fitted, modulates brake pressure to prevent locking.
The suspension controls wheel and body movement; it does not prevent tire overheating, which can result from overloading, for example.
The suspension controls wheel movement and road contact; increasing the turning radius is not its purpose.
Suspension needs inspection and maintenance according to the manufacturer, but not systematic adjustment before every long journey. Checking ride height does not necessarily mean adjusting it.
The suspension responds to movement between wheels and structure even at low speed; it does not start working only above 50 km/h.
The suspension supports the vehicle and controls oscillations; it is not ballast for increasing towing capacity.
Suspension components can wear or suffer damage and need inspection and maintenance; they are not guaranteed to remain effective for the vehicle’s entire life.
Overloading can impair stability and handling and put excessive strain on the suspension; it does not ensure perfect operation.
With a controlled air suspension system, the driver can raise or lower the chassis and thus the cargo body, for example to match a loading dock.
The suspension of autoveicoli, including trucks and buses, reduces oscillations transmitted from road irregularities to the structure.
Leveling valves regulate air in the air springs according to height, helping return the vehicle to its intended ride height.
The bar connects the two sides of the suspension and resists differences in their movement, limiting body roll in bends and over transverse level differences.
Suspension cushions impacts from uneven roads; combustion noise is dealt with by the exhaust and its silencer.

Do not add antifreeze to the suspension just because cold weather arrives. For example, the water-based Hydrolastic system uses a specific fluid already protected against freezing; maintenance follows the system specification.
Even with two rear axles a vehicle can have front suspension: the two rear axles do not remove the need to suspend the front axle.
Some air suspension systems have a manual control for raising or lowering the chassis as well as automatic adjustment.
Air suspension is also used on heavy vehicles: exceeding 3.5 tonnes does not prohibit its use.
A vehicle approved for towing can have air suspension: for example, road tractors exist with rear air suspension.
Increasing tyre pressure does not repair the leaf spring or restore the suspension. The break must be repaired before driving.
A leaf spring and its mountings need inspection and maintenance according to the manufacturer’s instructions: wear or breaks do not fix themselves.
The spring absorbs impacts but then continues to oscillate; the shock absorber damps these movements and helps the wheels stay in contact with the road.
Hydraulic and gas-charged shock absorbers are common. Gas-charged units also use oil to provide damping; the gas helps prevent aeration.
Double-acting means that the shock absorber resists movement both during compression and rebound, controlling both stages.
Shock absorber oil is formulated to retain suitable properties despite the heat generated in operation, keeping damping more consistent.
The shock absorber works between the sprung part connected to the chassis and the part following the wheel, connected to the axle or suspension. It damps their relative movement.
Shock absorbers are also used on heavy vehicles: they do not cease to be useful above 7 tonnes.
Seals retain the oil in the shock absorber; the driver does not routinely top it up every 3,000 km. A leak requires inspection.
With insufficient damping, the wheels follow the road less effectively and vehicle control deteriorates, particularly when manoeuvring and braking.
Worn shock absorbers can make tyre contact with the road less consistent, reducing braking effectiveness and increasing the distance needed to stop.
If the shock absorbers do not control suspension movement well, the vehicle can sway more in a bend and lose grip more easily.
On a wet road worn shock absorbers maintain less effective tyre contact with the surface, increasing the risk of aquaplaning.
The bouncing and less precise handling require more corrections and attention, increasing driver fatigue.
With ineffective shock absorbers the vehicle bounces for longer: the headlights move too and illuminate the road less steadily, reducing visibility.
Vehicle oscillation changes the direction of the headlights; when the beam rises it can dazzle oncoming drivers.
Effective shock absorbers limit oscillations and help the wheels maintain contact with the road, improving stability and braking.
Stiffening the springs does not replace damping: an ineffective shock absorber must be inspected and repaired or replaced.
A hydraulic shock absorber uses a specific fluid in its own circuit; antifreeze is not added as it is to the cooling system.
A worn shock absorber damps oscillations less effectively: wheel grip and control worsen, rather than improving through a supposed lowering of the centre of gravity.
Twin wheels do not replace shock absorbers: the suspension still needs to control axle oscillations.
Routine inspection checks the condition and effectiveness of shock absorbers and any leaks, not a pressure to be checked periodically like tyre pressure.
Replacement requires skill and appropriate procedures; it is not a simple job for just any driver.
There is no universal red warning light identifying one or more ineffective shock absorbers. Their condition requires an appropriate inspection.
A shock absorber damps suspension oscillations. When worn, it cannot properly damp the movement of the leaf springs.
The levelling valve adds or releases air from the bellows as the load changes to maintain ride height. If it fails, this pressure adjustment is lost.
Front shock absorbers help keep the wheels in contact with the road; removing them compromises vehicle control.
They are not exclusively mechanical: in hydraulic shock absorbers, fluid passes through valves that resist movement.
The levelling valve regulates suspension air and chassis height, not engine operation.
Inspector teaching specifies two chocks for autoveicoli, such as trucks and buses, and trailers over 3.5 tonnes; they help prevent wheel movement. Article 353 governs their use on steep slopes.
A chock placed against a wheel resists movement of a parked trailer, including when detached from the towing vehicle.
During a wheel change, chocks keep the other wheels from moving while the vehicle is raised.
Inspector teaching specifies two chocks for a single vehicle over 3.5 tonnes. They help prevent wheel movement when parked.
Heavy-vehicle teaching specifies two suitable chocks for a bus over 3.5 tonnes, helping keep it stationary.
Inspector teaching specifies two chocks for trailers and semi-trailers over 3.5 tonnes; they help prevent movement when parked.
Chocks resist movement of a stationary vehicle. On steep roads, vehicles over 3.5 tonnes must use them.
During removal and refitting, chocking the other wheels helps prevent the raised vehicle from moving.

The devices reduce water spray thrown up by the wheels. The quiz marks VERO, but Article 72(2-ter) covers goods-authorised motor vehicles, trailers and semi-trailers over 7.5 tonnes, new and registered in Italy from 1 January 2007. The question says only “motor vehicle” and is therefore broader; check the category and applicable rules.
Underrun protection reduces the risk of another road user going under the vehicle. Guards may be rear, side or front, according to the requirements for the vehicle type.
Chocks prevent vehicle movement; the portable warning sign alerts other road users to a vehicle stopped on the carriageway when required.
Inspector teaching specifies two chocks for a single vehicle over 3.5 tonnes, rather than four.
A chock prevents accidental wheel movement; it is not an anti-robbery device.
Front protection requirements depend on the vehicle category and any exemptions, not simply on motorway use. They do not apply to every heavy autoveicolo without distinction.
Twin wheels alone do not determine the obligation: requirements depend on vehicle category and characteristics, with specific exemptions.
The stated threshold is too low: spray suppression device requirements are not mandatory for category N vehicles with a maximum laden mass up to 7.5 tonnes.
These are physical parts fitted near the wheels, such as spray flaps; they are not switched off on dry roads.
Spray is reduced by components fitted near the wheels, not activated by a dashboard control.
Clean, intact mirrors adjusted for the driver provide the intended field of view and help identify other road users.
Mirrors widen the view but do not necessarily eliminate blind spots around the vehicle, even when properly adjusted.
The driver sees some areas through the windows and others in mirrors. Mirrors extend indirect vision without necessarily covering every area.
Adjustment improves the field of view, but blind spots can remain where other road users cannot be seen.
The mirror on the other side cannot restore the view lost through a dirty or damaged mirror; both must be kept in working order.

The quiz marks this FALSE. Camera placement alone is insufficient: the vehicle needs a camera-monitor system with the required fields of view and appropriate approval. Some truck configurations replace the main, wide-angle, close-proximity and front mirrors with camera views, so replacement is not universally prohibited. Check the vehicle’s approval.
A general check before a journey can reveal defects that compromise safety, for example in lights, tyres or brakes.
After starting, check the fault warning lights and instruments: a fault light that stays on may indicate a problem to investigate before departure.
Checking levels helps identify insufficient lubrication, coolant or brake fluid; the last applies to systems that use it.
Effective wiper blades and sufficient washer fluid allow the windscreen to be cleaned and visibility maintained.
Headlights help the driver see and be seen; indicators communicate turns. Checking them before departure helps reveal faults.
Reflectors must be intact and clean to reflect other vehicles’ lights and make the vehicle visible.
Cuts, incorrect pressure or insufficient tread can compromise safety. Check all tyres against the requirements applicable to the vehicle.
Required equipment depends on the vehicle and its use. Checking that it is present and intact makes it available when needed.
Where digital tachograph rules apply, the driver and operator must ensure correct operation and proper use of the driver card.
A charged spare battery is not generally required on board; instead, check that the installed battery is secure and in good condition.
Night travel does not generally require two 25-litre fuel cans. Before departure, check the vehicle and the fuel needed for the journey.
Checking roadworthiness does not necessarily require driving and stopping tests in an enclosed yard; check equipment and report defects.
Calling the company for permission is not a general mandatory check before every journey; the driver must ensure the vehicle is roadworthy.
There is no general requirement to carry a spare 10-litre can of water; checking the vehicle’s coolant level is useful.
There is no general requirement to carry 10 litres of spare oil; checking the engine oil level before a journey is useful.

The quiz marks this FALSE. Before cold weather, check the level and freeze protection of the specified coolant mixture; do not assume the reserve quantity in the question applies to every journey. Follow any vehicle or fleet instructions as well.
Roadworthiness checks are needed before a journey even for a new vehicle; they do not depend on two years having passed since registration.
The registration certificate identifies the vehicle and its characteristics; consult the manufacturer’s manual for checks and maintenance.

The quiz marks this FALSE. Check pressure periodically according to the manufacturer, using the cold-tyre reference; after driving, follow the instructions for hot tyres. The fleet or journey conditions may call for additional checks.
Lights should also be checked before a daytime journey: they are safety devices and may be needed on the way.
Tyres heat up during travel and their pressure rises. Measuring them cold allows comparison with the specified pressure.
Belts can deteriorate: periodically checking their condition and tension helps detect problems before a belt breaks.
Terminals need to be secure: a faulty connection can impair electrical contact. Check them safely.

On vehicles with hydraulic power steering, check the fluid level periodically as directed by the manufacturer: a low level may indicate a leak, and operating with too little fluid can damage the system.
In coolant already at the specified concentration, adding too much water can dilute the antifreeze and reduce freeze protection. Maintain the concentration specified by the manufacturer.
Checking washer fluid allows the washers to clean the windows when needed and maintain visibility.
The filter traps impurities in the intake air. Keeping it clean helps maintain the correct air-fuel mixture needed for combustion.
Recognising a warning light or another symptom promptly allows the driver to stop and act before the fault can worsen.
The driver may temporarily address minor problems within their competence and the vehicle instructions. A serious fault or unsafe vehicle instead requires stopping and seeking qualified help.
Reporting a serious defect promptly lets the company arrange repairs and avoid using an unsafe vehicle.
Knowing the instruments and warning lights helps the driver recognise problems promptly while driving and respond appropriately.
The owner’s manual contains instructions specific to the vehicle, including checks and periodic maintenance.
The periodic roadworthiness inspection must be current for the vehicle category. It does not replace pre-journey checks.
When a vehicle is subject to tachograph requirements, the device also needs periodic checks by an authorised workshop, separate from the vehicle inspection.
Periodic servicing helps keep the extinguisher effective. On buses subject to the equipment requirement, competent personnel perform checks and maintenance and record them on the label.
Tread over three millimetres does not permit every combination: for type approval of category M, N and O vehicles, tyres normally fitted to the same axle are of the same type.
The alternator supplies the electrical system and helps charge the battery; the indicator circuit controls flashing, not the alternator.
Connecting the two terminals of the same battery directly causes a short circuit and creates a fire risk. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions for assisted starting.
Do not add cooling-system antifreeze to gearbox or differential oil: use the lubricant specified by the manufacturer for those components.
Setting valve timing is a technical job for competent personnel; the driver’s role includes checks and reporting faults.
Identifying and reporting faults helps, but the driver need not personally diagnose every fault to reduce fuel use; driving and maintenance matter too.
After a successful inspection, the result is recorded on a label on the registration certificate; the driver does not have to sign it.
The driver must not dismantle it: the undertaking has an approved workshop or fitter repair the tachograph. Meanwhile the driver records the periods not recorded by it.
Do not test the extinguisher by discharging it: the inspection checks its condition and pressure or weight, among other things, so it remains ready for use.
Worn pads need competent brake-system service; the driver should report the problem, not necessarily replace them personally.
Navigation assists route finding; its failure does not itself require an immediate stop. If you need to plan a new route, do so safely.

The quiz marks FALSO: even small damage needs assessment of its position, visibility and glass condition. The 2026 MIT circular permits some repaired chips to pass inspection only if all conditions and certification requirements are met.
Check tyre pressure when the tyres are cold, using the specified values: after a long trip heating raises the measured pressure.
Damaged blades should be replaced: they must be able to clear the windscreen and provide visibility even when no rain is forecast.
The specified pressure can vary with the load: choose the value appropriate to the load using the manufacturer’s instructions.
Tread depth is assessed on each tyre: adding the depths of a twin pair can hide excessive wear on one tyre.

The quiz marks VERO: cracks need assessment and may require replacement. The 2026 MIT circular allows certain repaired chips to pass inspection if all conditions and certification requirements are met. Impact cracks can spread under thermal stress or vibration.

The quiz marks VERO: damage needs assessment because it may compromise the glass and visibility. The sources consulted do not establish that a jolt causes the glass to shatter; certain repaired chips may pass inspection under all the 2026 MIT circular conditions. Laminated glass has an interlayer that resists fragment scattering.

The quiz marks VERO: damaged laminated glass still needs assessment. The 2026 MIT circular allows certain repaired chips to pass inspection if all conditions and certification requirements are met; nonconforming damage requires replacement for a regular result.
Adhesive tape is not a windscreen repair: an accepted repair requires an appropriate technique and compliance with the applicable conditions and certification.
The kit is for providing first aid to passengers: before departure the driver checks that it is on board.
If glass emergency exits require hammers, check that they are present and accessible: they are used to break the glass in an emergency.

The quiz marks VERO: check the maintenance tag for periodic inspection, generally every six months under the applicable scheme. A scheduled technical overhaul is a different intervention, with an interval depending on type, standard and instructions.
The quiz expects a check for chocks before departure: they help prevent a parked vehicle from moving. The rule on use on steep slopes is separate from the equipment taught in quiz material.
The warning triangle is used to signal a stopped vehicle in the prescribed situations. The driver must check that it is present before departure.
Doors, steps and access equipment must work: checking them before departure helps passengers board and alight safely.
Doors and luggage compartments need to operate and close correctly; a pre-trip check helps identify faults that may endanger people or cargo.
The quiz does not require the driver personally to check gearbox oil before every departure. That check follows the vehicle maintenance schedule and instructions.
The quiz does not require the driver personally to check differential lubricant before every departure. Inspection follows the vehicle maintenance schedule.

The quiz marks FALSO, but pre-departure checks depend on the vehicle and its instructions. For example, the Thomas Built EFX manual includes an engine-belt check before starting. Follow the instructions applicable to the vehicle.

Pre-departure checks focus first on visible condition and safety equipment. A technical inspection of the injection system requires specific procedures and skills; it is not an ordinary check before every journey.

The quiz marks this FALSE. The air-conditioning filter is normally handled through scheduled maintenance; pre-trip checks focus mainly on safety. Follow the vehicle manual and operator instructions for that vehicle.
The panel is used when a protruding load must be marked; checking for it is not a requirement for every bus before departure.
Refreshments may be a passenger service, but they are not safety equipment that must be checked before departure.
Check coolant against the reservoir markings: it helps the engine cooling system work properly.
Pressure must suit the vehicle: underinflated or overinflated tires change their contact with the road.
When a tachograph is required, the driver must ensure it works properly so that the required activities are recorded.
Required documents depend on the vehicle, driver and journey. Checking them before departure helps demonstrate the necessary permissions and conditions during inspections.
Check the tread for wear and damage: it is the part of the tire that grips the road.
The brakes must work correctly: the check includes both service and parking brakes.
A visual suspension check can reveal obvious damage or an abnormal vehicle stance before the journey.
Safety equipment must work: for example, check emergency exits and any seat belts fitted.
The quiz marks this FALSE: the stated distance alone does not establish what spare equipment is required. Check the equipment and puncture procedure for the vehicle, route and operator.
Lease instalments are a contractual matter; pre-departure checks concern vehicle safety and documents required for the journey.

A separate ownership certificate need not be carried. For vehicles registered with the PRA, the single document replaces the older documents when issued; the previous documents remain valid until then.

The quiz marks this FALSE. Advertisement legibility serves to communicate the company’s name or message; it is distinct from vehicle safety or identification checks, such as checking the registration plate.
The quiz marks this FALSE: there is no general rule requiring tyres made less than two years ago. Check their condition, wear and suitability, taking any applicable tyre-age rules into account.
In hydraulic power steering, check the fluid level periodically: insufficient fluid can impair steering assistance.
The system requires the manufacturer-specified fluid; water is not a substitute. If the level is very low, identify the cause and follow the manual or seek assistance.
Use only fluid meeting the power-steering specification; generic lubricating oil is not automatically suitable. Some vehicles specify a particular transmission fluid: check the manual.

The quiz marks this FALSE: power steering normally provides assistance while driving, without a generic lever near the wheel to switch it off. Features and controls can vary by vehicle; consult the manual.

The quiz marks this TRUE. Replacing a steering wheel requires appropriate skills and procedures, especially when it contains an airbag. The sources consulted do not establish that every replacement is legally restricted to a workshop; use qualified personnel.

A larger steering wheel does not fix the cause of hard steering, which can include low pressure or fluid, or binding components. Have the system inspected and use components appropriate for the vehicle.

The quiz marks this TRUE, but a driver can perform preliminary checks, such as steering movement, play and assistance. A detailed technical assessment requires appropriate procedures and skills; not every check is possible only in a workshop.

The quiz marks this FALSE. A personal visual check can reveal some defects, but alone cannot guarantee a complete steering assessment. The driver can also check movement and play as applicable to the vehicle; faults require technical inspection.

The quiz marks FALSO, but an experienced colleague can assist with some checks. Their help does not replace a qualified inspection or repair when needed; the reason for the official answer is not specified.
Checking steering joint play does not necessarily require raised wheels: the joints can be stressed during inspection with the wheels on the ground.
Before departure, check any loading and unloading equipment too, since it must work properly for the intended operation.
The load must be secured so its parts cannot move during the journey; the driver checks its stability before departure.
Check that the load stays within the permitted capacity: overloading can impair stability, steering and braking.

The 5% is not an allowance to add to payload: the limit concerns the permitted total mass. For checks with certain instruments, the law reduces the measured value; that is distinct from the authorised load.
Check covers for good condition and secure fastening so they work properly without coming loose or letting the load scatter.
The manufacturer specifies the operations and intervals suited to the vehicle: following them helps detect and correct problems before they worsen.
Check tyre pressure regularly, preferably when cold, and adjust it according to the recommendations for the vehicle and load.
Avoiding overload limits stress on the vehicle: excessive load can, for example, accelerate tyre wear and damage tyres.
There is no universal one-third threshold that must always be maintained for maintenance. Check the level and refuel according to the vehicle instructions and journey needs.
Do not always add 0.2 bar to the stated value: the correct pressure depends on the manufacturer’s recommendations and the load and conditions of use.
Checks are not limited to hot days: check regularly with cold tyres, because pressure rises as they warm up.
Reporting the defect to the person responsible allows it to be assessed and repaired; the driver should not simply ignore it.
A dangerous defect must be repaired before continuing; other defects need assessment to decide whether and with what precautions the journey can continue.
Checks and repairs keep the vehicle fit for service and help prevent faults that could compromise transport safety and continuity.
Preventive maintenance keeps components in working order and reduces the risk of a breakdown interrupting service; it cannot eliminate every possible fault.
Smooth driving, avoiding unnecessary harsh acceleration and braking, reduces stress and wear on mechanical components.
Smooth driving reduces wear on parts such as brakes and tyres, limiting the need to replace them.
Reporting a fault promptly allows the company to assess and address it before it worsens or makes the vehicle dangerous.
Maintenance can limit noise: for example, a damaged silencer can make the exhaust noisy and needs repair.
Maintaining the vehicle according to the manufacturer’s instructions helps reduce harmful emissions caused by inefficient components.
Maintenance helps limit fuel consumption: for example, correctly inflated tyres reduce rolling resistance.
The owner’s and maintenance manual describes the manufacturer’s operations for that vehicle and provides the reference for scheduling them.
Maintenance intervals are often based on both distance and time: follow the vehicle’s schedule and observe the applicable deadline.
The supply pressure must be checked; in systems with a load-sensing brake valve, the device adjusts braking to the load rather than the driver adjusting pressure each time.
A leak may be audible, but do not rely on a hiss alone: check the pressure gauges and warnings too.

The quiz marks FALSO. Promptly report the defect to the person responsible for repairs under the operator’s procedure, and inform the next driver when appropriate. A dangerous vehicle must not continue until made safe. The reason for the official answer is not specified.
Wiping injectors with a cloth is not a routine pre-departure check. Work on the injection system requires appropriate procedures and careful cleanliness.
Use a suitable gear downhill to benefit from engine braking; switching off the engine while moving is not a maintenance measure.
Checking brakes is part of safety checks, but it does not require a full-force test stop at the end of every shift.
Routine maintenance keeps the vehicle safe and in working order; its purpose is not to raise service charges.
Routine maintenance keeps the vehicle safe and in working order; obtaining tax relief is not its purpose.
Look for maintenance operations and intervals in the manufacturer’s instructions, not the registration document.
Choose a gear suited to speed, load and gradient; avoiding gear changes at all costs is not a maintenance rule.
Maintenance follows the vehicle’s prescribed schedule; the periodic roadworthiness inspection is a separate check and need not coincide with every service.
A maintenance defect contributing to a collision can matter when assessing criminal negligence. Liability depends on the circumstances and causal link, and is not automatic.
Obeying traffic rules does not in itself remove liability for damage caused by a vehicle maintenance defect.
Recourse is possible if the policy permits the insurer to refuse or reduce its payment to the insured; it is not automatic for every defect.
A serious maintenance failure does not automatically result in immediate arrest: liability and measures depend on the facts and legal conditions.
A defect does not automatically double compensation; the amount concerns the compensable damage in the circumstances.

Under compulsory third-party liability insurance, the injured party can claim directly against the insurer within the insured limits. Contractual exclusions may instead lead to recourse against the insured.
A clogged filter restricts diesel flow: when demand rises, the pump may receive an insufficient or irregular supply.
A clogged filter restricts fuel supply: the engine can lose power or run unevenly and therefore perform less effectively.
A clogged filter can disrupt supply and combustion, reducing efficiency and increasing fuel consumption. The effect depends on the engine and operating conditions.
A clogged filter restricts supply and can cause loss of power; yellowish smoke is not a characteristic effect identifying this fault.
The fuel filter concerns the engine’s fuel supply; cylinder lubrication depends on the oil circuit, which is separate.

The quiz marks FALSO: a blocked filter restricts fuel to the pump and can reduce supply pressure upstream of injection. This does not establish a higher injection pressure; the effect depends on the system and operating conditions.
Shock absorbers control suspension movement. When worn, tyre contact and vehicle control can deteriorate.
Springs support the vehicle and form part of its suspension. A damaged leaf or coil spring can affect ride height and control.
The control system maintains air-suspension height. If it malfunctions, the vehicle’s stance and stability can suffer.
Shock absorbers damp suspension oscillations. When worn, the vehicle can continue bouncing after a disturbance.
Worn shock absorbers or their mounts can cause noise as the suspension moves without proper control.
If the suspension oscillates excessively, the body’s angle changes, as does the direction of the headlight beam.
